context: Halloween 2008 — six weeks after Lehman collapsed. Title: Bitcoin: A Peer-to-Peer Electronic Cash System. The mailing list was metzdowd.com cryptography.

question: The original Bitcoin white paper by Satoshi Nakamoto was approximately how long?
answer: Nine pages
choices: Nine pages
Three pages
Twenty-five pages
Fifty pages
context: Eight numbered pages plus title page. The brevity is striking given how much it changed. Read it in an evening; reread it the rest of your life.

question: Bitcoin's Genesis block, the first block on the chain, was mined on what date?
answer: January 3, 2009
choices: January 3, 2009
October 31, 2008
January 9, 2009
January 12, 2009
context: About 18:15 UTC. Block height 0. Satoshi mined it himself; the 50 BTC subsidy is unspendable due to a quirk of the original code.

question: The Genesis block's coinbase script embedded which Times of London newspaper headline as a timestamp?
answer: Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks
choices: Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks
Lehman collapse shocks markets
Fed cuts rates to zero
Banks ask for taxpayer rescue
context: From the front page of January 3, 2009. A deliberate political statement: Bitcoin was born in protest of the bank bailouts. The bailouts came; Bitcoin was the alternative.

question: The 50 BTC mined in Bitcoin's Genesis block — by Satoshi himself — is famously:
answer: Permanently unspendable
choices: Permanently unspendable
Held in cold storage
Lost to a forgotten password
Donated to charity
context: A quirk in the original code prevents spending the Genesis reward. Whether by design or accident, the very first coins are forever frozen — a permanent monument.

question: Bitcoin's first transaction sent between two people, on January 12, 2009, was from Satoshi to:
answer: Hal Finney
choices: Hal Finney
Nick Szabo
Adam Back
Wei Dai
context: 10 BTC sent at block 170. Finney tweeted 'Running bitcoin' on January 11. He died in 2014 of ALS; his body was cryopreserved.

question: Hal Finney's terse tweet on January 10, 2009 — eight days into the chain — read:
answer: Running bitcoin
choices: Running bitcoin
Bitcoin alive
Mining now
Block 78 mined
context: Two words. The first public mention of Bitcoin on Twitter. Finney was one of the earliest enthusiasts and the first known person besides Satoshi to run a node.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto's last verified communication, in a brief email to Gavin Andresen, dated approximately:
answer: April 26, 2011
choices: April 26, 2011
December 12, 2010
October 31, 2008
August 1, 2017
context: Wrote: 'I've moved on to other things... it's in good hands with Gavin and everyone.' Identity still unknown. The mining patterns suggest one consistent author.

question: Before disappearing in 2011, Satoshi handed development authority over Bitcoin to which contributor?
answer: Gavin Andresen
choices: Gavin Andresen
Hal Finney
Mike Hearn
Adam Back
context: Andresen had been the most active second developer. He passed the mantle further as Bitcoin grew. Today no single developer leads — a deliberate decentralization.

question: After Satoshi's disappearance in 2011, who served as Bitcoin's de facto lead developer for several years?
answer: Gavin Andresen
choices: Gavin Andresen
Wladimir van der Laan
Pieter Wuille
Greg Maxwell
context: Andresen later supported Bitcoin Cash in 2017 and his commit access was revoked. He briefly endorsed Craig Wright's Satoshi claim, damaging his standing.

question: Craig Wright, the Australian who repeatedly claimed to be Satoshi Nakamoto, was found by a UK court in 2024 to have:
answer: Lied about being Satoshi
choices: Lied about being Satoshi
Proven his identity convincingly
Forfeited remaining coins
Created Ethereum instead
context: Justice James Mellor, COPA v Wright. The fraud was thoroughly documented. Wright is now barred from claiming Satoshi status in British court.

question: On May 22, 2010, Laszlo Hanyecz famously paid 10,000 BTC for two pizzas — the first commercial Bitcoin transaction. Pizza Day is now observed:
answer: Annually on May 22
choices: Annually on May 22
Annually on January 3
Annually on October 31
Quarterly at halvings
context: 10,000 BTC then = $41. At various 2024 prices = roughly $700M-$1B. Hanyecz says he has no regrets — it was an important experiment.

question: The 2011-2013 darkmarket that drove Bitcoin's first wave of adoption and attention was called:
answer: Silk Road
choices: Silk Road
AlphaBay
Hansa
Black Market Reloaded
context: Operated by Ross Ulbricht (Dread Pirate Roberts). Shut down October 2013 in an FBI sting at the San Francisco public library. Ulbricht received a double life sentence.

question: Mt. Gox, the Tokyo exchange that handled the majority of Bitcoin volume in early years, collapsed in what month, losing approximately 850,000 BTC?
answer: February 2014
choices: February 2014
November 2022
January 2018
May 2010
context: Run by Mark Karpeles. Coins had been stolen incrementally over years through compromised hot wallets. Some users were partly reimbursed a decade later in 2024.

question: From 2015 to 2017, Bitcoin's community fought a deep dispute over scaling, ending with the activation of which upgrade?
answer: Segregated Witness (SegWit)
choices: Segregated Witness (SegWit)
Lightning Network
Taproot
Bitcoin Cash hard fork
context: Activated August 24, 2017, at block 481,824. Increases effective block capacity and enables Lightning. The big-blockers split off to form Bitcoin Cash a week earlier.

question: On August 1, 2017, the big-block faction split off, creating which forked chain that the market overwhelmingly rejected?
answer: Bitcoin Cash (BCH)
choices: Bitcoin Cash (BCH)
Bitcoin SV (BSV)
Bitcoin Gold (BTG)
Bitcoin Diamond (BCD)
context: Roger Ver and Jihan Wu led the split. BCH split further in 2018 into BSV under Craig Wright. Both trade at small fractions of BTC's value — markets ruled.

question: Bitcoin Cash itself split in November 2018, creating which further forked chain under Craig Wright?
answer: Bitcoin SV (BSV)
choices: Bitcoin SV (BSV)
Bitcoin ABC
Bitcoin Gold
Bitcoin Diamond
context: BSV: Bitcoin Satoshi Vision. Marketed as the 'true' Bitcoin by Wright. Markets disagreed; the price collapsed and most exchanges eventually delisted it.

question: The Taproot upgrade — adding Schnorr signatures and improved privacy — activated on the Bitcoin mainnet in:
answer: November 2021
choices: November 2021
August 2017
May 2020
March 2024
context: Block 709,632, November 14, 2021. The first major Bitcoin protocol upgrade since SegWit four years earlier. Smooth deployment after a long buildup.

question: El Salvador became the first country to make Bitcoin legal tender on what date in 2021 under President Nayib Bukele?
answer: September 7, 2021
choices: September 7, 2021
March 9, 2022
October 31, 2021
June 8, 2021
context: The Bitcoin Law passed June 8 and took effect three months later. The state Chivo wallet had a rocky rollout. Bukele tweets the country's BTC purchases.

question: Nayib Bukele, Bitcoin's first head-of-state champion, is the president of:
answer: El Salvador
choices: El Salvador
Argentina
Paraguay
Honduras
context: Re-elected in 2024 with around 85% of the vote after dramatically reducing gang violence. His Bitcoin advocacy has made him a global Bitcoin community figure.

question: El Salvador's planned Bitcoin-related sovereign bond, to fund infrastructure including geothermal mining, was nicknamed the:
answer: Volcano Bond
choices: Volcano Bond
Bitcoin Bond
Bukele Bond
Chivo Bond
context: Geothermal energy from El Salvador's volcanoes powers some Bitcoin mining. The bond has been repeatedly delayed; the geothermal mining is operational and growing.

question: Bitcoin's consensus mechanism — repeatedly hashing a candidate block until the result falls below a target — is called:
answer: Proof of work
choices: Proof of work
Proof of stake
Proof of authority
Proof of history
context: The required work is the unforgeable cost securing the chain. The energy spent is the security budget. No way to fake the work without doing the work.

question: Bitcoin automatically retargets mining difficulty to keep block times near 10 minutes, on what schedule?
answer: Every 2,016 blocks (~2 weeks)
choices: Every 2,016 blocks (~2 weeks)
Every 1,000 blocks
Every 4,032 blocks (~4 weeks)
Every halving (~4 years)
context: If recent blocks came too fast, the next difficulty epoch makes finding a block harder. The simple closed-loop control system is one of Satoshi's most elegant designs.

question: Bitcoin's protocol targets one new block roughly every:
answer: 10 minutes
choices: 10 minutes
1 minute
1 hour
30 seconds
context: Six blocks an hour, ~144 per day. Six confirmations is the conventional safety margin. The 10-minute interval balances orphan rate against transaction latency.

question: Bitcoin's block subsidy is cut in half roughly every four years, at intervals of exactly:
answer: 210,000 blocks
choices: 210,000 blocks
100,000 blocks
1,000,000 blocks
365,000 blocks
context: Four years times ~52,560 blocks per year. The halvings end around block 6,929,999 (~2140) when the last fractional satoshi is mined.

question: Bitcoin's first halving, reducing the block subsidy from 50 BTC to 25 BTC, occurred in what year?
context: November 28, 2012, at block 210,000. The first practical test of the halving mechanism. The price proceeded to rise dramatically in 2013.

question: Bitcoin's protocol caps total supply at approximately:
answer: 21 million
choices: 21 million
100 million
1 billion
10 million
context: 21 million BTC, never more. Hardcoded into consensus rules; changing it would require near-unanimous agreement among independent nodes. Won't happen.

question: By 2024, the circulating Bitcoin supply was approximately:
answer: 19.7 million BTC (94% of cap)
choices: 19.7 million BTC (94% of cap)
10 million BTC (48% of cap)
21 million BTC (100% of cap)
5 million BTC (24% of cap)
context: Asymptotic approach to 21M. The last fractional satoshi will be mined around the year 2140, when block rewards drop to zero.

question: The last fractional satoshi will be mined approximately in what year, after which fees alone will pay miners?
choices: Never
context: Block 6,929,999. After that, miners earn only transaction fees. Bitcoin's monetary policy is the most predictable in human history.

question: The original Bitcoin block size limit, in place from 2010 to the 2017 SegWit upgrade, was:
answer: 1 MB
choices: 1 MB
32 MB
100 KB
8 MB
context: Satoshi added the 1 MB cap in July 2010 to prevent spam during early growth. SegWit (2017) effectively raised it via a witness-discounted weight metric to ~4 MB max.

question: Bitcoin's scripting language is deliberately limited — non-Turing-complete — to prevent infinite loops. The language is called:
answer: Script
choices: Script
Solidity
Rust
Move
context: Stack-based, no recursion, no unbounded loops. The simplicity is a feature: Bitcoin must remain reliably verifiable on commodity hardware for decades.

question: Bitcoin's provably unspendable output type, used to embed small arbitrary data in the chain, is:
answer: OP_RETURN
choices: OP_RETURN
OP_CHECKSIG
OP_HASH160
OP_CHECKMULTISIG
context: Originally limited to 40 bytes; later 80. Used for Ordinals inscriptions, Counterparty assets, and many less savory data-embedding schemes.

question: Bitcoin transactions can require multiple signatures to unlock — useful for shared custody. This feature is called:
answer: Multi-signature (multisig)
choices: Multi-signature (multisig)
Time-lock
Pay-to-script-hash
Schnorr aggregation
context: Common setup: 2-of-3, 3-of-5. Used by exchanges, family treasuries, corporate boards, and security-conscious individuals. Cold-storage best practice for years.

question: Bitcoin's second-layer payment network, enabling instant low-fee transactions through bilateral payment channels, is called:
answer: Lightning Network
choices: Lightning Network
Liquid Network
RGB Protocol
Stacks Layer
context: White paper: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja, February 2015. Mainnet launched January 2018. Channel routing uses HTLCs with onion routing for privacy.

question: Lightning Network's white paper, the technical foundation, was published in 2015 by Thaddeus Dryja and:
answer: Joseph Poon
choices: Joseph Poon
Adam Back
Pieter Wuille
Andreas Antonopoulos
context: Title: The Bitcoin Lightning Network: Scalable Off-Chain Instant Payments. Poon later created Plasma for Ethereum and Handshake for naming.

question: Lightning Network's mainnet launch — and the start of practical real-world Lightning usage — was in:
answer: January 2018
choices: January 2018
February 2015
November 2021
May 2020
context: Lightning Labs released LND v0.4 with mainnet support. Strike, Cash App, Wallet of Satoshi, Phoenix, and Muun followed; tens of millions of channels exist.

question: Bitcoin wallets are now typically backed up by a list of 12 or 24 ordinary English words drawn from a fixed 2048-word list. This scheme is called:
answer: BIP-39 seed phrase
choices: BIP-39 seed phrase
BIP-32 hierarchical wallet
PGP keychain
PKCS#12 archive
context: BIP-39 standardized in 2013. The word list is hashed and used to derive an entire tree of private keys. Lose your 12 words, lose your coins forever.

question: The practice of generating and storing Bitcoin private keys on a device permanently disconnected from the internet is called:
answer: Cold storage
choices: Cold storage
Hot wallet
Custodial storage
Brain wallet
context: Air-gapped hardware wallets, paper wallets, even engraved metal. The opposite of hot wallets connected to the internet. Best practice for long-term holdings.

question: The first commercially successful Bitcoin hardware wallet, released in 2014 by SatoshiLabs in Prague, was called:
answer: Trezor
choices: Trezor
Ledger
Coldcard
Jade
context: A small one-button device that signs transactions while keeping keys offline. Marek Palatinus and Pavol Rusnak founded SatoshiLabs.

question: The most widely sold Bitcoin hardware wallet brand worldwide, founded in 2014 in Paris, is called:
answer: Ledger
choices: Ledger
Trezor
Coldcard
BitBox
context: Founded in Paris by Pascal Gauthier and others. The Nano S and Nano X sold tens of millions of units. A 2020 customer-data breach taught users hard lessons.

question: The Bitcoin-only hardware wallet brand favored by maximalist users for air-gap operation is called:
answer: Coldcard
choices: Coldcard
Trezor
Ledger Nano X
BitBox02
context: Made by Coinkite in Toronto. The device has an air-gap mode using QR codes and microSD cards. Aimed at users who want zero network exposure.

question: The maxim warning that coins held on an exchange or custodian are not really yours is:
answer: Not your keys, not your coins
choices: Not your keys, not your coins
Be your own bank
Verify, don't trust
Stay humble, stack sats
context: Andreas Antonopoulos popularized the phrase. Mt. Gox, QuadrigaCX, Celsius, BlockFi, FTX — each collapse vindicated the maxim. Self-custody is core to Bitcoin's purpose.

question: PlanB's quantitative model for Bitcoin price based on the ratio of existing supply to annual new issuance is called:
answer: Stock-to-flow
choices: Stock-to-flow
Metcalfe's law
Realized cap
MVRV ratio
context: Inspired by Saifedean Ammous's gold analysis. Widely cited 2019-2021, then notably broke during the 2022 bear market. PlanB remains active; the model is contested.

question: Saifedean Ammous's 2018 bestseller introducing Bitcoin through the lens of monetary history and Austrian economics was titled:
answer: The Bitcoin Standard
choices: The Bitcoin Standard
The Fiat Standard
Layered Money
Broken Money
context: Subtitled: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking. Built the intellectual bridge between hard-money Austrians and the technical Bitcoin community.

question: Nik Bhatia's 2021 book mapping Bitcoin onto the multi-tier structure of historical monetary systems was titled:
answer: Layered Money
choices: Layered Money
The Bitcoin Standard
Broken Money
The Price of Tomorrow
context: Subtitle: From Gold and Dollars to Bitcoin and Central Bank Digital Currencies. A useful framework for understanding Lightning, exchanges, and ETFs as layers.

question: Vijay Boyapati's widely shared 2018 long-form essay arguing Bitcoin would attain global monetary status was titled:
answer: The Bullish Case for Bitcoin
choices: The Bullish Case for Bitcoin
Bitcoin Is Time
Gradually, Then Suddenly
Why Bitcoin Matters
context: Boyapati framed Bitcoin's monetization in stages — collectible, store of value, medium of exchange, unit of account. Distilled into a 2021 book of the same name.

question: Lyn Alden's 2023 book tracing money's history and Bitcoin's role as a fix to broken monetary systems was titled:
answer: Broken Money
choices: Broken Money
Layered Money
The Bitcoin Standard
The Price of Tomorrow
context: Alden writes accessibly on macro and Bitcoin. Frequent guest on podcasts; sometimes lumped with Austrians though she carries no formal Austrian credentials.

question: Jeff Booth's 2020 short book arguing technology's natural deflation is suppressed by central banks, making Bitcoin essential, was titled:
answer: The Price of Tomorrow
choices: The Price of Tomorrow
Broken Money
The Bitcoin Standard
Layered Money
context: Booth: real productivity gains should lower prices; central banks inflate to mask this, transferring wealth to asset holders. A widely cited short read.

question: Parker Lewis's series of essays published 2019-2022, later collected as a book, took its title from a Hemingway line: gradually then suddenly. The collection was titled:
answer: Gradually, Then Suddenly
choices: Gradually, Then Suddenly
The Bullish Case for Bitcoin
Broken Money
Bitcoin Is Time
context: From The Sun Also Rises: 'How did you go bankrupt? Two ways. Gradually, then suddenly.' Applied to fiat's collapse — and Bitcoin's monetization.

question: The Hemingway quote popular in Bitcoin circles for describing both fiat collapse and Bitcoin adoption comes from which novel?
answer: The Sun Also Rises
choices: The Sun Also Rises
For Whom the Bell Tolls
A Farewell to Arms
The Old Man and the Sea
context: Mike's line in the 1926 novel. Two ways: gradually, then suddenly. Captures non-linear phase transitions — perfect metaphor for monetary regime change.

question: Gigi's poetic short book of meditations on Bitcoin's significance was titled:
answer: 21 Lessons
choices: 21 Lessons
The Bitcoin Standard
Inventing Bitcoin
Bitcoin Audible
context: Pseudonymous author. The book is a poetic counterpoint to dense economic treatments — closer to a Rilke than a Friedman. Free PDF widely circulated.

question: Robert Breedlove hosts which Bitcoin philosophy podcast that ran a famous 17-hour series with Michael Saylor in 2021?
answer: What Is Money Show
choices: What Is Money Show
Tales from the Crypt
The Pomp Podcast
Bitcoin Magazine Show
context: Saylor's appearance generated millions of views. Breedlove explores Bitcoin's economic, philosophical, and theological implications at length.

question: Andreas Antonopoulos's definitive technical text on Bitcoin, with multiple editions for developers, was titled:
answer: Mastering Bitcoin
choices: Mastering Bitcoin
The Internet of Money
Bitcoin From the Inside Out
Bitcoin: The Complete Guide
context: Published by O'Reilly. The standard developer reference. Antonopoulos also wrote The Internet of Money for general audiences and is one of Bitcoin's great public educators.

question: Andreas Antonopoulos's series of accessible talks on Bitcoin's social significance, compiled as books, was titled:
answer: The Internet of Money
choices: The Internet of Money
Mastering Bitcoin
Bitcoin Audible
Layered Money
context: Three volumes by 2019. Antonopoulos's talks at conferences explained Bitcoin to non-technical audiences without watering down the substance.

question: Saifedean Ammous's 2021 follow-up book analyzing the cultural and economic costs of fiat money was titled:
answer: The Fiat Standard
choices: The Fiat Standard
The Bitcoin Standard
Principles of Economics
Layered Money
context: Subtitle: The Debt Slavery Alternative to Human Civilization. A polemic. Sometimes more rhetorically heated than the first book; many useful arguments.

question: MicroStrategy CEO Michael Saylor, who turned his company into a Bitcoin treasury starting August 2020, holds approximately how many BTC corporately by 2024?
answer: Over 200,000 BTC
choices: Over 200,000 BTC
Around 50,000 BTC
Under 10,000 BTC
Around 1,000,000 BTC
context: MicroStrategy renamed itself Strategy in 2025. The largest corporate BTC holder, accumulated through debt and equity issuance. Saylor became a major Bitcoin advocate.

question: Bitcoin's hard supply cap is often abbreviated in marketing as a single number:

100 million BTC

question: Each Bitcoin is divisible to eight decimal places. The smallest unit is named:
answer: Satoshi
choices: Satoshi
Finney
Szabo
Hal
context: 100,000,000 satoshis = 1 BTC. Named after the protocol's anonymous creator. Casual usage has stabilized around 'sats' for everyday discussion of small amounts.

question: A full Bitcoin node is software that:
answer: Validates and stores the entire blockchain

Mines new blocks for rewards
Operates a Lightning channel
Routes Tor traffic
context: Anyone can run a node on commodity hardware. Validating yourself is what makes Bitcoin's rules truly decentralized — nodes reject blocks violating the protocol.

question: Bitcoin miners are nodes that additionally:
answer: Compete to solve proof-of-work for new blocks
choices: Compete to solve proof-of-work for new blocks

Process Lightning payments

question: Bitcoin transactions broadcast but not yet included in a block sit in each node's:
answer: Mempool
choices: Mempool
Block cache
UTXO set
Wallet queue
context: Memory pool. When a miner builds a candidate block, they typically choose from the mempool by fee rate (sats per virtual byte), prioritizing the highest fee transactions.

question: Bitcoin transaction fees are typically quoted as:

choices: Satoshis per virtual byte (sats/vB)
Percentage of transaction value
Flat amount per transaction
Number of confirmations needed
context: After SegWit, fees are denominated against virtual bytes (vbytes), a weight-based size measure. During fee spikes, this can mean dollars per simple transfer.

question: The maxim 'don't trust, verify' captures Bitcoin's protocol-level commitment, embodied technically by:
answer: Every user running their own full node
choices: Every user running their own full node
Trusting a few elected validators
Relying on a federation
Government-issued certificates
context: Running a node is the act of personally verifying Bitcoin's monetary rules — supply cap, block reward, signatures — rather than trusting any third party.

question: Bitcoin's total network hashrate — the security budget — has by 2024 reached approximately what scale?

choices: Hundreds of exahashes per second
Hundreds of gigahashes per second
Thousands of petahashes per second
Hundreds of zettahashes per second
context: An exahash is 10^18 hashes. The global hashrate represents the all-time-high level of computational security backing any monetary asset in human history.

Bitcoin Corp

answer: Bitcoin (and Lightning via Strike, etc.)

Ethereum DeFi
USDC stablecoin transfers

question: Claims that Russian oligarchs would evade 2022 sanctions through Bitcoin proved largely overblown because:

question: An annual January 3 ritual where Bitcoin holders withdraw their coins from exchanges to demonstrate self-custody is called:

HODL Day
Bitcoin Independence Day

question: Bitcoin maximalists often describe Satoshi as 'the first economic actor' — the founder who:

question: Bitcoin's launch is described by advocates as 'immaculate conception' because:

question: The technical term Bitcoiners use to distinguish Bitcoin's debut from VC-launched cryptocurrencies is:

Genesis distribution

question: Bitcoin's defenders argue its rule-set qualifies as 'credibly neutral' — neither favoring nor disfavoring any party — in contrast to:

question: Bitcoin is unique among major monetary networks because it has:

question: Bitcoin's permissionless transaction inclusion is preserved as long as some miners refuse to comply with sanctions filtering. A node operator's role is:

Spiral
context: Founded 2022. Modeled partly on the Internet Archive. Distributes grants based on community recommendations to FOSS contributors across Bitcoin, Lightning, and Nostr.

question: Jameson Lopp, a leading Bitcoin advocate and security expert known for his personal-security framework after being SWATted, runs which company?
answer: Casa
choices: Casa
Unchained Capital
Coinbase
Strike
context: Casa offers multi-key collaborative custody. Lopp also publishes detailed analyses of Bitcoin's technical evolution. A widely respected steady voice.

question: The company providing collaborative multisig custody services for Bitcoin, founded by Jameson Lopp among others, is:
answer: Casa
choices: Casa
Unchained Capital
Trezor
Ledger
context: Provides 2-of-3 or 3-of-5 setups where Casa is one key, not all keys. Strong security guarantees with usability — solving the self-custody on-ramp problem.

question: The Texas-based multisig vault and IRA service founded by Joe Kelly and Dhruv Bansal for Bitcoin-only clients is called:
answer: Unchained Capital
choices: Unchained Capital
Casa
BitGo
Swan Bitcoin
context: Long-running Bitcoin-only firm. Provides multisig vaults where the user holds keys but Unchained provides ops and inheritance services. Austin-based, paywall-free podcast (The Gathering).

question: The Bitcoin-only auto-DCA savings platform founded by Cory Klippsten in 2019 in Los Angeles is called:
answer: Swan Bitcoin
choices: Swan Bitcoin
Strike
River
Bull Bitcoin
context: Cory Klippsten emerged from FTX-era criticism as a vocal Bitcoin-only advocate. Swan emphasizes self-custody and Bitcoin-only education.

question: The San Francisco Bitcoin-only brokerage that publishes detailed annual industry reports and offers Lightning services is:
answer: River Financial
choices: River Financial
Swan Bitcoin
Strike
Coinbase
context: Founded by Alex Leishman and Andrew Benson. Known for the River Annual Lightning report tracking real-world Lightning usage growth.

question: Jack Mallers's Bitcoin-and-Lightning payments company, central to El Salvador's rollout and known for its Lightning remittance product, is:
answer: Strike
choices: Strike
Swan Bitcoin
Cash App
Casa
context: Strike operates Lightning rails behind the scenes for remittances to multiple countries. Mallers was a key figure in El Salvador's Bitcoin adoption.

question: Block Inc.'s Cash App enabled Bitcoin buying in 2018 and Lightning withdrawals in 2022, putting Lightning in the hands of:
answer: Tens of millions of US users
choices: Tens of millions of US users
A few thousand power users
Only El Salvadorans
Enterprise clients only
context: Dorsey's Bitcoin commitment turned Cash App into a major Bitcoin on-ramp. Lightning withdrawals brought instant cheap Bitcoin payments to the mainstream US.

question: The Tor-routed Bitcoin wallet that pioneered Chaumian CoinJoin mixing for ordinary users is called:
answer: Wasabi Wallet
choices: Wasabi Wallet
Samourai Wallet
Sparrow Wallet
BlueWallet
context: Wasabi paused its CoinJoin coordinator in 2024 amid the Samourai prosecution risk. Sparrow Wallet integrates Whirlpool client-side; alternatives proliferate.

question: The 2023 unofficial fungible token standard built on top of Ordinals inscriptions was called:
answer: BRC-20
choices: BRC-20
Runes
Stamps
Counterparty
context: Created by anonymous developer Domo. Cheaper alternative to Ethereum ERC-20 in the inscription craze. The Runes protocol replaced it April 2024.

question: When Bitcoin prices fall below efficient miners' production cost, weaker miners shut down. This phenomenon is called:
answer: Miner capitulation
choices: Miner capitulation
Mining halving
Difficulty crash
Hashrate squeeze
context: Difficulty adjusts downward to compensate, helping remaining miners. The negative-feedback loop is part of what makes Bitcoin mining resilient.

question: The Bitcoin community phrase for regularly buying small amounts to accumulate over time, regardless of price, is:
answer: Stacking sats
choices: Stacking sats
Bitcoin DCA
HODL strategy
Buy the dip
context: Borrowed from dollar-cost averaging. The Bitcoin culture treats stacking as a multi-year discipline aligned with low time preference.

question: Each anniversary of Pizza Day (May 22), Bitcoin community members commemorate by:
answer: Buying pizza with Lightning Network
choices: Buying pizza with Lightning Network
Holding silent reflection
Selling 10,000 sats
Mining a special block
context: Strike, Bitrefill, and others enable instant Lightning pizza orders. The ritual underscores how far the payments stack has come since 2010.

question: The first metallic coins struck under royal authority, around 600 BC, were minted in which Anatolian kingdom?
answer: Lydia
choices: Lydia
Phrygia
Persia
Egypt
context: Lydian king Croesus issued electrum coins of standardized weight. The innovation spread to Greek city-states and reshaped trade across the Mediterranean.

question: The Byzantine gold coin minted at consistent purity from Constantine to the 11th century — perhaps the most stable money in history — was the:
answer: Solidus
choices: Solidus
Denarius
Bezant
Stater
context: Roughly 700 years of unchanging gold content. Foreign merchants from Sri Lanka to Sweden treated it as benchmark money. Called the 'dollar of the Middle Ages'.

question: The Roman silver coin that started near 95% pure silver under Augustus and ended near 2% pure under Aurelian was the:
answer: Denarius
choices: Denarius
Aureus
Sestertius
Antoninianus
context: Three centuries of progressive debasement. The Roman emperors funded armies and games by clipping the coinage. Inflation followed; trust evaporated.

question: The 301 AD attempt to halt Roman inflation by setting maximum prices, on penalty of death, was issued by emperor:
answer: Diocletian
choices: Diocletian
Aurelian
Constantine
Justinian
context: Edict on Maximum Prices. Failed predictably: black markets opened, goods disappeared from shops, executions followed. Among the most well-documented failures of price controls.

question: Henry VIII's Great Debasement of the English silver coinage, beginning in earnest in 1542, was driven by:
answer: His wars in France and Scotland
choices: His wars in France and Scotland
The Black Death's continuing toll
Discovery of New World silver
Reformation seizure of monasteries
context: He cut silver content from 93% down to 33%. The pound sterling lost two thirds of its value within a decade. Elizabeth I later restored sound coinage.

question: Massive silver imports from American mines, especially Potosi after 1545, caused what 16th-century European phenomenon?
answer: Price revolution
choices: Price revolution
Industrial Revolution
Gold standard collapse
Commercial revolution
context: Prices in Spain rose roughly six-fold across the 1500s. The quantity-theory case for inflation as a monetary phenomenon was established by 16th-century writers like Jean Bodin.

question: The Spanish colonial silver mine that produced perhaps half the world's silver in the 16th-17th centuries was located at:
answer: Potosi (Bolivia)
choices: Potosi (Bolivia)
Zacatecas (Mexico)
Guanajuato (Mexico)
Taxco (Mexico)
context: 16,000 feet up the Andes. By 1600 Potosi had 150,000 inhabitants — one of the largest cities on Earth. Most of the silver flowed to Europe, then via Manila to China.

question: The 1720 French speculative bubble engineered by Scottish economist John Law around colonial trade shares was the:
answer: Mississippi Scheme
choices: Mississippi Scheme
South Sea Bubble
Tulip Mania
Darien Scheme
context: Paper money flooded France. The bubble inflated the company's shares 30-fold, then collapsed. Law fled France in disgrace; France swore off paper money for generations.

question: England's parallel 1720 bubble, in shares of a company holding South American trade monopolies, was the:
answer: South Sea Bubble
choices: South Sea Bubble
Mississippi Scheme
Tulip Mania
Darien Scheme
context: Isaac Newton famously lost a fortune. He later said: 'I can calculate the motion of heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people.' The political fallout shaped British finance.

question: The 1636-37 Dutch speculative episode often cited as the first recorded bubble in a modern commodity was:
answer: Tulip Mania
choices: Tulip Mania
South Sea Bubble
Mississippi Scheme
Boston Land Bubble
context: Bulb prices spiked then crashed within months. Modern economic historians like Earl Thompson have argued the conventional story exaggerates the scale; the cultural legend endures.

question: American Revolutionary War paper money, issued by the Continental Congress and hyperinflated by the war's end, gave rise to which phrase?
answer: Not worth a Continental
choices: Not worth a Continental
Wildcat banking
Greenback inflation
Free silver crash
context: By 1781 Continentals traded at 1000-to-1 against specie. Voters' bitterness about paper inflation shaped the Constitution's prohibition on state-issued bills of credit.

question: The paper money the French Revolution issued backed by confiscated church lands, which hyperinflated by 1796, was the:
answer: Assignat
choices: Assignat
Continental
Mandat territorial
Livre tournois
context: Started 1789. Within seven years, 1000-livre notes were worthless. Andrew Dickson White's 1896 essay Fiat Money Inflation in France is the classic short account.

question: The classical international gold standard — fixed dollar/pound/franc/mark gold parities supporting massive trade — operated roughly:
context: Pax Britannica's monetary side. Trade boomed; capital flowed freely. WWI broke it; the interwar restoration failed; only Bretton Woods's looser version followed.

question: The Coinage Act of 1873, demonetizing silver in the US during a populist push for bimetallism, was nicknamed the:
answer: Crime of '73
choices: Crime of '73
Free Silver Act
Specie Act
Gold Standard Act
context: Silver advocates argued it was a sneaky goldbug coup. The William Jennings Bryan 'Cross of Gold' speech in 1896 was the populist response. Gold won, silver lost.

question: William Jennings Bryan's 1896 Democratic Convention speech demanding free silver coinage was titled:
answer: Cross of Gold
choices: Cross of Gold
Free Silver Now
Silver and Liberty
The People's Money
context: 'You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.' The convention nominated him for president; McKinley defeated him in November. Gold remained.

question: The US formally defined the dollar in terms of gold through which 1900 law passed under William McKinley?
answer: Gold Standard Act
choices: Gold Standard Act
Federal Reserve Act
Bretton Woods Agreement
Sherman Silver Purchase Act
context: $1 = 23.22 grains of pure gold (~1/20.67 oz). The act ended the bimetallism debate that had roiled politics since the Civil War. Held until 1933.

question: FDR's Executive Order 6102 of April 5, 1933 required American citizens to surrender their gold to the Federal Reserve at $20.67 per ounce. Penalty for noncompliance was:
answer: 10 years prison and $10,000 fine
choices: 10 years prison and $10,000 fine
Confiscation only
Disbarment from federal service
Loss of voting rights
context: After collection, Roosevelt revalued gold to $35 per ounce in January 1934 — a 41% one-shot devaluation against the metal Americans had just been forced to surrender.

question: FDR's 1933 Joint Resolution voiding gold-payment clauses in private contracts was upheld in 1935 by the Supreme Court in:
answer: The Gold Clause Cases
choices: The Gold Clause Cases
Norman v Baltimore Ohio
Schechter Poultry v US
Roosevelt v Federal Reserve
context: 5-4 decision. Contracts requiring payment in gold were rewritten to fiat. A fundamental break in property rights and contract law that has never been fully repaired.

question: FDR officially revalued the dollar against gold in January 1934 at what new price?
answer: $35 per ounce
choices: $35 per ounce
$50 per ounce
$20.67 per ounce
$100 per ounce
context: A 41% devaluation of the dollar against gold. The Treasury made an enormous one-time bookkeeping profit, which was used to capitalize the Exchange Stabilization Fund.

question: US silver certificates, redeemable for silver at the Treasury, ceased being convertible in:
context: Lyndon Johnson's Treasury withdrew redeemability. The 1965 Coinage Act had already begun debasing dimes and quarters. By 1968, US silver coinage was finished.

question: The 1944 conference establishing the postwar dollar-anchored gold-exchange standard was held at Bretton Woods, New Hampshire, in July. The dollar was pegged at:
answer: $35 per ounce of gold
choices: $35 per ounce of gold
$20.67 per ounce
$50 per ounce
$100 per ounce
context: 44 nations sent delegates. Keynes wanted a supranational currency (the 'bancor'); Harry Dexter White won for the US dollar. The system lasted 27 years.

question: John Maynard Keynes's rejected 1944 proposal for a supranational reserve currency was called the:
answer: Bancor
choices: Bancor
Eurodollar
SDR
Federal note
context: Harry Dexter White won; the dollar became the anchor. Years later Robert Triffin showed why dollar-anchored gold standards must fail — exactly as Bretton Woods did.

question: Richard Nixon ended dollar convertibility to gold in a televised speech on what date?
answer: August 15, 1971
choices: August 15, 1971
October 19, 1987
September 11, 2001
March 14, 1933
context: Nixon, John Connally, and Paul Volcker met secretly at Camp David. The 'temporary' suspension is still in effect. A defining moment of 20th-century economic history.

question: Gold's nominal peak during the late-1970s inflation surge, reached briefly in January 1980, was approximately:
answer: $850 per ounce
choices: $850 per ounce
$2000 per ounce
$500 per ounce
$1500 per ounce
context: From ~$35 in 1971 — a 24-fold rise in nine years. Volcker's rate hikes broke the bullion run; gold fell into a 20-year bear market.

question: The most famous postwar hyperinflation, in which a German mark fell from prewar parity to 4.2 trillion marks per dollar by November 1923, was the:
answer: Weimar Republic hyperinflation
choices: Weimar Republic hyperinflation
Hungarian pengo collapse
Zimbabwean hyperinflation
Yugoslav dinar collapse
context: Caused by war reparations + Reichsbank printing. People burned banknotes for heat. The hyperinflation traumatized German society; many historians link the trauma to later extremism.

question: The Weimar inflation was finally halted in November 1923 by introduction of a new currency partially backed by mortgages on German real estate. It was called the:
answer: Rentenmark
choices: Rentenmark
Reichsmark
Goldmark
Papiermark
context: Hjalmar Schacht administered the introduction. The Rentenmark was later replaced by the Reichsmark; both maintained value after the Papiermark was retired.

question: The iconic photographs of Weimar inflation show Germans transporting cash in:
answer: Wheelbarrows for everyday purchases
choices: Wheelbarrows for everyday purchases
Steel drums
Suitcases at border crossings
Train cars
context: Children played with bricks of worthless marks. The photograph of a woman lighting her stove with cash circulated worldwide. A warning kept alive by every German central banker since.

question: The German banker credited with engineering the November 1923 currency stabilization was:
answer: Hjalmar Schacht
choices: Hjalmar Schacht
Rudolf Havenstein
Ludwig Erhard
Karl Helfferich
context: Schacht served as Reichsbank president, then later under Hitler. Tried at Nuremberg, acquitted. His monetary stabilization is studied; his Nazi-era role remains debated.

question: The worst hyperinflation in recorded history occurred in 1946 in:
answer: Hungary
choices: Hungary
Weimar Germany
Zimbabwe
Yugoslavia
context: Prices doubled every 15 hours at peak. The pengo lost essentially all value; the forint replaced it August 1, 1946. Soviet occupation policies and reparations drove the collapse.

question: Hungary issued the largest-denomination banknote in human history during its 1946 hyperinflation. The denomination was:
answer: 100 quintillion pengo
choices: 100 quintillion pengo
1 quadrillion mark
100 trillion Zimbabwe dollar
500 billion dinar
context: 10^20 pengo. The note was printed but rarely actually circulated by the time it was issued. Hungary introduced the gold-backed forint days later.

question: Hungary's currency replacing the hyperinflated pengo, introduced August 1, 1946, is the:
answer: Forint
choices: Forint
Pengo II
Hungarian mark
Zloty
context: Initially backed by Hungarian gold reserves repatriated from German territory. The forint has been Hungary's currency since.

question: The Chinese Nationalist gold yuan certificate's failure in 1948 contributed to the collapse of which government?
answer: The Chinese Nationalist (KMT) government
choices: The Chinese Nationalist (KMT) government
The Qing Dynasty
The Republican government before Mao
Sun Yat-sen's Republic
context: Hyperinflation destroyed urban support for Chiang Kai-shek's government. Within a year, the KMT had retreated to Taiwan. Monetary collapse aided the communist takeover.

question: Yugoslavia under Milosevic experienced one of the worst hyperinflations in European history in:
context: Prices doubled every 1.4 days at peak. The 500-billion-dinar note was issued — the largest European banknote denomination. The new dinar replaced it January 1994.

question: Zimbabwe's 2008 hyperinflation, driven by Mugabe-era money printing, is famous for the issuance of which large-denomination banknote?
answer: 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollar note
choices: 100 trillion Zimbabwean dollar note
1 trillion Zimbabwean dollar note
10 quadrillion mark
1 million dollar note
context: Issued January 2009. By the time it appeared, the local economy had largely dollarized informally. The note has become a popular collectible.

question: Zimbabwe officially abandoned its currency for the US dollar in:
context: After hyperinflation destroyed remaining purchasing power. The country used USD as its primary unit of account for more than a decade. Reintroduced a gold-backed currency in 2024.

question: Venezuela's 2016-2019 hyperinflation under Hugo Chavez's successor Nicolas Maduro was driven primarily by:
answer: Money printing to fund subsidies
choices: Money printing to fund subsidies
External oil price shocks alone
US sanctions alone
Earthquakes
context: Combined with oil price decline and Chavez-era central planning destruction of productive capacity. Inflation topped 1 million percent per year at peak. Caracas largely dollarized.

question: Argentina has experienced repeated currency collapses; the 1989-1990 hyperinflation under President Alfonsin reached over what monthly rate?
answer: 3000% annually at peak
choices: 3000% annually at peak
100% annually
20% monthly
Below 50% annually
context: The austral replaced the peso 1985; the peso replaced the austral 1992. Argentine governments routinely confiscate savings through devaluations.

question: From 1991 to 2001, Argentina pegged its peso to the US dollar at 1:1 in what stabilization regime?
answer: Convertibility Plan
choices: Convertibility Plan
Currency Board
Dollarization Lite
ARS Standard
context: Under economy minister Domingo Cavallo. Initially halted inflation; eventually collapsed in 2001 amid sovereign default, bank freezes, and political chaos.

question: Argentina's libertarian president Javier Milei, elected November 2023, has championed which monetary reform?
answer: Full dollarization
choices: Full dollarization
Bitcoin as legal tender
Gold standard
Currency board
context: Milei is an open Austrian economist. The plan has been pursued partially; entrenched political opposition has slowed full implementation. The peso has stabilized somewhat under his administration.

question: The Lebanese pound, after decades of de facto dollar peg, collapsed in:
context: The Lebanese banking system collapsed; depositors lost most of their savings. The lira lost 98% of its value against the dollar. Hyperinflation and political collapse intertwined.

question: The Turkish lira has suffered persistent decline under President Erdogan, whose unorthodox theory holds that:
answer: High interest rates cause inflation
choices: High interest rates cause inflation
Hyperinflation must be permitted
Currency boards never work
Capital controls always work
context: Erdogan repeatedly fired central bankers who raised rates. The lira lost about 90% of its value 2018-2024. A real-world test of unorthodox monetary theory.

question: Egypt has repeatedly devalued its pound under IMF program conditions throughout the 2010s and 2020s. The most recent major devaluation was in:
answer: March 2024
choices: March 2024
October 2008
January 1934
August 1971
context: From ~30 EGP per USD to ~50 EGP. The Egyptian government had defended an unsustainable peg for years while inflation eroded purchasing power.

question: Sri Lanka defaulted on its sovereign debt for the first time in:
context: Following a combination of poor macroeconomic management, the COVID tourism collapse, and chemical-fertilizer ban consequences. Mass protests forced the president's resignation.

question: Iran's rial has collapsed dramatically under Western sanctions, from ~10,000 IRR per USD in 2010 to approximately what level by 2024?
answer: Above 600,000 IRR per USD
choices: Above 600,000 IRR per USD
Around 50,000 IRR per USD
Below 30,000 IRR per USD
Below 10,000 IRR per USD
context: Iran experimented with crypto, gold imports, and barter trade to evade sanctions. Inflation has consistently exceeded 30% annually. Sound money would solve much of this.

question: Cuba operated a notable two-currency system from 1994 to 2021, with the convertible peso (CUC) alongside the:
answer: Cuban peso (CUP)
choices: Cuban peso (CUP)
US dollar
Russian ruble
Venezuelan bolivar
context: The CUC was used for tourism and dollar transactions; the CUP for ordinary citizens. The unification in 2021 caused inflation. Cuba's economy has continued to deteriorate.

question: The Economist magazine's whimsical index comparing the price of a Big Mac across countries to measure currency purchasing-power parity began in:
context: Created by Pam Woodall. Simple, visceral, surprisingly informative. A burger contains tradable goods + non-tradable labor and rent in standardized proportions.

question: The economic concept asserting that exchange rates should adjust so identical goods cost the same across countries is called:
answer: Purchasing power parity
choices: Purchasing power parity
Interest rate parity
Real exchange rate
Effective exchange rate
context: PPP rarely holds in the short run because of transport costs, tariffs, and non-tradable goods. It holds reasonably well over long horizons and remains a useful benchmark.

question: Gold's 21st century run, from ~$280 in 2000 to ~$2400 by 2024, has been driven primarily by:
answer: Central bank monetary expansion
choices: Central bank monetary expansion
Industrial demand growth
Jewelry demand surge
Mine production decline
context: Volcker-era discipline gave way; QE, ZIRP, and now post-2020 stimulus have driven hard-asset bids. Gold and Bitcoin both serve as escape valves from fiat debasement.

question: The Byzantine solidus was so widely accepted across medieval Eurasia that Italian merchants used a generic term for it:
answer: Bezant
choices: Bezant
Ducat
Florin
Sequin
context: From 'Byzantium'. Marco Polo encountered it from Constantinople to Beijing. Stable monetary units make long-distance trade possible; debased ones don't.

question: The Spanish silver peso that became the global trade currency was called 'pieces of eight' because:
answer: It was scored to break into eight reales
choices: It was scored to break into eight reales
Eight were minted per silver bar
It contained eight grades of silver
It bore eight royal seals
context: The coin's scoring made it convertible into smaller change. The eight-reales coin (the dollar) circulated freely; cutting yielded 'two bits' = a quarter — still slang for 25 cents.

question: China operated a silver standard for centuries; it officially abandoned the standard in:
context: The Nationalist government switched to managed paper money — the fabi — in 1935 after silver outflows. Hyperinflation in 1948 followed. Silver had been Chinese money for a thousand years.

question: The 'Crisis of the Third Century' (235-284 AD) in the Roman Empire saw severe coin debasement, military collapse, and:
answer: Hyperinflation lasting decades
choices: Hyperinflation lasting decades
Mass conversions to Christianity only
Population growth
Successful currency reform
context: Real wages collapsed. Aurelian's later reforms only partially restored stability. The crisis prefigured many later civilizational failures linked to monetary degradation.

question: After WWI, the Habsburg empire's successor states suffered severe currency collapses; the Austrian krone hyperinflated in:
context: The new schilling replaced the krone in 1924. Mises's Theory of Money and Credit (1912) had anticipated such collapses in central-bank-dominated war economies.

question: World War I ended the classical international gold standard because:
answer: Belligerents suspended convertibility to fund war
choices: Belligerents suspended convertibility to fund war
Gold reserves were physically destroyed
The UK formally renounced gold
Civilians demanded paper money
context: All major participants suspended specie payments and inflated to finance the war. The interwar attempt to restore the standard was half-hearted and short-lived.

question: The 1925 British return to the prewar gold parity, championed by Winston Churchill as Chancellor, was attacked as a major economic mistake by:
answer: John Maynard Keynes
choices: John Maynard Keynes
Friedrich Hayek
Irving Fisher
Ludwig von Mises
context: Keynes's pamphlet The Economic Consequences of Mr Churchill argued Britain pegged the pound too high. The decision contributed to British deflation and unemployment in the late 1920s.

question: Paul Volcker broke the 1970s inflation by raising the federal funds rate as high as approximately:
context: The prime rate hit 21.5% in 1981. The economy entered deep recession; unemployment peaked above 10%. Inflation fell from above 13% in 1980 to under 4% by 1983. Brutal but effective.

question: By the late 1960s, foreign central banks held more dollars than the US held gold at $35/oz. This Triffin-dilemma-driven imbalance led to:
answer: The 1971 Nixon shock closing the gold window
choices: The 1971 Nixon shock closing the gold window
Increased gold reserves at Fort Knox
Successful realignment of pegs
Renewal of Bretton Woods
context: Robert Triffin had warned in 1960 that the dollar-anchored standard would inevitably fail. The system held by inertia until France and others demanded gold.

question: The US government's main gold bullion depository, established in 1937, is located at:
answer: Fort Knox, Kentucky
choices: Fort Knox, Kentucky
West Point, New York
Denver, Colorado
Washington, DC
context: Officially holds 147.3 million troy ounces. The Treasury has never permitted a comprehensive public audit. The opacity has fed conspiracy theories for decades.

question: US official gold holdings, the world's largest, total approximately:
answer: 8133 metric tons
choices: 8133 metric tons
1000 metric tons
25,000 metric tons
Less than 100 metric tons
context: About 261 million troy ounces, valued at $42.22/oz on the Treasury's books — an absurd convention. At market prices, the holdings would be hundreds of billions of dollars.

question: The world's second-largest official gold reserve, with around 3350 tons, is held by:
answer: Germany
choices: Germany
France
Italy
China
context: Held by the Bundesbank. Germany repatriated significant portions from New York and Paris in the 2010s — a notable signal about trust in foreign custody.

question: Among major nations, the most rapid 21st-century accumulation of central bank gold reserves has been by:
answer: China
choices: China
Russia
Saudi Arabia
Switzerland
context: China reports gold reserves periodically. Unofficial estimates are higher. The accumulation appears tied to longer-term de-dollarization strategy.

question: Russia's central bank's gold reserves, plus its experiments with gold-backed ruble settlement, have been actively expanded since:
answer: 2014 Crimean sanctions
choices: 2014 Crimean sanctions
2008 financial crisis
1998 ruble crisis
1971 Bretton Woods collapse
context: Russia has been accumulating gold steadily; after 2022 it accelerated. The frozen reserves abroad showed dollar/euro vulnerability to political weaponization.

question: US dimes and quarters ceased to contain meaningful silver under which law?
answer: Coinage Act of 1965
choices: Coinage Act of 1965
Coinage Act of 1873
Federal Reserve Act of 1913
Bretton Woods Agreement
context: Cupronickel sandwiches replaced 90% silver. Silver had been money in the West for thousands of years; the US replaced it under LBJ in less than a century after Bryan's Cross.

question: US one-cent coins ceased to be made of mostly copper and became copper-plated zinc in:
context: When copper prices made the coin's intrinsic value exceed its face. Eisenhower's IKE dollar coins from 1971-78 contained no silver despite their large size.

question: The American Silver Eagle one-ounce silver bullion coin, struck by the US Mint since 1986, has a nominal face value of:
answer: One dollar
choices: One dollar
Twenty dollars
Fifty cents
Ten dollars
context: Absurdly low compared to silver content (~$25-30). The face value preserves legal-tender status. The American Gold Eagle parallels it.

question: The American Gold Eagle bullion coin was first struck by the US Mint in:
context: Authorized under President Reagan, struck from American mined gold. The one-ounce coin's $50 nominal face value bears no relation to its market value of thousands.

question: The first widely traded modern gold bullion coin, introduced in 1967 by South Africa, was the:
answer: Krugerrand
choices: Krugerrand
Maple Leaf
American Eagle
Sovereign
context: Named for Paul Kruger. Used to circumvent apartheid-era export restrictions on raw gold. Canadians introduced the Maple Leaf in 1979; the Americans followed in 1986.

question: The first .9999 fine gold bullion coin, struck by the Royal Canadian Mint starting in 1979, is the:
answer: Canadian Maple Leaf
choices: Canadian Maple Leaf
Australian Kangaroo
Chinese Panda
British Sovereign
context: Set the new purity standard. Subsequent issues moved to .99999. Highly collectible; the bullion-coin market exploded in popularity during the late-1970s gold rush.

question: Among modern alternatives to fiat money, the two assets most discussed as sound-money successors are:
answer: Gold and Bitcoin
choices: Gold and Bitcoin
Silver and SDRs
Real estate and equities
Treasury bonds and gold
context: Bitcoiners and goldbugs often spar; many serious investors hold both as complementary. Gold has 5000 years of monetary history; Bitcoin offers digital portability and absolute scarcity.

question: Zimbabwe introduced a gold-backed national currency called the ZiG in:
answer: April 2024
choices: April 2024
January 2009
context: ZiG = Zimbabwe Gold. Replaced the unstable Zimbabwean dollar. Whether the gold backing is genuine and the regime credible is being tested.

question: An alternative inflation measurement maintained by John Williams, often cited by sound-money advocates as showing higher inflation than CPI, is:
answer: ShadowStats
choices: ShadowStats
Truflation
Chapwood Index
MIT Billion Prices Project
context: Williams reconstructs CPI using older methodologies. Methodologically debatable; the basic idea — that official CPI has been adjusted in ways that lower the print — has some merit.

question: A Bitcoin-native inflation index that publishes daily real-time price-change estimates from millions of data points is:
answer: Truflation
choices: Truflation
ShadowStats
Chapwood
MIT BPP
context: Founded by Stefan Rust. Aggregates retail and online prices. Often diverges sharply from BLS CPI prints, particularly during inflationary episodes.

question: A controversial CPI adjustment technique that lowers reported inflation by accounting for quality improvements in products is:
answer: Hedonic adjustment
choices: Hedonic adjustment
Substitution effect
Owner's equivalent rent
Chain-weighting
context: If a new computer is faster, BLS may count part of the price increase as 'quality' rather than inflation. Defensible in principle; subjective in practice; widely criticized by hard-money advocates.

question: The CPI uses imputed rent — rather than actual house prices — to measure homeowner housing costs. This measure is:
answer: Owner's equivalent rent
choices: Owner's equivalent rent
Hedonic price index
House Price Index
Case-Shiller adjustment
context: Treats homes as consumption goods rather than assets. Defended by economists; criticized by sound-money advocates who note it masks the inflationary impact on housing prices.

question: The German political party Adolf Hitler led, which exploited Weimar hyperinflation grievances, was founded as the NSDAP in:
context: His failed 1923 Munich putsch came at the peak of inflation. The Nazi vote stayed marginal until the second crisis hit — the Depression. Both economic shocks contributed.

question: US paper money issued during the Civil War, not backed by specie, was called:
answer: Greenbacks
choices: Greenbacks
Confederate dollars
Continentals
Silver certificates
context: Issued under the Legal Tender Act of 1862. Lost roughly half their value during the war, then restored to par by 1879. Their constitutionality was upheld 1871.

question: The Confederate States' wartime fiat currency, which lost essentially all value by April 1865, was the:
answer: Confederate dollar
choices: Confederate dollar
Confederate gold note
Cotton certificate
Richmond mark
context: Massively over-printed to fund the war. Combined with crop failures, blockade pressure, and battlefield losses, the currency's collapse contributed to Southern surrender.

question: The American era of state-chartered banks issuing their own paper money, with widely varying reliability, was called:
answer: Wildcat banking
choices: Wildcat banking
Free banking
Independent treasury
National banking
context: 1837-1862, after Jackson killed the Second Bank. Notes were redeemed at discounts based on the issuing bank's reputation. The Civil War led to the National Banking Acts replacing the system.

question: The National Banking Acts of 1863-64 imposed federal standards on banks and:
answer: Taxed state bank notes out of existence
choices: Taxed state bank notes out of existence
Created the Federal Reserve directly
Suspended the gold standard
Required all dollars be gold-backed
context: Created a uniform national currency (greenbacks + national bank notes). The 10% tax on state notes effectively ended their circulation. The Federal Reserve came 50 years later.

question: The US suspended dollar convertibility to gold during World War I in:
context: Wartime emergency. Restored quickly after the war. The Federal Reserve, founded 1913, was just beginning to exercise its powers.

question: William Jennings Bryan's three-time presidential run on free silver represents what enduring American political tradition?
answer: Populist demand for monetary inflation
choices: Populist demand for monetary inflation
Austrian sound-money preference
Bipartisan technocratic consensus
Anarcho-capitalist self-rule
context: Bryan's Cross of Gold speech vibrates with rural debtors' grievance against gold-standard creditors. The populist temptation to inflate has recurred in every generation.

question: Argentinian middle-class households have repeatedly lost savings to currency devaluations because:
answer: The government routinely inflates
choices: The government routinely inflates
Banks are nationalized
International sanctions devalue savings
Real estate is confiscated
context: Every Argentine generation since the 1940s has experienced a major monetary loss. The cultural distrust of pesos drives a deep informal dollar economy and growing Bitcoin adoption.

question: Venezuela has redenominated its currency multiple times to remove zeros caused by inflation; in 2021 it removed:
answer: Six zeros
choices: Six zeros
Three zeros
Ten zeros
One zero
context: After earlier 2008 and 2018 redenominations. Combined, the bolivar has lost about 14 zeros of value since 1983. The bolivar's history is a museum exhibit of currency collapse.

question: The Byzantine solidus, considered by many monetary historians as the most stable currency ever issued, maintained essentially constant gold content for approximately:
answer: Seven centuries
choices: Seven centuries
One century
Three centuries
Twelve centuries
context: From Constantine's reform (~309 AD) until the Komnenian dynasty's debasement (~1080). Long-distance trade across Eurasia depended on its reliability.

question: The Latin word for soldier's stipend, paid partly in salt, gives English what surviving word for compensation?
answer: Salary
choices: Salary
Stipend
Wage
Bonus
context: Roman legions received salt rations because preservation in pre-refrigeration economies was critical. Salt was money. Worth its salt: another surviving idiom.

question: A famous image from Weimar Germany shows children playing with bricks made of:
answer: Bundled banknotes worthless as money
choices: Bundled banknotes worthless as money
Real bricks marked with prices
Iron Cross medals
Confederate flags
context: When notes became worth less than their wood-pulp paper, they were used as fuel, wallpaper, kite material, and play blocks. The visceral memory passed down generations.

question: Lyn Alden's 2023 history of money and monetary failure was titled:
answer: Broken Money
choices: Broken Money
The Bitcoin Standard
Layered Money
The Price of Tomorrow
context: Subtitle: Why Our Financial System Is Failing Us and How We Can Make It Better. A genuine modern primer combining sound-money critique with Bitcoin advocacy.

question: Lewis Lehrman, the financier and intellectual leader of the modern American gold-standard movement, co-authored which 1980s book defending sound money?
answer: Money and the Coming World Order
choices: Money and the Coming World Order
The Bitcoin Standard
The Politics of Hard Money
The Federalist Papers Today
context: His Lehrman Institute funded sound-money scholarship for decades. Cosponsored the Reagan-era Gold Commission, which voted not to restore the standard.

question: Beyond End the Fed, Ron Paul's earlier book on monetary policy, co-authored with Lewis Lehrman, was:
answer: The Case for Gold
choices: The Case for Gold
Liberty Defined
A Foreign Policy of Freedom
Pillars of Prosperity
context: Their 1982 minority report to the Gold Commission, published as a book. Paul has been the leading congressional sound-money advocate of the past half century.

question: The First Bank of the United States, championed by Alexander Hamilton and opposed by Thomas Jefferson, was chartered in:
context: Twenty-year charter. Jefferson and Madison thought the federal government had no power to charter a corporation; Hamilton won. Charter expired 1811 without renewal.

question: Andrew Jackson's celebrated 1832 veto message rejecting renewal of the Second Bank's charter denounced it as a den of vipers and:
answer: Thieves
choices: Thieves
Foreign meddlers
Slave drivers
Aristocrats
context: Jackson considered the Bank a threat to the republic — politically powerful, foreign-influenced, unaccountable to the people. The veto stood; Jackson won the 1832 election decisively.

question: Andrew Jackson made his veto of the Second Bank's recharter the central issue of which election?
answer: 1832 presidential election
choices: 1832 presidential election
1828 presidential election
1816 presidential election
1840 presidential election
context: Jackson defeated Henry Clay 219 to 49 in the electoral college. The 'Bank War' is a defining episode in American political history. Jackson's Democrats opposed central banks for generations.

question: The president of the Second Bank of the United States, who defied Jackson and contracted credit to provoke recession, was:
answer: Nicholas Biddle
choices: Nicholas Biddle
Robert Morris
Albert Gallatin
Stephen Girard
context: Biddle deliberately caused the Panic of 1837 to pressure Jackson into renewing the charter. It failed; he lost. The episode shapes Bitcoin maximalist views of central-bank power.

question: The 1907 banking panic, resolved when JP Morgan organized a private rescue, set the political stage for:
answer: Founding the Federal Reserve in 1913
choices: Founding the Federal Reserve in 1913
Bretton Woods
Gold standard restoration
FDIC creation
context: The panic exposed America's lack of a lender of last resort. Morgan's personal intervention worked but made clear America couldn't depend on one banker forever. Reform pressure built.

question: The early Federal Reserve framework, drafted secretly by senators and bankers on Jekyll Island, Georgia in 1910, was called the:
answer: Aldrich Plan
choices: Aldrich Plan
Glass-Owen Bill
Federal Banking Act
Warburg Plan
context: Named for Senator Nelson Aldrich. Rejected as politically toxic because of its Wall Street origins. Reframed and passed as the more politically acceptable Glass-Owen bill in 1913.

question: The November 1910 secret meeting at the Jekyll Island Club that drafted the framework of the Federal Reserve was attended by approximately:
answer: Six men
choices: Six men
Twenty men
Two men
Fifty men
context: Senator Aldrich, Paul Warburg, Frank Vanderlip, Henry P. Davison, Charles Norton, A. Piatt Andrew. They posed as duck hunters. The meeting was secret for decades.

question: Among the Jekyll Island Club attendees who designed the Federal Reserve framework was which Kuhn Loeb banker, brother to a German central banker?
answer: Paul Warburg
choices: Paul Warburg
JP Morgan
Andrew Mellon
John D Rockefeller
context: Warburg's brother Max ran a German private bank later folded into the Nazi system. Paul Warburg later served on the first Federal Reserve Board.

question: The Jekyll Island meeting's intended secrecy was achieved by:
answer: Travelling as duck hunters using only first names
choices: Travelling as duck hunters using only first names
Publishing a decoy meeting agenda
Conducting it in code
Using diplomatic cover
context: Frank Vanderlip himself later wrote about the secrecy in his memoirs. He claimed disclosure in 1910 would have killed any bill resembling what eventually became the Federal Reserve Act.

question: Paul Warburg, a key Federal Reserve architect, advocated for a US central bank based on which European model?
answer: The German Reichsbank
choices: The German Reichsbank
The Bank of England
The Banque de France
The Austrian National Bank
context: Warburg considered the German model the most modern in 1910. The Federal Reserve adopted some features of all three major European central banks.

question: The Federal Reserve Act was signed by Woodrow Wilson on what date?
answer: December 23, 1913
choices: December 23, 1913
January 1, 1914
August 15, 1913
November 1, 1913
context: Two days before Christmas, with much of Congress already departed for the holidays. Wilson signed the bill amidst significant procedural controversy. The Fed's foundational moment.

question: Which US president signed the Federal Reserve Act into law in December 1913?
answer: Woodrow Wilson
choices: Woodrow Wilson
William Howard Taft
Theodore Roosevelt
Warren Harding
context: Wilson is reported to have later said: 'I am a most unhappy man. I have unwittingly ruined my country.' The quote is sometimes disputed; the policy was real.

question: The Federal Reserve System consists of how many regional banks plus a Board of Governors in Washington?
answer: Twelve
choices: Twelve
Seven
Twenty-five
Three
context: Created as a federal compromise. The 12 regional Fed banks have different presidents; the New York Fed plays the largest role. The Board has 7 governors in DC.

question: The Federal Open Market Committee, which sets monetary policy, has how many voting members at each meeting?
answer: Twelve
choices: Twelve
Seven
Five
Nineteen
context: The 7 governors plus 5 of the 12 regional bank presidents (New York permanent; others rotate). FOMC meetings occur eight times a year and set the federal funds target.

question: The Federal Reserve's standing facility for emergency lender-of-last-resort loans to banks is called the:
answer: Discount window
choices: Discount window
Open market desk
Repo facility
FOMC operations
context: Originally the primary tool. Stigma attached to its use; banks avoided it in 2008, requiring the Fed to invent new facilities. Restored to importance in March 2020 emergency.

question: The Federal Reserve's purchase or sale of Treasury securities in markets, to expand or contract reserves, is called:
answer: Open market operations
choices: Open market operations
Discount window lending
Quantitative easing
Reserve requirement adjustment
context: Executed by the New York Fed's open market desk. Conventional QE is open market operations scaled up dramatically — buying not just Treasuries but mortgage-backed securities and beyond.

question: In September 2019, an unexpected disruption forced the Federal Reserve to inject emergency liquidity into which money market?
answer: The repo market
choices: The repo market
The treasury bond market
The interbank lending market
The mortgage market
context: Repo rates spiked to 10% briefly. The Fed re-began balance sheet expansion months before COVID. Underlying causes are still debated; structural fragilities persist.

question: The 1933 Banking Act separating commercial banking from investment banking was called:
answer: Glass-Steagall Act
choices: Glass-Steagall Act
Federal Reserve Reform Act
Banking Holiday Act
FDR Banking Act
context: Repealed in 1999 under the Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act. Many observers argue the repeal contributed to the conditions that led to the 2008 crisis.

question: The 1999 act repealing parts of Glass-Steagall, allowing commercial and investment bank combinations, was:
answer: Gramm-Leach-Bliley
choices: Gramm-Leach-Bliley
Riegle-Neal
Sarbanes-Oxley
Dodd-Frank
context: Signed by President Clinton. Citicorp and Travelers had already merged anticipating the change. The repeal accelerated bank consolidation.

question: The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation was created in:
context: Standard deposit insurance levels rose over time: $5,000 originally; $250,000 since 2008. The FDIC backstop is funded by industry premiums, with implicit Treasury backing.

question: The 2008 financial crisis prompted the FDIC's standard deposit insurance limit to be raised to:
context: Up from $100,000. Defended as crisis stabilization; criticized as a one-way ratchet expanding the federal backstop and moral hazard for risk-taking banks.

question: Federal Reserve chairman Arthur Burns (1970-78) is often cited for letting inflation run during the 1970s under pressure from which president?
answer: Richard Nixon
choices: Richard Nixon
Jimmy Carter
Gerald Ford
Lyndon Johnson
context: Nixon-Burns tapes record explicit pressure to keep money loose ahead of the 1972 election. Burns delivered. The 1970s inflation followed, and Volcker had to break it.

question: Paul Volcker served as Federal Reserve chairman during what years?
context: Appointed by Carter, reappointed by Reagan. Broke the 1970s inflation through high rates. Returned briefly under Obama to lead the Volcker Rule effort restricting bank trading.

question: Alan Greenspan served as Federal Reserve chairman during what years?
context: Initially a Rand-influenced gold standard advocate; in practice he ran an increasingly accommodative monetary policy. Praised as 'Maestro' through 2007; widely criticized after.

question: On October 23, 2008, during congressional testimony, former Fed chairman Alan Greenspan admitted he had found a 'flaw' in his:
answer: Ideology about self-regulating markets
choices: Ideology about self-regulating markets
Methodology for predicting inflation
Theory of the Phillips curve
Approach to gold pricing
context: A remarkable public concession. Critics argued the 'flaw' was straightforward — banks given lender-of-last-resort backstops will take excessive risks. Austrians warned of this for decades.

question: Ben Bernanke, Federal Reserve chairman 2006-2014, was previously a Princeton economist specializing in:
answer: The Great Depression
choices: The Great Depression
International trade
Labor economics
Industrial organization
context: His academic work on the 1930s shaped his crisis responses. Bernanke shared the 2022 economics Nobel for banking-crisis research — for analyzing the very crisis he helped manage.

question: Bear Stearns, the first major Wall Street firm to collapse in 2008, was sold to JP Morgan with Federal Reserve guarantees in:
answer: March 2008
choices: March 2008
September 2008
October 2008
August 2008
context: Initial price: $2 per share, later raised to $10. The Fed guaranteed $30 billion of Bear's questionable assets. The Bear deal foreshadowed and arguably encouraged Lehman's later defenders.

question: Lehman Brothers, the largest bankruptcy in US history, filed for Chapter 11 on:
answer: September 15, 2008
choices: September 15, 2008
March 14, 2008
October 19, 2008
August 9, 2007
context: Total assets $639 billion. The Fed and Treasury did not bail out Lehman — a still-debated decision. Within 48 hours, the AIG bailout began. Crisis cascade intensified.

question: TARP, the 2008 bank bailout package signed by George W. Bush, authorized initial spending of:
answer: $700 billion
choices: $700 billion
$100 billion
$2 trillion
$300 billion
context: Eventually disbursed less; the program was largely repaid. The political precedent — that Washington would underwrite major bank losses — has shaped expectations ever since.

question: The Federal Reserve's three rounds of post-2008 large-scale asset purchases, between 2008 and 2014, were collectively known as:
answer: QE1, QE2, QE3 (quantitative easing)
choices: QE1, QE2, QE3 (quantitative easing)
Open Market Operations
Interest Rate Targets
Reserve Requirement Cuts
context: The Fed's balance sheet grew from about $900 billion in 2008 to $4.5 trillion by 2014. Then it grew further to $9 trillion during the 2020 COVID emergency.

question: By the end of QE3 in 2014, the Federal Reserve's balance sheet had grown from $900 billion pre-crisis to approximately:
answer: $4.5 trillion
choices: $4.5 trillion
$2 trillion
$10 trillion
$1 trillion
context: Mostly Treasuries and mortgage-backed securities. The Fed had become the largest holder of MBS in the world. Reducing this took years; March 2020 reversed the reduction completely.

question: In May-June 2013, markets convulsed when Ben Bernanke suggested the Fed might soon slow asset purchases. This episode was called the:
answer: Taper Tantrum
choices: Taper Tantrum
Volcker Shock
Greenspan Standoff
Bernanke Bounce
context: Treasury yields spiked. Emerging market currencies sold off sharply. The Fed learned that tightening would be hard; it took until December 2015 to raise rates by 25 basis points.

question: Jerome Powell has served as Federal Reserve chair since:
answer: February 2018
choices: February 2018
January 2014
August 2006
December 2010
context: Appointed by Trump, reappointed by Biden. Initially raised rates and shrank the balance sheet; reversed course in 2020; then engineered the most aggressive tightening cycle since Volcker.

question: The Federal Reserve crossed a significant Rubicon in March 2020 by, for the first time in its history, buying:
answer: Corporate bonds directly via SPV
choices: Corporate bonds directly via SPV
Foreign sovereign debt
Equities directly
Real estate
context: Through a special-purpose vehicle backed by Treasury equity. The mere announcement was enough; actual purchases were modest. Distorted credit markets durably.

question: The Federal Reserve's balance sheet peaked in April 2022 at approximately:
answer: $9 trillion
choices: $9 trillion
$4.5 trillion
$15 trillion
$2 trillion
context: Massive post-2020 expansion. The Fed has been reducing it via quantitative tightening (QT) since June 2022, but the pace of reduction is slow. Still over $7 trillion in 2024.

question: The Federal Reserve began allowing assets to roll off its balance sheet — quantitative tightening — in:
answer: June 2022
choices: June 2022
January 2014
October 2008
March 2020
context: Initially $47.5B per month, then $95B. Slower than markets initially anticipated. Even after years of QT, the Fed balance sheet remains vastly larger than pre-2020.

question: Federal Reserve chair Jerome Powell described the 2021 inflation surge throughout most of that year using what word he later admitted was wrong?
answer: Transitory
choices: Transitory
Temporary
Stable
Contained
context: He retired the term in late November 2021. By then, headline CPI was already 6.8% and rising. The transitory framing delayed tightening by nearly a year.

question: US CPI inflation peaked in June 2022 at year-over-year rate of approximately:
context: Highest reading since November 1981 under Volcker. Driven by post-COVID demand, supply chains, energy prices, and lagged effects of money supply expansion. Painful for wage earners and savers.

question: By mid-2023, the Federal Reserve had raised the federal funds target range to:
context: The most aggressive tightening cycle since Volcker. Inflation fell back toward 3% range. Critics: the rate destruction of long-duration bonds prefigured Silicon Valley Bank's March 2023 collapse.

question: Congress assigned the Federal Reserve a dual mandate in 1977 covering:
answer: Maximum employment and stable prices (with 2% inflation target)
choices: Maximum employment and stable prices (with 2% inflation target)
Currency stability and monetary independence
Sound money and unemployment minimization
Treasury financing and banking supervision
context: The Fed adopted the formal 2% target only in 2012 under Bernanke. The 'maximum employment' definition is open-ended, giving the Fed wide discretion.

question: The Federal Reserve formally adopted a 2% inflation target in:
answer: January 2012 under Bernanke
choices: January 2012 under Bernanke
December 1913 at founding
1979 under Volcker
2020 under Powell
context: Already implicit since the 1990s under Greenspan. The number was conceived to keep nominal rates above zero in case of recession. Austrians argue any chronic positive inflation target is a debasement program.

question: The doctrine of Federal Reserve 'independence' is challenged by both left and right critics, who argue it really means:
answer: Unaccountable monetary power
choices: Unaccountable monetary power
Apolitical technocracy
Voter judgment of rates
Election-proof policy
context: Both populist and libertarian critics question 'independence' as a euphemism for unaccountable expert rule. Audit-the-Fed initiatives have been pushed for decades.
