answer: The Mississippi Company (Compagnie du Mississippi)
choices: The Mississippi Company (Compagnie du Mississippi)
The South Sea Company, which was the parallel English bubble
The Royal African Company, an older English chartered company
The British East India Company, an older English chartered company
context: Law's experiment was the first major paper-money inflation by a modern European state. The Mississippi Company crash bankrupted thousands of French speculators and set French monetary policy back by a century. Law fled and died in Venice in 1729. His General Maxims (1705) anticipated modern central banking ideas.

question: Between 1775 and 1781, the Continental Congress issued paper notes to finance the American Revolution. The notes depreciated so rapidly against silver and gold that they entered the language as a synonym for worthlessness. What phrase comes from this episode?
answer: 'Not worth a Continental'
choices: 'Not worth a Continental'
'Greenback' (from a different Civil War-era issuance)
'Inflation chickens come home to roost'
'Bad money drives out good' (which is Gresham's older Law)
context: Continental notes inflated by roughly 100:1 against specie by 1780. Congress effectively defaulted in 1780-1781 when the notes ceased to be legal tender. Hamilton's later assumption of state debts and creation of the First Bank of US restored confidence in federal finances. The Continentals are the founding monetary trauma of the American republic.

question: By March 1781, after six years of accelerating depreciation, the Continental Congress effectively abandoned its paper currency. The notes ceased being acceptable for tax payments at face value. What approximate exchange rate had emerged by that point between Continental notes and silver coins?
answer: Roughly 1000 Continentals per silver dollar
choices: Roughly 1000 Continentals per silver dollar
Roughly parity (1:1) between Continentals and silver
Roughly 10 Continentals per silver dollar
Roughly 1,000,000 Continentals per silver dollar
context: By March 1781, Continentals had depreciated to roughly 1000:1. Congress effectively recognized the default by allowing tax collection in commodity-equivalents rather than face-value Continentals. The episode left the United States deeply skeptical of paper money for the next eight decades.

question: By November 1923, German hyperinflation had reached the wheelbarrow stage. A new financial regime took office and introduced an emergency currency backed nominally by German land mortgages. Within weeks, prices stabilized. Who was the German central banker who engineered this rescue?
answer: Hjalmar Schacht (as Reichswahrungskommissar and then Reichsbank president)
choices: Hjalmar Schacht (as Reichswahrungskommissar and then Reichsbank president)
Rudolf Havenstein, who had presided over the inflation and died in November 1923
Walther Funk, who later became Reichsbank president under the Nazis
Hans Luther, who was Reichschancellor during the crisis
context: Schacht engineered the November 1923 stabilization on the Rentenmark, then the 1924 transition to the Reichsmark. The Rentenmark trick was confidence engineering: the marks were technically backed by mortgage claims, but the real anchor was a credible commitment to stop printing.

question: Iconic photographs from the late stages of German hyperinflation in 1923 show citizens transporting cash in wheelbarrows for ordinary purchases. By November 1923, what was the approximate price of a single loaf of bread in marks?
answer: Roughly 200 billion marks
choices: Roughly 200 billion marks
Roughly 200 marks
Roughly 200,000 marks
Roughly 200 trillion marks
context: 200 billion marks for bread in November 1923. Hyperinflations have a distinctive social pattern: wage earners and savers are destroyed; debtors and asset holders win. The political consequences in Weimar — pushing the middle class toward extremist parties — are part of why honest macroeconomic policy matters morally.

question: The worst hyperinflation in recorded history occurred not in Weimar Germany but in post-war Hungary in 1945-1946. At the peak in July 1946, prices were doubling every 15 hours. What currency was being destroyed in this episode?
answer: The Hungarian pengo (replaced by the forint in August 1946)
choices: The Hungarian pengo (replaced by the forint in August 1946)
The Hungarian krone (which was replaced in the 1920s)
The Hungarian dinar (which does not exist)
The Hungarian rupee (which does not exist)
context: Hungary 1946 holds the record for worst hyperinflation. Daily inflation of 207%, monthly inflation of 13.6 quadrillion percent. The 100-quintillion-pengo note (10^20) was the largest denomination banknote ever issued. The forint introduced August 1, 1946 stabilized the situation.

question: Hungary's 1945-1946 hyperinflation produced the largest denomination banknote ever issued anywhere in human history — a note with a face value of 100 quintillion (10^20) of the depreciating currency. What was this note officially valued at?
answer: 100 quintillion pengo (one hundred million billion pengo)
choices: 100 quintillion pengo (one hundred million billion pengo)
100 trillion pengo (one hundred thousand billion pengo)
100 quadrillion pengo (one hundred thousand trillion pengo)
100 sextillion pengo (one hundred thousand quintillion pengo)
context: The 100 quintillion pengo (10^20) note is preserved in museums. Hungary printed an even larger denomination (10^21) but never actually issued it before stabilizing. The forint replaced the pengo at 4 x 10^29 pengo to 1 forint — currency reform on an unprecedented scale.

question: In 2008, Zimbabwe under Robert Mugabe experienced the highest hyperinflation of the 21st century to date — official annual inflation reached 89.7 sextillion percent at peak. The Reserve Bank of Zimbabwe issued banknotes in denominations including a 100 trillion dollar note. How did Zimbabwe ultimately stabilize?
answer: By dollarizing — adopting the US dollar as primary currency in 2009
choices: By dollarizing — adopting the US dollar as primary currency in 2009
By introducing a gold-backed currency in 2009
By adopting the euro as primary currency in 2009
By introducing a Bitcoin-backed currency in 2009
context: Zimbabwe's dollarization in 2009 ended the hyperinflation immediately. The Zimbabwe dollar was not officially abandoned until 2015. In 2024, Zimbabwe attempted a return to local currency with the gold-backed ZiG (Zimbabwe Gold) — early results are mixed. The 2008 episode taught generations about fiat collapse.

question: Between 2016 and 2019, Venezuela suffered one of the worst hyperinflations of the 21st century, peaking at over 1.7 million percent annual inflation in 2018. The official minimum wage in dollar terms fell to roughly $2 per month at the worst point. What underlying political-economic regime produced this collapse?
answer: Chavismo: Hugo Chavez's and Nicolas Maduro's socialist-style economic management
choices: Chavismo: Hugo Chavez's and Nicolas Maduro's socialist-style economic management
Free-market capitalism with no currency controls
Pure barter economy with no government intervention
Dollarization combined with strict fiscal discipline
context: Venezuela's collapse is the textbook 21st-century cautionary tale. Chavez nationalized oil, imposed price controls, and printed money. Maduro continued the policies. The country had the world's largest oil reserves and somehow produced famine conditions. Mass emigration of 7+ million Venezuelans by 2024 reshaped South American demographics.

question: Argentina has had one of the most pathological monetary histories of any major economy, with currency redenominations, capital controls, default, and inflation crises recurring approximately every decade since the 1940s. Which dramatic monetary episode occurred in 2001-2002, ending a decade of dollar peg under the 'convertibility plan'?
answer: The default and 'corralito' freezing of bank accounts in December 2001
choices: The default and 'corralito' freezing of bank accounts in December 2001
The 1989 hyperinflation episode of the austral period
The 2018 IMF rescue package and run on the peso
The 1955 Revolucion Libertadora coup against Peron
context: Argentina's 2001-2002 crisis ended a decade of 1:1 dollar peg under the convertibility plan. Bank accounts were frozen ('corralito'). Five presidents in two weeks. The default was the largest sovereign default to that point. Milei's 2023 election was Argentina's response to the latest iteration of monetary collapse — promising dollarization.

question: From 2019 through 2024, Lebanon experienced one of the worst sustained monetary collapses of the early 21st century. The Lebanese pound lost over 98% of its dollar value as the Banque du Liban Ponzi-like central-banking arrangements unraveled. The IMF described it as one of the worst economic crises since 1850 in any country. What underlying mechanism was at the heart?
answer: Central bank 'financial engineering' that masked deep losses through new dollar deposits
choices: Central bank 'financial engineering' that masked deep losses through new dollar deposits
A direct gold-standard collapse with no intervening pathology
A US-imposed sanctions regime targeting financial institutions
A natural-disaster-induced collapse following the 2020 Beirut port explosion
context: Lebanon's collapse is among the worst peacetime monetary catastrophes ever recorded. The Banque du Liban's Riad Salameh ran a complex scheme channeling new dollar deposits to pay older depositors. When the new inflows stopped, the entire system collapsed. Salameh was indicted in multiple jurisdictions.

question: Between 1993 and 1994, Yugoslavia under Slobodan Milosevic suffered a hyperinflation that peaked at over 313 million percent monthly — among the worst of the post-Cold-War era. The National Bank issued a note that became the largest denomination ever circulated in Europe. What was the face value?
answer: 500 billion dinar
choices: 500 billion dinar
5 billion dinar
50 trillion dinar
5 trillion dinar
context: The 500 billion dinar note (1993) holds the European hyperinflation denomination record. Yugoslavia's collapse was financing the wars in Croatia and Bosnia by printing money. The 1994 'super-dinar' (1 super-dinar = 10 million old dinars) stabilized things temporarily. Yugoslav inflation is a less-famous but textbook case.

question: In 1948-1949, as the Communists advanced against the Nationalist (Kuomintang) government, the Nationalist regime under Chiang Kai-shek attempted a desperate currency reform — introducing a new 'gold yuan' supposedly backed by gold. Within months the gold yuan was worthless. What political event coincided with the collapse?
answer: The Communist victory in the Chinese Civil War and the founding of the PRC in October 1949
choices: The Communist victory in the Chinese Civil War and the founding of the PRC in October 1949
The Japanese surrender ending World War II in August 1945
The Korean War starting in June 1950
The Cultural Revolution starting in 1966
context: The 1948-1949 KMT hyperinflation severely undermined Nationalist credibility and helped the Communist victory. The Communists initially issued a 'people's yuan' in 1948 in liberated areas, then the renminbi from 1949 onward, which (despite many issues) avoided the worst hyperinflation outcomes. The episode is part of why China's communist regime takes inflation seriously.

question: In July 1944, 730 delegates from 44 Allied nations met for three weeks at a New Hampshire resort hotel to design the postwar international monetary system. The agreement they reached fixed exchange rates against the US dollar, fixed the dollar against gold at $35 per ounce, and created the IMF and World Bank. What was the resort called?
answer: The Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire
choices: The Mount Washington Hotel in Bretton Woods, New Hampshire
The Greenbrier in West Virginia
The Banff Springs Hotel in Alberta
The Mohonk Mountain House in New York
context: Bretton Woods July 1-22, 1944. The dollar-gold standard at $35 per ounce lasted until Nixon closed the gold window in 1971. Keynes (UK) and Harry Dexter White (US Treasury) led the negotiations. Keynes's bancor proposal (a supranational reserve currency) was rejected in favor of the dollar-anchored system.

question: At the 1944 Bretton Woods conference, John Maynard Keynes — representing the United Kingdom — proposed an alternative to a dollar-anchored system: a supranational reserve currency that no single country would issue or control. The proposal was rejected in favor of Harry Dexter White's dollar-centric design. What did Keynes name this proposed currency?
answer: The bancor
choices: The bancor
The dinar
The international monetary unit (IMU)
The special drawing right (SDR), which was a later 1969 IMF construct
context: The bancor would have rebalanced trade flows by penalizing both chronic surplus and deficit countries. The US, the surplus country of the era, rejected it. The dollar-anchored system created exorbitant privilege for the US — at the cost of the contradictions Triffin later identified.

question: On Sunday evening August 15, 1971, US President Richard Nixon went on television and announced what he called a temporary suspension of the dollar's convertibility to gold. The 'temporary' suspension has now lasted over half a century. Where had Nixon made the decision that weekend?
answer: Camp David, Maryland, after a weekend meeting with Treasury Secretary John Connally
choices: Camp David, Maryland, after a weekend meeting with Treasury Secretary John Connally
The White House, after a meeting with Federal Reserve chair Arthur Burns
The Pentagon, after a meeting with Secretary of Defense Melvin Laird
Key Biscayne, Florida, where Nixon was vacationing
context: Camp David, August 13-15, 1971. The 'Camp David weekend' included the gold-window closure, wage-price controls, and 10% import surcharge. Connally, Volcker (then Treasury under-secretary), and Burns were key figures. Bretton Woods was dead; the modern fiat regime had begun.

question: When Nixon announced on August 15, 1971 the suspension of dollar-to-gold convertibility, the dollar's official gold price had been fixed at what amount per troy ounce since 1934 (when FDR had devalued from the pre-Roosevelt $20.67)?
answer: $35 per troy ounce
choices: $35 per troy ounce
$20 per troy ounce
$50 per troy ounce
$100 per troy ounce
context: $35 per troy ounce had been the Bretton Woods anchor since 1944, confirming the FDR 1934 devaluation level. After August 1971, gold floated. By January 1980 it had spiked to $850. As of 2024, gold trades around $2,300 — meaning the dollar has depreciated against gold by over 60x since Nixon's 'temporary' suspension.

question: On April 5, 1933, President Franklin Roosevelt issued Executive Order 6102, forbidding the hoarding of gold coin, gold bullion, and gold certificates by Americans. Most US citizens were required to deliver their gold to the Federal Reserve at $20.67 per ounce. Penalty for noncompliance was up to ten years in prison plus what fine?
choices: $100 fine
$1,000 fine
context: EO 6102 effectively confiscated American gold for $20.67 per ounce. Less than a year later, FDR set the dollar's new official gold price at $35 per ounce — a 41% devaluation. Americans who had complied with EO 6102 lost. Private gold ownership remained illegal until 1975 under Ford. The episode is the founding modern American case of monetary expropriation.

question: In 301 AD, the Roman Emperor Diocletian, facing rampant inflation following decades of currency debasement, issued an Edict on Maximum Prices fixing prices and wages across the empire with death as the penalty for violation. What happened to the edict in practice?
answer: Massive price-control evasion, market disappearance, and ultimate withdrawal of the edict
choices: Massive price-control evasion, market disappearance, and ultimate withdrawal of the edict
Successful price stabilization for several decades
Discovery of new silver mines making the edict obsolete
Diocletian's voluntary abdication leading to the edict's quiet repeal
context: Diocletian's price edict is the classical example of price controls during inflation. Markets disappeared underground; supplies became scarce; the death penalty was reportedly applied at least sometimes. The edict was effectively dead within a decade. Constantine's later monetary stabilization on gold (the solidus) was the actual fix.

question: The Roman silver denarius, introduced around 211 BC at roughly 95% silver content, maintained its standard for over two centuries. From Nero (54-68 AD) onward, successive emperors progressively debased the coin. By the time of Aurelian (270-275 AD), what was the approximate silver content?
answer: Roughly 5% silver (down from 95%)
choices: Roughly 5% silver (down from 95%)
Roughly 50% silver
Roughly 25% silver
Still roughly 95% silver
context: The denarius's silver content fell from 95% to 5% over two centuries. The third-century crisis (235-284 AD) saw the worst debasement, accompanied by economic and political crisis. Diocletian's reforms (and later Constantine's) ended the denarius and introduced new gold and silver standards. The pattern — debasement leading to crisis leading to reform — recurs.

question: The Roman Empire from approximately 235 to 284 AD experienced what historians call the Third Century Crisis: roughly fifty years of military upheaval, economic dislocation, and currency collapse. By the end of the period, the silver content of the denarius had fallen to near zero. What initiated the systematic debasement?
answer: Sustained military expenditure outstripping tax revenues; emperors paid troops in debased coin
choices: Sustained military expenditure outstripping tax revenues; emperors paid troops in debased coin
A natural disaster eliminating Roman silver mines
A trade collapse with China and India for silk and spices
The Antonine Plague of the previous century reducing population
context: The third-century crisis is one of history's great cautionary tales about fiscal-monetary linkage. Emperors needed to pay armies; tax revenues fell; debasement filled the gap; debasement caused inflation; inflation undermined the system further. Diocletian and Constantine eventually restored stability — but on a new monetary basis.

question: Throughout the 19th century, the United States operated on a bimetallic gold-and-silver standard with a fixed legal ratio between the two metals. When market ratios diverged from the legal ratio, one metal would tend to disappear from circulation. What economic principle predicts this disappearance?
answer: Gresham's Law: 'bad money drives out good' under fixed exchange
choices: Gresham's Law: 'bad money drives out good' under fixed exchange
Say's Law: supply creates its own demand
Walras's Law: in general equilibrium markets clear simultaneously
Friedman's Law: inflation is everywhere a monetary phenomenon
context: Gresham's Law (named for Tudor financier Thomas Gresham) explains why bimetallism is operationally unstable. If gold is undervalued by law, people hoard gold and spend silver. The US 1834 ratio favored gold; the 1873 demonetization of silver ('Crime of 73') resolved the question — but produced the silver-vs-gold political wars of the 1880s-1890s.

question: In 1873, Congress passed legislation revising the US Mint statutes and notably omitting the silver dollar from the list of coins authorized for free coinage. Silver advocates later called this legislation a conspiracy. What was the legislation called by them?
answer: The Crime of '73 (to silver advocates) or simply the Coinage Act of 1873
choices: The Crime of '73 (to silver advocates) or simply the Coinage Act of 1873
The Free Silver Act, which was a later silver advocate proposal
The Cross of Gold Act, named for Bryan's later speech
The Bryan Act, named for William Jennings Bryan
context: The 1873 Act demonetized silver effectively. Whether the omission was intentional or careless became politically contested through the 1880s. The Free Silver movement, William Jennings Bryan's 1896 'Cross of Gold' campaign, and Populist agrarian politics all flowed from the 1873 decision. Gold Standard Act of 1900 made it explicit.

question: At the 1896 Democratic National Convention in Chicago, a 36-year-old former Nebraska congressman delivered a thunderous speech advocating for free silver coinage and ending with imagery comparing the gold standard to crucifixion. The speech won him the presidential nomination. Who was he and what was the speech called?
answer: William Jennings Bryan, 'Cross of Gold' speech
choices: William Jennings Bryan, 'Cross of Gold' speech
Robert La Follette, 'Defense of the Common Man' speech
Eugene Debs, 'Industrial Freedom' speech
Theodore Roosevelt, 'Square Deal' speech
context: Bryan's 'Cross of Gold' speech (July 9, 1896) is one of the most famous in American political history. 'You shall not crucify mankind upon a cross of gold.' He lost the 1896 election to McKinley but ran twice more (1900, 1908). The Gold Standard Act of 1900 settled the monetary question against silver advocates.

question: After World War I, the major economies attempted to return to the gold standard but found there was not enough gold to support the higher postwar price levels. The 1922 international conference designed a system in which countries would hold reserves in gold and in foreign currencies pegged to gold. What was this system called?
answer: The gold exchange standard
choices: The gold exchange standard
The Bretton Woods system, which came later in 1944
The dollar-gold standard
The bimetallic standard
context: The gold exchange standard (1922-1931) was a halfway-house. Reserves could be held in gold or in sterling/dollar claims. The 1931 sterling devaluation collapsed the system. Britain went off gold; the gold-exchange period had ended with a crash. The 1944 Bretton Woods system was a more sustainable variation but ended in 1971.

question: Between approximately 1815 (after Waterloo) and 1914 (the outbreak of World War I), the world's dominant reserve currency and trade-financing currency was issued by the largest naval and commercial power. What was the currency, and what is this era sometimes called?
answer: The British pound sterling; the era is the 'Pax Britannica'
choices: The British pound sterling; the era is the 'Pax Britannica'
The French franc germinal; the era is the 'Belle Epoque'
The US dollar; the era is the 'American Century'
The German mark; the era is the 'Wilhelmine peace'
context: The Pax Britannica saw sterling function as the world's reserve currency for a century. London became the global financial center. The classical gold standard was effectively a sterling standard. World War I and its financial aftermath shifted reserve-currency status to the US dollar — a transition not officially completed until Bretton Woods 1944.

question: Many US private contracts in the early 1930s included 'gold clauses' specifying payment in gold-dollar terms — a hedge against possible devaluation. After FDR's 1933 gold confiscation and devaluation, what happened to these contractual gold clauses?
answer: They were declared void by joint resolution of Congress in 1933 and upheld by the Supreme Court in 1935
choices: They were declared void by joint resolution of Congress in 1933 and upheld by the Supreme Court in 1935
They were upheld as private contractual rights enforceable in court
They were upheld but only for contracts with foreign parties
They were upheld but only at the new $35 gold price
context: The June 1933 Joint Resolution voided gold clauses. The 1935 Supreme Court Gold Clause Cases narrowly upheld the resolution (5-4). Holders of gold-clause bonds were paid in depreciated paper dollars. Gold clauses were re-permitted in 1977. The episode showed that 'private property' under fiat regimes depends on the regime not declaring it otherwise.

question: On January 31, 1934, following the gold confiscation of April 1933 and the formal devaluation, the US Treasury fixed the dollar's new official gold price at a specific level — a level that prevailed for the next 37 years until the August 1971 Nixon shock. What was this new official gold price?
answer: $35 per troy ounce (up from $20.67)
choices: $35 per troy ounce (up from $20.67)
$20.67 per troy ounce (unchanged)
$50 per troy ounce
$25 per troy ounce
context: The January 31, 1934 Gold Reserve Act fixed the dollar at $35 per ounce — a 41% devaluation from the prior $20.67. Americans who had complied with EO 6102 in April 1933 had been paid $20.67 per ounce. The Treasury profited about $2.8 billion. The $35 price held through Bretton Woods and ended only with Nixon's August 1971 closing of the gold window.

question: From 1878 through 1964, US Silver Certificates circulated as currency redeemable in silver coin or bullion at the Treasury. The certificates featured prominent 'silver dollar' language. When did the Treasury finally end silver certificate redemption?
answer: Final redemption deadline was June 1968
choices: Final redemption deadline was June 1968
Final redemption deadline was 1934 with gold confiscation
Final redemption deadline was 1971 with the Nixon shock
Final redemption deadline was 1873 with silver demonetization
context: Silver Certificate redemption ended June 24, 1968. By then, market silver prices had risen above the official $1.29/oz redemption price, creating an arbitrage. The Treasury stopped redeeming. Silver Certificates remain legal tender but functionally are just dollar bills. The 1968 endpoint is the last shred of US silver-monetary linkage.

question: Before the 19th century, silver — not gold — was the dominant monetary metal worldwide. Chinese, Indian, and Spanish-American economies all operated effectively on silver bases. When did most major Western economies transition from silver-dominant or bimetallic to a pure gold standard?
answer: Roughly the 1870s and 1880s, led by Germany after the 1871 Franco-Prussian war indemnity
choices: Roughly the 1870s and 1880s, led by Germany after the 1871 Franco-Prussian war indemnity
Roughly the 1500s, with the discovery of Potosi silver
Roughly the 1700s, with the founding of the Bank of England
Roughly the 1930s, with the abandonment of bimetallism
context: Germany used the Franco-Prussian War indemnity (5 billion gold francs) to transition to gold in 1871-1873. Other Western powers followed. The 'crime of 73' (US silver demonetization) is part of the same shift. By 1900 essentially every major Western economy was on gold. India and China stayed on silver until the 1930s.

question: China was one of the last major economies to abandon the silver standard. Until 1935, the Chinese yuan was anchored to silver, which had served as China's primary monetary metal for centuries. What event triggered the 1935 currency reform?
answer: The US Silver Purchase Act of 1934 raising world silver prices and draining Chinese silver
choices: The US Silver Purchase Act of 1934 raising world silver prices and draining Chinese silver
The Japanese invasion of Manchuria in 1931
The Chinese civil war's intensification
Adoption of the gold standard following the 1933 World Economic Conference
context: FDR's 1934 Silver Purchase Act raised world silver prices, sucking silver out of China and triggering deflation. The Nationalist government's November 1935 currency reform replaced silver with a managed fiat — the fapi. The 1948-1949 hyperinflation followed when the KMT printed fapi to fund the civil war. China's monetary trajectory through 1949 is a textbook fiscal-dominance failure.

question: In August 1998, the Russian government defaulted on domestic ruble-denominated debt (the GKOs) and the central bank devalued the ruble. The 'August crisis' was triggered by what combination of factors?
answer: Collapse of oil prices, Asian financial contagion, and unsustainable government short-term borrowing
choices: Collapse of oil prices, Asian financial contagion, and unsustainable government short-term borrowing
Direct Russian intervention in the Ukraine, which began later
Sanctions imposed by Western powers, which came in 2014
Soviet-era debt assumed by the Yeltsin government, which had been restructured
context: The 1998 Russian crisis is a textbook emerging-market currency-and-debt crisis. The combination of falling oil revenues, capital flight from Asia, and overreliance on short-term ruble debt produced a classic 'first generation' currency crisis in Krugman's terminology. Long-Term Capital Management (LTCM) was the famous Western collateral damage.

question: The Turkish lira lost over 90% of its dollar value between 2017 and 2024 amid persistent high inflation and unconventional monetary policy under President Recep Tayyip Erdogan. What is Erdogan's controversial economic theory about the relationship between interest rates and inflation?
answer: That high interest rates cause inflation, so cutting rates fights inflation
choices: That high interest rates cause inflation, so cutting rates fights inflation
Standard Keynesian theory that low rates stimulate aggregate demand
Standard monetarist theory that money supply controls inflation
Austrian theory that artificially low rates create unsustainable booms
context: Erdogan's claim — that interest rates cause inflation — inverts standard economics. Under his pressure, Turkey cut rates while inflation was 80%+, accelerating the lira's collapse. The 2024 reversal under new central bank leadership (raising rates dramatically) has begun to stabilize matters but at enormous cost. The episode is an instructive contemporary case.

question: The Iranian rial collapsed dramatically following the 2018 US re-imposition of sanctions (after withdrawal from the JCPOA nuclear deal). Black market exchange rates diverged from official rates by factors of 5-10x. What is the dual exchange rate system Iran adopted?
answer: An official rate for essential imports, a black market rate for everything else
choices: An official rate for essential imports, a black market rate for everything else
A floating rate identical to the black market rate
A gold-anchored rate independent of foreign exchange
A bitcoin-anchored rate adopted in 2022
context: Iran's dual exchange rate system creates opportunities for corruption and arbitrage. Sanctions-aware traders distinguish official rate, NIMA system rate, and free-market rate. The rial's collapse has driven Iranian middle-class savings into gold, bitcoin, and dollars. The episode is the contemporary cautionary tale of sanctions-induced currency stress.

question: The Pakistani rupee declined from approximately 100 per dollar in 2015 to over 280 per dollar by 2024 — losing nearly two-thirds of its dollar value in less than a decade. What underlying macroeconomic pattern characterizes Pakistan's recurring crises?
answer: Chronic current-account deficits financed by IMF programs combined with fiscal expansion
choices: Chronic current-account deficits financed by IMF programs combined with fiscal expansion
Direct printing of money to fund Hindu pilgrimage programs
Gold standard with insufficient gold reserves
Bitcoin overuse drawing IMF criticism
context: Pakistan's recurring crises follow a familiar pattern: trade deficits, fiscal expansion, foreign reserves depletion, IMF rescue, brief stabilization, and back. As of 2024, Pakistan is in its 24th IMF program. The cycle has hollowed out the rupee. Sound-money advocates point to such cases as illustrations of the fiat-system pathology.

question: In late 2009, the North Korean government carried out a sudden currency revaluation, requiring citizens to exchange their old won for a new currency at 100:1 with strict limits on how much per family could be exchanged. The policy's stated goal was suppressing private market activity. What was the practical effect?
answer: Mass destruction of accumulated middle-class savings and a wave of public anger
choices: Mass destruction of accumulated middle-class savings and a wave of public anger
Successful currency stabilization and economic growth
A peaceful transition to a more stable monetary regime
Adoption of the South Korean won as the new standard
context: North Korea's 2009 revaluation may have been the most explicit modern instance of a state confiscating savings via currency reform. The finance minister Pak Nam-gi was reportedly executed in 2010 over the policy's failure. Black market dollars and yuan now dominate. The case is an extreme illustration of the fragility of paper money under authoritarian regimes.

question: From 1994 to 2021, Cuba operated a unique dual-currency system with two officially recognized currencies — one for ordinary domestic use and one ostensibly pegged to the US dollar for tourism and foreign-currency transactions. What were they called?
answer: The Cuban peso (CUP) and the Cuban convertible peso (CUC)
choices: The Cuban peso (CUP) and the Cuban convertible peso (CUC)
The peso oro and the dollar oro
The Cuban dinar and the Cuban dollar
The patacón and the cuban real
context: Cuba's dual-peso system was unique among modern economies. The CUC traded at 1:1 with USD officially; the CUP at 24-25 per CUC. The unification in January 2021 (Tarea Ordenamiento) was the largest single price-adjustment shock to ordinary Cubans in three decades. Subsequent inflation has been substantial.

question: Argentine president Javier Milei, who took office in December 2023 with the slogan 'la casta tiene miedo', proposed dollarization (abandoning the peso for the US dollar) as part of his shock therapy program. Why has full dollarization not yet occurred?
answer: Insufficient dollar reserves to retire the existing peso monetary base at market rates
choices: Insufficient dollar reserves to retire the existing peso monetary base at market rates
Opposition from the IMF, which has actually supported milder reform
Constitutional prohibitions on currency replacement
Trade union pressure for retention of pesos
context: Argentina lacks the dollar reserves needed for full dollarization. Milei's program has focused instead on dramatic fiscal cuts to stabilize the peso. As of 2024, monthly inflation has fallen substantially but reserves remain low. Whether full dollarization comes later or the program transitions to mere stabilization is one of the most interesting open monetary questions.

question: The 1923 hyperinflation in Weimar Germany destroyed the savings of the German middle class. Real wages, pensions, and bank accounts denominated in marks were essentially wiped out. What political consequences followed in the subsequent decade?
answer: Rising support for extremist parties of both left and right, including the early Nazi movement
choices: Rising support for extremist parties of both left and right, including the early Nazi movement
Strengthening of centrist Weimar coalition parties through 1932
Successful left-liberal restoration of mainstream politics
Decline of right-wing politics into the 1930s
context: The 1923 inflation's destruction of middle-class savings is widely understood by historians as a crucial precondition for the rise of extremist politics. The Nazi Beer Hall Putsch (November 1923) occurred at the inflation's peak. The post-Schacht stabilization brought brief relief, but the 1929-1932 slump completed the political collapse. Sound money is moral infrastructure.

question: Saifedean Ammous, Lyn Alden, and other Austrian-leaning monetary economists argue that Bitcoin functions as a 21st-century equivalent of historical sound-money assets like gold — with comparable scarcity properties but improved portability and verification. What specific Bitcoin property is most analogous to gold's traditional scarcity?
answer: The 21-million-coin protocol cap and the energy-cost of mining new coins
choices: The 21-million-coin protocol cap and the energy-cost of mining new coins
The blockchain's transaction-history visibility
The Lightning Network's payment-channel scalability
The Taproot upgrade's privacy enhancements
context: Bitcoin's supply scarcity is mathematically guaranteed by the protocol. Gold's scarcity is physically guaranteed by geology and mining cost. Both have non-state issuance. The Ammous-Alden case treats Bitcoin as 'engineered gold' with better portability and verification but the same fundamental monetary function. Whether one accepts the case or not, the analogy is the central Bitcoin-as-money argument.

question: Bitcoin advocates argue that Bitcoin has certain monetary properties superior to gold. Which of the following is an actual advantage Bitcoin has over physical gold for monetary use?
answer: Portability: any amount can be moved globally with no special transport infrastructure
choices: Portability: any amount can be moved globally with no special transport infrastructure
Industrial demand: Bitcoin has more industrial uses than gold
Historical track record: Bitcoin has been monetary for longer than gold
Government acceptance: more central banks hold Bitcoin reserves than gold
context: Bitcoin's portability is its operational advantage over gold. The verification of authenticity is also fundamentally easier — Bitcoin is cryptographically verifiable in seconds; gold requires assay equipment. The 5000-year track record favors gold; the technological properties favor Bitcoin. Different optimization choices.

question: William Jennings Bryan's 1896 'Cross of Gold' speech won him the Democratic and Populist presidential nominations on a free-silver platform. He lost the general election to Republican William McKinley, who ran on the gold standard. What was the popular vote margin?
answer: Approximately 51% McKinley vs 47% Bryan — closer than the electoral margin
choices: Approximately 51% McKinley vs 47% Bryan — closer than the electoral margin
Approximately 70% McKinley vs 28% Bryan — a landslide
Approximately 49% Bryan vs 48% McKinley — Bryan won the popular vote
Approximately 45% Bryan vs 41% McKinley — a three-way race
context: McKinley won 51-47% in the popular vote (271-176 electoral votes). The 1896 election settled the gold-vs-silver question. The 1900 Gold Standard Act made gold legally official. Bryan ran twice more (1900, 1908) and lost both times. Free silver as a political force ended; the gold standard held until World War I.

question: Argentina has redenominated its currency multiple times since 1969 to lop zeros off depreciated bills. The sequence has been peso ley (1970), peso argentino (1983), austral (1985), peso convertible (1992), peso (2002). Each redenomination effectively wiped out trailing zeros. What is the cumulative redenomination factor since 1969?
answer: Roughly 10 trillion to one (10^13)
choices: Roughly 10 trillion to one (10^13)
Roughly 10 thousand to one
Roughly 10 million to one
Roughly 10 billion to one
context: Argentina's cumulative redenomination is around 10 trillion to one since 1969. Each redenomination is the political-economic moment when the state formally acknowledges its currency has been depreciated. The 2024 Milei program is trying to break the cycle through fiscal discipline rather than currency reform.

question: After the Soviet collapse, several former Soviet republics adopted currency boards or strict pegs as anti-inflation policy. The Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania) eventually joined the euro. Which Eastern European country adopted a particularly strict currency board in 1997 after a devastating banking crisis?
answer: Bulgaria, with a currency board pegging the lev to the German mark (later euro)
choices: Bulgaria, with a currency board pegging the lev to the German mark (later euro)
Russia, which never had a currency board
Ukraine, which had floating exchange rates
Belarus, which retained Soviet-style monetary policy
context: Bulgaria's 1997 currency board (under IMF pressure) followed hyperinflation that destroyed the lev's prior value. The lev was pegged at 1000 old lev = 1 new lev = 1 deutsche mark. The arrangement has held for over 25 years. Currency boards provide credibility by removing central-bank discretion — a 21st-century approximation of gold standard.

question: Between roughly 1965 and 1980, the US experienced sustained high inflation that became known as the Great Inflation. CPI inflation peaked at 13.5% in 1980 before Volcker broke it. What underlying combination of factors is typically blamed?
answer: Vietnam War spending, Great Society spending, oil shocks, and accommodative monetary policy under Burns
choices: Vietnam War spending, Great Society spending, oil shocks, and accommodative monetary policy under Burns
Sole responsibility of OPEC oil shocks with no monetary component
Tight monetary policy by the Federal Reserve through the period
The gold standard restricting monetary growth
context: The Great Inflation has multiple causes but central among them was accommodative monetary policy under Arthur Burns (Fed chair 1970-1978). Burns yielded to Nixon administration political pressure to keep rates low. Carter's appointment of Volcker (August 1979) was the inflection point. The episode shaped a generation of central-bank thinking about credibility.

question: Around 1908, after the Panic of 1907 in which JP Morgan personally rescued the US banking system from his library at 36th Street and Madison Avenue, Senator Nelson Aldrich of Rhode Island convened a secret meeting on a private island off the Georgia coast. The six attendees disguised themselves as duck hunters and operated under fake first-name-only protocol for ten days. What did they design?
answer: The blueprint for what became the Federal Reserve System (1913)
choices: The blueprint for what became the Federal Reserve System (1913)
The original Securities Exchange Act later passed in 1934
The Sherman Antitrust Act framework eventually passed 1890
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation design adopted 1933
context: Jekyll Island, November 1910. The Aldrich Plan was replaced by the politically more palatable Glass-Owen Bill (Federal Reserve Act) signed December 23, 1913 by Woodrow Wilson during the holiday session.

question: The November 1910 secret meeting at Jekyll Island, Georgia — convened by Senator Nelson Aldrich to design what became the Federal Reserve — had six attendees. They traveled to Aldrich's private rail car under first-name-only protocol. The names did not become public for over a decade. Which of these was NOT among the six?
answer: John D. Rockefeller Sr., who was not present
choices: John D. Rockefeller Sr., who was not present
Paul Warburg, the German-born investment banker
Frank Vanderlip, president of National City Bank
Henry Davison, JP Morgan partner
context: The six were: Senator Aldrich, Paul Warburg (Kuhn Loeb), Frank Vanderlip (National City Bank), Henry Davison (JP Morgan), Charles Norton (First National Bank), and A. Piatt Andrew (Treasury). The first revelation of names came in B.C. Forbes's 1916 magazine. Frank Vanderlip later confirmed the meeting in his 1935 autobiography. Mainstream historians acknowledge the meeting; Austrians treat it as evidence of insider design.

question: After the political process replaced the unpopular Aldrich Plan with the politically more palatable Glass-Owen Bill, Congress passed the Federal Reserve Act in late 1913. The bill became law during a holiday-season session that critics argued was designed to minimize public scrutiny. On what specific date was it signed?
answer: December 23, 1913, signed by President Woodrow Wilson
choices: December 23, 1913, signed by President Woodrow Wilson
April 5, 1933, signed by FDR
August 15, 1971, signed by Nixon
September 30, 1909, signed by Taft
context: December 23, 1913 — two days before Christmas, when Congress was sparsely attended. Wilson had campaigned on monetary reform; the timing was deliberate. The Fed opened operations November 16, 1914. Whether one regards the Fed as benign technocracy or insider capture depends largely on one's prior framework — but the specific historical timeline is well-established.

question: In 1791, against Thomas Jefferson's opposition, Treasury Secretary Alexander Hamilton successfully proposed a chartered central bank modeled on the Bank of England. The institution was chartered for 20 years and operated with mixed federal and private ownership. What was it called?
answer: The First Bank of the United States
choices: The First Bank of the United States
The Bank of New York, which Hamilton helped found earlier
The Federal Reserve, which is a much later 1913 institution
The Second Bank of the United States, chartered in 1816
context: The First Bank's charter expired in 1811 and Congress declined to renew. Hamilton-Jefferson dispute over the Bank was the first major American constitutional dispute over central banking. The Second Bank (1816-1836) followed; Andrew Jackson killed it. The Fed (1913) is the third major American central-banking experiment.

question: In 1832, President Andrew Jackson vetoed the recharter of the Second Bank of the United States and won re-election on the issue. Jackson then ordered Treasury deposits removed from the Bank and distributed to state-chartered 'pet banks'. The Bank's charter expired in 1836. What was Jackson's famous phrase characterizing the Bank?
answer: 'A den of vipers and thieves'
choices: 'A den of vipers and thieves'
'A pernicious aristocracy of money'
'A wicked invention of foreign powers'
'A tribute to the British Crown'
context: Jackson's bank war (1832-1836) is one of the founding political-economic battles in American history. His veto message attacked the Bank as an 'unconstitutional' privilege for the wealthy. The Whig Party formed in opposition. The destruction of the Second Bank arguably contributed to the Panic of 1837 — a debate that continues.

question: Between 1836 (when the Second Bank's charter expired) and 1862 (when the National Banking Act established federal bank regulation), American banking was characterized by state-chartered banks issuing their own currencies, with frequent bank failures and notes trading at varying discounts. What is this era often called?
answer: The Free Banking era (or 'Wildcat Banking' era)
choices: The Free Banking era (or 'Wildcat Banking' era)
The National Banking era, which is the period 1862-1913
The Federal Reserve era, which is 1913-present
The State Banking era, which is not the standard term
context: Free banking 1836-1862 has been heavily debated. Selgin and White argue the worst depictions are unfair; many state systems operated well. Rothbard argued the era was less stable than supporters claimed but more stable than Federal Reserve era. The 1862 National Banking Act standardized currency through federally chartered banks issuing greenbacks.

question: On March 6, 1933 — two days after taking office — President Franklin Roosevelt declared a four-day national bank holiday under the Trading With the Enemy Act of 1917. Banks were closed; gold withdrawals were suspended; new emergency banking legislation was prepared. What was the longer-term consequence on private gold ownership?
answer: Executive Order 6102 on April 5, 1933 prohibited private gold ownership above $100
choices: Executive Order 6102 on April 5, 1933 prohibited private gold ownership above $100
The Bretton Woods system replaced private gold ownership in 1944
The Gold Reserve Act of 1934 restored private gold ownership rights
Gold ownership remained unrestricted; only banking practices changed
context: The March 1933 bank holiday led directly to EO 6102 in April 1933 (gold confiscation) and the 1934 Gold Reserve Act (dollar devaluation to $35/oz). Private gold ownership remained illegal until 1975. The episode marked the most dramatic monetary regime change in US history outside of wartime.

question: In 1933, in response to the Great Depression, Congress passed legislation separating commercial banking from investment banking. The law also created federal deposit insurance. What was the legislation called?
answer: The Glass-Steagall Act (officially the Banking Act of 1933)
choices: The Glass-Steagall Act (officially the Banking Act of 1933)
The Federal Reserve Act, which is the 1913 legislation
The Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation Act, a partial element
The Securities Act, which is a separate 1933 law
context: Glass-Steagall separated commercial and investment banking for 66 years (1933-1999). The 1999 Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act effectively repealed the separation, allowing the formation of mega-banks like Citigroup. Some economists argue the repeal contributed to the 2008 crisis; others disagree. The repeal-vs-cause debate continues.

question: Federal deposit insurance was created as part of the 1933 banking reforms. The agency guarantees deposits up to a specified limit, replacing the panic-runs that had been a recurrent feature of American banking. What was the original limit and what is the current limit?
answer: $2,500 originally (1933); $250,000 currently (since 2008 crisis)
choices: $2,500 originally (1933); $250,000 currently (since 2008 crisis)
$1,000 originally; $100,000 currently
$25,000 originally; $2.5 million currently
$250 originally; $25,000 currently
context: FDIC insurance started at $2,500 in 1933, was raised multiple times, and reached $250,000 in 2008 (initially temporary, made permanent in 2010). The 2023 banking turmoil (Silicon Valley Bank) demonstrated that even $250K is below contemporary business deposit levels. The 2023 episode raised questions about whether the limit should be raised again.

question: In 1963, Milton Friedman and Anna Schwartz published a 900-page empirical history of US monetary policy from 1867 to 1960. Their argument about the Great Depression became influential: the Depression's severity was caused not by capitalism's instability but by a specific Fed failure. What was that failure?
answer: Allowing the M1 money supply to contract by roughly one-third between 1929 and 1933
choices: Allowing the M1 money supply to contract by roughly one-third between 1929 and 1933
Adopting unlimited quantitative easing without congressional authorization
Maintaining the gold standard rigidly through 1933
Cutting interest rates too aggressively in 1929
context: Friedman-Schwartz argued the Fed should have aggressively expanded credit during 1930-1933 to prevent the money-supply collapse. The argument shifted blame for the Depression from markets to monetary policy. Bernanke, a Depression scholar, took the argument very seriously — and as Fed chair in 2008-2014 acted on the lesson with aggressive QE.

question: At a November 8, 2002 conference celebrating Milton Friedman's 90th birthday, Federal Reserve Governor Ben Bernanke gave a speech publicly acknowledging the Friedman-Schwartz thesis about Fed responsibility for the Great Depression. What was the famous closing line of his speech?
answer: 'You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.'
choices: 'You're right, we did it. We're very sorry. But thanks to you, we won't do it again.'
'You're wrong, we did not cause it, but we have learned much from your work.'
'You're right, but the next crisis will be different.'
'You're right, and we now know exactly what to do.'
context: Bernanke's 2002 acknowledgment was a remarkable moment of institutional acknowledgment. Six years later, as Fed chair during the 2008 crisis, Bernanke acted on the Friedman-Schwartz lesson: QE1, QE2, QE3, and massive balance-sheet expansion to prevent monetary contraction. Whether this was the right response remains debated.

question: Federal Reserve Chairman Arthur Burns (1970-1978) presided over the worst peacetime inflation in modern US history. Inflation rose from 4% when he took office to 9% by 1978. Burns has been criticized for yielding to political pressure to keep rates low. Whose political pressure was most documented?
answer: President Richard Nixon's, particularly in the lead-up to the 1972 re-election
choices: President Richard Nixon's, particularly in the lead-up to the 1972 re-election
President Jimmy Carter's, who actually appointed Volcker to replace Burns
President Lyndon Johnson's, whose term predated Burns
President Gerald Ford's, who was more inflation-hawkish than Burns
context: Nixon's White House tapes captured explicit pressure on Burns to keep money loose for the 1972 re-election. The Burns Fed delivered. The subsequent inflation acceleration ran through Watergate, Vietnam end, oil shocks, and beyond. Carter's August 1979 appointment of Volcker was the inflection point. Burns is the canonical example of central-bank credibility loss to political pressure.

question: On August 6, 1979, President Jimmy Carter appointed Paul Volcker as Federal Reserve Chairman. Volcker's policy framework, announced in October 1979, targeted monetary aggregates rather than interest rates and tolerated the historic spike in rates that resulted. What was Volcker's specific monetary policy doctrine?
answer: Targeting M1 growth, allowing interest rates to find whatever level was consistent with the target
choices: Targeting M1 growth, allowing interest rates to find whatever level was consistent with the target
Targeting unemployment, with monetary expansion until target rates achieved
Targeting the dollar's gold price, restoring a quasi-gold standard
Targeting the Phillips curve sweet spot of inflation and unemployment
context: Volcker's October 1979 monetarist turn was inspired by Friedman's framework. The fed funds rate spiked above 19% in 1981; prime rate hit 21.5%. CPI inflation fell from 13.5% in 1980 to 4% by 1983. The recession was severe but inflation broke. The episode reset the credibility of US monetary policy for a generation.

question: Alan Greenspan served as Federal Reserve Chairman from 1987 to 2006 — the longest serving Fed chair until Powell. Bob Woodward called him 'Maestro' in a worshipful 2000 biography. By the time of the 2008 crisis, his reputation had collapsed. What did Greenspan tell Congress on October 23, 2008?
answer: That he had found 'a flaw in the ideology' that he had relied on for forty years
choices: That he had found 'a flaw in the ideology' that he had relied on for forty years
That the crisis was caused entirely by Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac
That the crisis was caused entirely by foreign capital flows
That the crisis was caused entirely by Bear Stearns
context: Greenspan's October 23, 2008 testimony was a remarkable public acknowledgment. The 'flaw' he identified was his belief that financial institutions would self-regulate prudently. Austrians had argued this for decades. The Greenspan era is now widely seen as having sowed seeds of 2008 through low rates 2001-2004 and laissez-faire regulation.

question: On September 15, 2008, after Treasury Secretary Henry Paulson and Federal Reserve Chairman Ben Bernanke declined to arrange a rescue or backstop, what was at the time the largest bankruptcy filing in US history was filed. What firm collapsed?
answer: Lehman Brothers, with $613 billion in assets
choices: Lehman Brothers, with $613 billion in assets
Bear Stearns, which had been rescued earlier in March 2008
Merrill Lynch, which was acquired by Bank of America
Citigroup, which received TARP support
context: Lehman's September 15, 2008 filing was the most dramatic moment of the 2008 crisis. The decision to let Lehman fail (versus rescue Bear Stearns six months earlier) remains controversial. AIG was rescued two days later; the financial system seized; TARP followed within weeks. The Lehman moment defined modern central-bank doctrine about being prepared to act.

question: On October 3, 2008, after a House defeat triggered a one-day market panic, Congress passed and President Bush signed the Emergency Economic Stabilization Act authorizing the Treasury to spend up to $700 billion to purchase troubled financial assets. The program was originally proposed by Treasury Secretary Paulson. What is the program commonly called?
answer: TARP (Troubled Asset Relief Program)
choices: TARP (Troubled Asset Relief Program)
ARRA (American Recovery and Reinvestment Act, the 2009 stimulus)
Dodd-Frank, which is regulatory reform legislation
Quantitative easing, which is monetary not fiscal
context: TARP $700B was passed in October 2008. Authorized for asset purchases, it was rapidly repurposed to inject capital directly into bank balance sheets. Roughly $440B was deployed; most was recovered with interest by 2014. Whether TARP saved the economy or just bailed out reckless lenders is the standard right-vs-left debate; both arguments have merit.

question: In September 2008, the largest insurance company in the United States required emergency federal intervention after its credit-default-swap portfolio collapsed. The Federal Reserve and Treasury combined to provide a rescue package eventually totaling roughly $182 billion. What was this company?
answer: AIG (American International Group)
choices: AIG (American International Group)
Berkshire Hathaway, which was actually a beneficiary
Travelers Insurance, which was not in crisis
Allstate, which was not in crisis
context: AIG's collapse on September 16, 2008 (day after Lehman) brought the financial system to its knees. AIG had written hundreds of billions in credit default swaps without adequate capital. The rescue passed value to its CDS counterparties (notably Goldman Sachs at par). The episode is exhibit A for moral-hazard concerns about Fed-Treasury bailouts.

question: Between 2008 and 2014, the Federal Reserve conducted three rounds of large-scale asset purchases, expanding its balance sheet from approximately $900 billion to $4.5 trillion. The programs are usually labeled by their sequence. What are they called?
answer: QE1, QE2, and QE3 (Quantitative Easing)
choices: QE1, QE2, and QE3 (Quantitative Easing)
Operation Twist, which is a separate maturity-extension program
Helicopter money, which has not been deployed by the Fed
Open Market Operations, which is the general term not specific to QE
context: QE1 (November 2008-March 2010, $1.4T); QE2 (November 2010-June 2011, $600B); QE3 (September 2012-October 2014, $1.6T). Plus Operation Twist (2011-2012). The Fed's balance sheet went from $900B to $4.5T. The 2022 post-COVID balance sheet peaked above $9T.

question: Between December 2008 and December 2015, the Federal Reserve held its target interest rate at 0 to 0.25 percent — a seven-year run of effectively zero interest rates. What is the standard term for this monetary regime?
answer: Zero Interest Rate Policy (ZIRP)
choices: Zero Interest Rate Policy (ZIRP)
Negative Interest Rate Policy (NIRP), which has been adopted in Europe and Japan
Open Market Policy, which is too generic
Yield Curve Control, which is a different policy
context: ZIRP 2008-2015 transformed asset markets. Pension funds and savers were starved; risk-taking was forced; asset prices inflated. Whether this was the right policy or a generational malinvestment is the textbook Austrian-vs-Keynesian debate. Bernanke's defense rests on the Friedman-Schwartz lesson; Austrians point to malinvestment that surfaced in 2022-2023 rate-shock losses.

question: In March 2020, the Federal Reserve deployed unprecedented emergency monetary and lending programs in response to the COVID pandemic, cutting rates to zero and announcing essentially unlimited QE within days. Roughly how much did the Fed's balance sheet expand in the first few months of the response?
answer: Roughly $3 trillion, from $4 trillion to $7 trillion between March and June 2020
choices: Roughly $3 trillion, from $4 trillion to $7 trillion between March and June 2020
Roughly $300 billion, from $4 trillion to $4.3 trillion
Roughly $30 billion, a minor adjustment
Roughly $30 trillion, an order of magnitude too large
context: March 2020's Fed response was the most aggressive monetary expansion in history. Within weeks the balance sheet went from $4.2T to over $7T. Direct purchases of corporate bonds occurred for the first time. The 2021-2023 inflation was the predictable consequence. Whether it was preventable or a price worth paying is the central monetary-policy debate of the decade.

question: In March 2020, the Federal Reserve announced for the first time in its history that it would purchase corporate bonds — both directly and through ETFs — using two emergency lending facilities created under the CARES Act. What were these facilities called?
answer: The Primary Market Corporate Credit Facility (PMCCF) and Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility (SMCCF)
choices: The Primary Market Corporate Credit Facility (PMCCF) and Secondary Market Corporate Credit Facility (SMCCF)
The Federal Open Market Committee operations
The discount window, which has long existed for banks
The repo facilities, which deal with overnight funding not corporate bonds
context: The PMCCF and SMCCF were unprecedented Fed expansions. The Fed bought BlackRock-managed corporate-bond ETFs. The implicit message was that the Fed would prevent corporate bankruptcies in a crisis. The moral-hazard implications are real. The facilities expired in 2020-2021 but the precedent — Fed support of corporate bond markets — was established.

question: Between March 2020 and April 2022, the Federal Reserve expanded its balance sheet from approximately $4 trillion to a peak. The size at peak was the largest in any central bank's history relative to its country's GDP outside of wartime. What was the approximate peak?
answer: Roughly $9 trillion (about 40% of US GDP)
choices: Roughly $9 trillion (about 40% of US GDP)
Roughly $5 trillion (about 25% of US GDP)
Roughly $15 trillion (about 70% of US GDP)
Roughly $30 trillion (about 140% of US GDP)
context: The $9 trillion peak (April 2022) represented an unprecedented experiment in monetary expansion. Subsequent quantitative tightening has reduced the balance sheet but not anywhere near pre-2020 levels. Whether this scale of intervention is the new normal or an emergency aberration is a defining question for monetary policy in the coming decade.

question: After the massive 2020-2021 monetary and fiscal expansion, US inflation began rising in early 2021 and accelerated through 2022. CPI inflation reached a 40-year peak. What was the peak month, and what was the rate?
answer: 9.1% in June 2022
choices: 9.1% in June 2022
5.0% in January 2022
15.0% in December 2022
2.0% in January 2022
context: 9.1% CPI in June 2022 was the highest reading since November 1981. Core PCE peaked at 5.6% in February 2022. The Powell Fed had labeled the early 2021 inflation 'transitory' through November 2021. The aggressive rate-hiking cycle began March 2022 — long after the inflation had taken hold. The episode damaged Fed credibility substantially.

question: Through most of 2021, Federal Reserve Chairman Jerome Powell described rising US inflation using a particular word. He retired the term in late November 2021. What was the word?
answer: 'Transitory'
choices: 'Transitory'
'Permanent'
'Embedded'
'Structural'
context: Powell's 'transitory' framing held from spring 2021 to November 30, 2021, when he explicitly retired the term in Senate testimony. By that point CPI was 6.8%. The Fed didn't begin raising rates until March 2022 with CPI already at 8.5%. The 'too slow to act' charge against Powell is the central Fed-critique of the post-COVID era.

question: From March 2022 through July 2023, the Federal Reserve raised the federal funds target rate from 0-0.25% to a peak that held through 2024 — the most aggressive hiking cycle since Volcker. What was the peak federal funds target range?
answer: 5.25% to 5.50% (with prime rate 8.5%)
choices: 5.25% to 5.50% (with prime rate 8.5%)
10.00% to 10.25% (no cycle reached this level)
2.50% to 2.75% (well below actual peak)
20.00% to 20.25% (Volcker-era level not reached again)
context: The Fed funds target peaked at 5.25-5.50% in July 2023 and held there through September 2024 before cutting. The cycle was rapid (11 hikes in 16 months) but did not reach Volcker-era levels of restriction. Inflation came down to roughly 3% by mid-2024 — slower than hoped but without the deep recession many had predicted.

question: Since the Federal Reserve Reform Act of 1977, the Federal Reserve has operated under a 'dual mandate' established by Congress. What two specific economic outcomes is the Fed obligated to pursue?
answer: Maximum employment and stable prices
choices: Maximum employment and stable prices
Maximum GDP and low taxes
Stable exchange rates and balanced budgets
Maximum bank profits and low interest rates
context: The 1977 dual mandate added employment to the long-standing price-stability mission. The 2% inflation target was adopted in January 2012 by the FOMC's revised statement. The two targets can conflict — the textbook Phillips-curve framework — but in practice the Fed has often treated them as compatible. The 2021-2023 inflation tested that assumption.

question: For over a decade, Senator Rand Paul (and previously Congressman Ron Paul) has championed legislation that would subject the Federal Reserve to comprehensive audit by the Government Accountability Office, removing current limitations on what GAO can examine. What is this legislation typically called?
answer: Audit the Fed (formally the Federal Reserve Transparency Act)
choices: Audit the Fed (formally the Federal Reserve Transparency Act)
Glass-Steagall, which is 1933 banking-separation legislation
Dodd-Frank, which is 2010 financial-regulation legislation
Sarbanes-Oxley, which is 2002 corporate-governance legislation
context: The GAO can currently audit the Fed's operational areas but not its monetary-policy decisions. Audit the Fed bills have passed the House multiple times but never overcome Senate filibuster. The Fed's institutional opposition to broader audit has been consistent across chairs. Whether one views this as appropriate independence or unaccountable power is a contested question.

question: In February 1936, the most influential English economist of the 20th century published a book whose title deliberately invoked Einstein's relativity work. The book reoriented academic economics around aggregate-demand management. Who wrote it and what was the title?
answer: John Maynard Keynes, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
choices: John Maynard Keynes, The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money
Alfred Marshall, Principles of Economics
Joan Robinson, The Economics of Imperfect Competition
Friedrich Hayek, The Pure Theory of Capital
context: Keynes 1936 became the most influential economics book of the 20th century. The 'general' adjective deliberately positioned the work as making the classical framework a special case. Critics — Hayek, Hazlitt, Pigou, Robertson — argued the book was empirically and theoretically inadequate. The Hicks IS-LM rendering (1937) became the textbook synthesis.

question: In Keynes's 1923 Tract on Monetary Reform, he wrote a famous response to classical economists who pointed to long-run equilibrium effects of monetary mismanagement. The quote has been used (often misleadingly) ever since to characterize Keynes's policy orientation. What did Keynes write?
answer: 'In the long run we are all dead'
choices: 'In the long run we are all dead'
'In the long run the market always wins'
'In the long run we are all rich'
'In the long run the past determines the future'
context: Keynes's 'in the long run we are all dead' was specifically about the inadequacy of classical economists who said monetary distortions self-correct over the long run. Critics (especially Austrians) have used it to characterize Keynesianism as short-term-fixated and irresponsible. The quote is often quoted without the immediate context.

question: In 1919, after attending the Versailles peace conference as a UK Treasury representative, John Maynard Keynes resigned in protest at the terms imposed on Germany and published a polemic predicting catastrophic consequences. The book made him internationally famous and is often cited as prophetic of the 1920s-1930s German trajectory. What was the title?
answer: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
choices: The Economic Consequences of the Peace
The General Theory of Employment, Interest and Money (his later major work)
A Tract on Monetary Reform (a different 1923 work)
How to Pay for the War (his 1940 essay)
context: Keynes's Economic Consequences of the Peace (1919) is a famous indictment of Versailles. The argument: punitive reparations would impoverish Germany without securing peace. The 1923 hyperinflation, 1929 collapse, and 1933 Nazi rise validated much of Keynes's prediction. The book established Keynes as a public intellectual of the highest rank, well before the General Theory.

question: In 1958, a New Zealand economist working at the LSE published an empirical paper showing a long-running statistical relationship between UK unemployment and nominal wage growth. The paper became the founding empirical citation for what later economists called the 'Phillips curve'. Who was the author?
answer: A.W. Phillips (Alban William Phillips)
choices: A.W. Phillips (Alban William Phillips)
Paul Samuelson, who later used Phillips's data
Robert Solow, who collaborated with Samuelson
Milton Friedman, who later attacked Phillips's interpretation
context: Phillips's 1958 paper covered UK data 1861-1957. The 'curve' showed an apparent inflation-unemployment tradeoff that became the central tool of 1960s Keynesian macroeconomics. Friedman 1968 ('The Role of Monetary Policy') predicted the relationship would break down in the long run — vindicated empirically by the 1970s stagflation.

question: In 1976, the Chicago economist Robert Lucas published a paper arguing that econometric policy evaluation based on historical correlations was fundamentally flawed because economic agents adjust their behavior in response to policy changes — invalidating the historical correlations as a guide to policy effects. What is this argument called?
answer: The Lucas Critique
choices: The Lucas Critique
The Volcker Doctrine
The Friedman Hypothesis
The Cochrane Conjecture
context: Lucas 1976 'Econometric Policy Evaluation: A Critique' transformed macroeconomic methodology. Rational expectations — the idea that agents anticipate and respond to systematic policy patterns — became central to subsequent macro modeling. Lucas won the Nobel in 1995. The Critique is foundational for the methodological turn in mainstream macro post-1970s.

question: In February 2009, the Obama administration's first major legislation was a $787 billion stimulus package combining tax cuts, transfer payments, and infrastructure spending. The package was justified using Keynesian multiplier estimates that subsequent CBO revisions and academic studies brought down substantially. What was the package called?
answer: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA)
choices: The American Recovery and Reinvestment Act (ARRA)
TARP, which was the prior 2008 financial-sector bailout
Dodd-Frank, which is regulatory legislation
Build Back Better, which was a later 2021 proposal
context: ARRA was the original 2009 Keynesian stimulus. The administration's economic team (Romer, Summers) projected unemployment would peak below 8% with the package; actual unemployment peaked at 10%. Multiplier estimates of 1.5-2.0 used to justify the package have been substantially revised down in subsequent academic work.

question: In February 2021, former Treasury Secretary Lawrence Summers published a Washington Post op-ed warning that the $1.9 trillion American Rescue Plan was too large given the US output gap and would likely produce inflation 'the likes of which we have not seen in a generation'. The warning was dismissed at the time. How did events vindicate Summers?
answer: Inflation rose from 1.4% in January 2021 to 9.1% by June 2022 — 'a generation' high
choices: Inflation rose from 1.4% in January 2021 to 9.1% by June 2022 — 'a generation' high
Inflation stayed below 2% throughout 2021-2022
Deflation occurred instead, vindicating Krugman not Summers
Stagflation occurred but unemployment also rose dramatically
context: Summers's February 2021 warning is one of the most vindicated economic predictions in recent memory. Krugman, Yellen, Powell, and others dismissed the warning. Within 18 months inflation had hit a 40-year high. The episode produced substantial damage to the credibility of post-2008 mainstream macroeconomic consensus.

question: In 2020, Bernie Sanders's former chief economist published a popular book arguing that sovereign currency issuers face no operational financing constraint, that taxes do not 'fund' government spending in the usual sense, and that inflation is the only meaningful constraint on government spending. Who is the author and what is the title?
answer: Stephanie Kelton, The Deficit Myth
choices: Stephanie Kelton, The Deficit Myth
Warren Mosler, Soft Currency Economics
L. Randall Wray, Understanding Modern Money
Bill Mitchell, Macroeconomics
context: Kelton 2020 is the most popular accessible statement of Modern Monetary Theory (MMT). The book reached the NYT bestseller list. MMT's central claim — that inflation is the operational constraint, not deficit financing — was tested almost immediately by the 2021-2023 inflation. Critics (Summers, Krugman, Cochrane, Sumner, Selgin) argue MMT was falsified; MMT advocates disagree.

question: Modern Monetary Theory's founder, the former hedge-fund manager Warren Mosler, published in 2010 a short manifesto laying out the MMT framework as a series of 'innocent frauds' — popular economic beliefs he argued were systematically misleading. What is the title?
answer: Seven Deadly Innocent Frauds of Economic Policy
choices: Seven Deadly Innocent Frauds of Economic Policy
The Deficit Myth, which is Kelton's 2020 book
Soft Currency Economics, his earlier 1996 paper
Understanding Modern Money, L. Randall Wray's 1998 book
context: Mosler's Seven Deadly Innocent Frauds is the canonical statement of MMT's policy implications. His seven 'frauds' are claims like 'governments must finance spending through taxation' that MMT argues are misleading for currency-issuing sovereigns. Whether MMT is a major theoretical contribution or a reframing of older Keynesian ideas remains contested.

question: Paul Krugman, the New York Times columnist and 2008 Nobel laureate, has made many high-profile macroeconomic predictions over the past two decades. His track record on the 2021-2023 inflation has been criticized. What was his characteristic position in 2021?
answer: Dismissed concerns about inflation as 'team transitory' through late 2021
choices: Dismissed concerns about inflation as 'team transitory' through late 2021
Predicted record inflation early in 2021 before consensus
Predicted record deflation throughout 2021-2022
Predicted stagflation but was substantially correct on timing
context: Krugman's 2021 'team transitory' framing has been characteristic of his post-2010 record. Earlier predictions on Trump-induced market crashes, Brexit consequences, Obama recovery speed, and others have also been substantially incorrect. The pattern raises questions about the academic-celebrity-economist class's epistemic discipline.

question: On September 17, 2019 — months before COVID — overnight repo rates in US dollar markets spiked from approximately 2% to over 10% in a single trading day. The Federal Reserve intervened with emergency lending, the first time in over a decade it had needed to do so for systemic plumbing reasons. What does this episode reveal about post-2008 financial structure?
answer: That US dollar funding markets had become structurally fragile despite years of regulatory reform
choices: That US dollar funding markets had become structurally fragile despite years of regulatory reform
That cryptocurrency had begun replacing dollar markets
That Chinese currency had begun displacing the dollar in funding
That repo markets functioned perfectly without need for Fed support
context: September 2019 was a warning that the Fed missed at the time. Within six months, COVID required even larger emergency intervention. The repo episode highlighted that post-2008 reforms had reduced bank balance-sheet capacity to intermediate funding markets, structurally requiring more Fed intervention. The Fed's standing repo facility (2021) is the institutional response.

question: Critics of the Federal Reserve and Treasury point to the pattern of personnel rotation between these institutions and major Wall Street firms (Goldman Sachs especially). Hank Paulson, Steven Mnuchin, Robert Rubin, and Jay Powell all share affiliations with both spheres. What is this pattern commonly called?
answer: The revolving door (between government and finance)
choices: The revolving door (between government and finance)
The Bretton Woods system, which is unrelated
The Mundell-Fleming trilemma, which is unrelated
The Phillips curve, which is unrelated
context: Revolving-door criticism is bipartisan. Public choice theorists (Buchanan, Tullock, Stigler) predicted such patterns. Regulatory capture (Stigler 1971) is the academic framework. Whether one views the revolving door as inevitable expertise circulation or as systematic capture is the central political-economic disagreement about modern financial regulation.

question: John Williams's ShadowStats website publishes alternative inflation calculations attempting to mirror the methodologies the US Bureau of Labor Statistics used in earlier decades, before various adjustments. ShadowStats's alternative inflation measures are systematically higher than official CPI. Roughly how much higher do they tend to run?
answer: Roughly 4-6 percentage points higher than official CPI in recent years
choices: Roughly 4-6 percentage points higher than official CPI in recent years
Roughly 0.1 percentage points higher than official CPI
Roughly identical to official CPI within margin of error
Roughly 50 percentage points higher than official CPI
context: ShadowStats's methodology and conclusions are contested by mainstream economists. The point isn't that ShadowStats is necessarily correct — but that the methodological choices in CPI construction are not innocent and matter substantially. Austrians have generally been sympathetic to skepticism about official inflation measurement. The truth is probably between the official and ShadowStats figures.

question: In 2009, Kenneth Rogoff (Harvard) and Carmen Reinhart (then Maryland) published a major empirical history of financial crises across centuries, arguing that the patterns are remarkably consistent and that the standard 'this time is different' justifications for excessive debt typically presage crisis. What was the title?
answer: This Time Is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly
choices: This Time Is Different: Eight Centuries of Financial Folly
End the Fed, by Ron Paul (a different polemic)
The Big Short, by Michael Lewis (a different crisis-era book)
Animal Spirits, by Akerlof and Shiller (a different crisis-era book)
context: Rogoff-Reinhart 2009 is one of the most empirically rich post-crisis economics books. The 90% debt-to-GDP threshold controversy (over a spreadsheet error in a 2010 paper) produced some embarrassment but the broader book stands. The cross-century pattern of financial-crisis history is real, however one wants to characterize the policy implications.
