context: Rothbard's two completed volumes (Economic Thought Before Adam Smith and Classical Economics) take pre-Smithian and 19th-century economic thought through an Austrian lens. The series might have been completed if Rothbard had lived. The volumes remain influential and provide alternative readings of figures (especially the Scholastics) often neglected by mainstream histories.

question: Roger Garrison's 2001 Time and Money presented Austrian Business Cycle Theory in a series of structural diagrams — production possibilities frontier, loanable funds market, Hayekian triangle — that finally gave ABCT the diagrammatic-pedagogical clarity it had lacked since 1931. What is this graphical framework called?
answer: Capital-based macroeconomics (or the 'Garrison diagrams')
choices: Capital-based macroeconomics (or the 'Garrison diagrams')
Goods-market-vs-money-market analysis (which is IS-LM)
Aggregate-supply-aggregate-demand analysis (which is AD-AS)
Real-business-cycle analysis (which is RBC)
context: Garrison's diagrams made ABCT teachable to undergraduates in a way Mises and Hayek had not achieved. The Hayekian triangle showing the time structure of production is the centerpiece. The diagrams render Austrian capital theory and business cycle theory comparable to mainstream macro frameworks — an important step toward broader acceptance.

question: Peter Boettke's 2001 book Calculation and Coordination collected essays applying Hayekian-Austrian analysis to a wide range of topics — Soviet economic history, the transition economies of post-communist Europe, comparative economic systems. What is the central organizing question of the book?
answer: How do market economies coordinate without central planning, and why does central planning fail?
choices: How do market economies coordinate without central planning, and why does central planning fail?
How do labor markets achieve full employment without government intervention?
How do financial markets price risk without regulatory oversight?
How do international trade flows balance without exchange rate adjustment?
context: Boettke 2001 represents the GMU-Hayekian Austrian wing's mature treatment of the calculation-and-knowledge problem. The book is partly a sustained critique of socialist calculation, partly an empirical examination of postcommunist transitions, partly a defense of Hayekian methodology. The Vienna-Lavoie-Boettke lineage is on full display.

question: In 1973, Murray Rothbard published a popular libertarian manifesto for general readers — an introduction to libertarian political philosophy applied to specific policy domains (education, welfare, foreign policy, criminal law). The book has been continuously in print. What is the title?
answer: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto
choices: For a New Liberty: The Libertarian Manifesto
Power and Market: Government and the Economy (his 1970 academic work)
Man, Economy, and State (his 1962 academic work)
The Ethics of Liberty (his 1982 academic work)
context: Rothbard's For a New Liberty is one of the most influential popular libertarian books ever written. The book applied Rothbardian principles to specific policy domains in accessible style. Combined with Atlas Shrugged (1957) and Free to Choose (1980), it forms part of the trio of 20th-century popular libertarian texts that reached mass audiences.

question: Ludwig von Mises's Human Action went through three substantially revised editions in Mises's lifetime — each incorporating his updated views on contemporary economic policy debates. The first edition was 1949; the second was 1963 (when he was 82). The third edition came in?
answer: 1966, the last major revision before his 1973 death
choices: 1966, the last major revision before his 1973 death
1959, an intermediate revision often missed
1972, the year before his death
1953, an intermediate revision often missed
context: Mises continued working on Human Action throughout the 1950s and 1960s. The 1966 third edition incorporates his latest thinking on inflation, central planning, and the rising fashion of Keynesianism. The book runs about 900 pages and integrates a complete deductive system from the action axiom through international economics.

question: In 1956, Ludwig von Mises published a slim essay analyzing why so many intellectuals despise free-market capitalism despite living comfortably from its products. He argued the resentment stems from intellectuals' positional anxiety in a market society that rewards entrepreneurs more than intellectuals. What was the title?
answer: The Anti-Capitalistic Mentality
choices: The Anti-Capitalistic Mentality
Bureaucracy (his 1944 book)
Planned Chaos (his 1947 essay)
Theory and History (his 1957 longer work)
context: Mises's Anti-Capitalistic Mentality is a polemical short read addressing a puzzle: why are intellectuals systematically hostile to market society when they live well from it? His answer — resentment of relative status — has analogs in Schumpeter, Hayek (The Intellectuals and Socialism), and many others. The framework remains relevant for understanding much contemporary intellectual culture.

question: In 1949, Friedrich Hayek published a famous essay analyzing how socialism captures intellectuals — the same puzzle Mises later addressed. Hayek argued intellectuals are 'secondhand dealers in ideas' who often adopt fashionable views without doing the underlying work to evaluate them. What was the essay's title?
answer: The Intellectuals and Socialism
choices: The Intellectuals and Socialism
Why I Am Not a Conservative, his later 1960 essay
Individualism: True and False, his 1945 essay
Economics and Knowledge, his 1937 presidential address
context: Hayek's Intellectuals and Socialism explains the intellectual class's persistent leftward bias through their position in the social-knowledge ecosystem. Intellectuals don't produce primary knowledge — they popularize and arrange what specialists produce. The work creates dependence on fashionable opinion. Hayek's analysis remains a powerful tool for understanding contemporary cultural dynamics.

question: In 1955, Friedrich Hayek published a methodological essay collection critiquing the rise of scientism in social science — the tendency to imitate physics by quantification, measurement, and prediction without recognizing the deep methodological differences between physical and social phenomena. What was the title?
answer: The Counter-Revolution of Science: Studies on the Abuse of Reason
choices: The Counter-Revolution of Science: Studies on the Abuse of Reason
The Sensory Order, his 1952 psychology book
The Constitution of Liberty, his 1960 political philosophy book
Law, Legislation and Liberty, his later 1973-1979 work
context: Hayek's Counter-Revolution of Science extends the Methodenstreit into 20th-century social science. The argument: social phenomena involve subjective meaning, dispersed knowledge, and emergent complexity that physical phenomena do not. Imitating physics through aggregation and statistical estimation has produced systematic policy errors. The book remains a fundamental statement of Austrian methodology.

question: Between 1950 and 1962, Friedrich Hayek held a position at the University of Chicago's Committee on Social Thought — a distinctive interdisciplinary unit that did not require him to teach economics in the standard sense. Why was he not in the Economics Department?
answer: The Economics Department refused to hire him, in part because of conservative discomfort with The Road to Serfdom
choices: The Economics Department refused to hire him, in part because of conservative discomfort with The Road to Serfdom
The Committee on Social Thought offered him a higher salary than the Economics Department
Hayek preferred interdisciplinary teaching to standard economics teaching
The Committee on Social Thought provided easier access to research funding
context: Hayek's Chicago appointment was made possible by the Volker Fund's support, since the Economics Department would not have him. The Committee on Social Thought (founded by John Nef in 1941) had been a refuge for interdisciplinary scholars. Hayek's Chicago years (1950-1962) produced The Constitution of Liberty and many essays.

question: In 1963, Murray Rothbard published a very short essay (around 100 pages) introducing Austrian monetary theory and arguing for the gold standard. The essay was originally a chapter excerpt from Man, Economy, and State and became Rothbard's most-distributed introduction to monetary economics. What is the title?
answer: What Has Government Done to Our Money
choices: What Has Government Done to Our Money
The Mystery of Banking (his longer 1983 work)
A History of Money and Banking in the United States (his posthumous work)
Mises and Hayek on Money and Banking (which is not the title)
context: Rothbard's What Has Government Done to Our Money has sold hundreds of thousands of copies and been translated into many languages. The text presents Austrian monetary theory in a brief, accessible form — making it the standard gateway for new readers. The current Mises Institute edition is freely available online; the print edition has gone through multiple printings.

question: Beginning in fall 1945 and continuing until 1969, Ludwig von Mises ran a graduate seminar at NYU that became the gathering place of American Austrian economics through the postwar period. The seminar met weekly during academic terms. Approximately how many students attended over the 24-year run?
answer: Hundreds of students attended over the years, including Rothbard, Kirzner, Sennholz, Salerno, and many others
choices: Hundreds of students attended over the years, including Rothbard, Kirzner, Sennholz, Salerno, and many others
Only a handful (fewer than ten) attended over the entire period
Thousands attended each year, like a typical large university lecture
The seminar was canceled in 1948 and never resumed
context: Mises's NYU seminar attracted students for 24 years. The list of attendees reads like a roll-call of postwar American Austrian economics. Murray Rothbard was the most prominent, but Israel Kirzner, Hans Sennholz, George Reisman, Ralph Raico, Joseph Salerno, and many others passed through. The seminar's institutional importance to Austrian economics is hard to overstate.

question: Ludwig von Mises's unpaid NYU faculty position from 1945 to 1969 was sustained by a small network of private donors who recognized that the Keynesian-dominated economics department would not have him. The most important early donor was a businessman who also funded the Foundation for Economic Education. Who was he?
answer: Lawrence Fertig (and the William Volker Fund also provided substantial support)
choices: Lawrence Fertig (and the William Volker Fund also provided substantial support)
John D. Rockefeller, who actually funded Keynesian-aligned economists
Andrew Carnegie, who died before Mises came to America
Henry Ford, who funded different causes
context: Lawrence Fertig and the William Volker Fund were the most important early sponsors. The arrangement that allowed Mises to continue teaching despite institutional hostility was a remarkable case of philanthropic preservation of a tradition that would otherwise have been suppressed. The Mises Institute later honored Fertig's role.

question: Leonard Read founded the Foundation for Economic Education in 1946, the same year that Henry Hazlitt published Economics in One Lesson. FEE has been continuously producing free-market educational materials since. Where is FEE located?
answer: Originally in Irvington-on-Hudson, NY (later moved to Atlanta, GA)
choices: Originally in Irvington-on-Hudson, NY (later moved to Atlanta, GA)
Manhattan, NY, where Mises was teaching
Auburn, AL, where the Mises Institute later moved
Washington, DC, where many think tanks are concentrated
context: FEE was for decades in Irvington-on-Hudson, a Hudson Valley village. The location was chosen partly for tranquility and partly to keep distance from political pressure. FEE published The Freeman magazine, organized seminars, and trained generations of free-market activists. Leonard Read's 1958 'I, Pencil' essay was a FEE production.

question: In 1955, Antony Fisher founded a London-based research institute to make Hayekian-Misesian classical-liberal ideas accessible to British policymakers and journalists. The institute became one of the most influential center-right policy organizations of the postwar era and shaped Margaret Thatcher's intellectual development. What is the institute called?
answer: The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA)
choices: The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA)
The Adam Smith Institute, which is a different and later London think tank
The Atlas Network, which is a different and later organization
The Mont Pelerin Society, which is the academic society Hayek founded
context: The IEA in London under Ralph Harris and Arthur Seldon was the institutional center of British free-market intellectual life in the 1960s-1970s. The IEA's publications shaped Thatcher's policy education. Antony Fisher later founded the Atlas Economic Research Foundation (Atlas Network) to replicate the model globally — with hundreds of think tanks now in the network.

question: In 1947, Friedrich Hayek convened a meeting of 38 classical-liberal intellectuals at a Swiss resort hotel to discuss how to preserve and reinvigorate the classical-liberal tradition in the postwar context. The resulting society has continued to meet annually for over 75 years. What was the founding location?
answer: Mont Pelerin, Switzerland (overlooking Lake Geneva)
choices: Mont Pelerin, Switzerland (overlooking Lake Geneva)
Lake Como, Italy
St Moritz, Switzerland
Davos, Switzerland (now associated with the World Economic Forum)
context: The Mont Pelerin Society's 1947 founding gathered Hayek, Mises, Friedman, Knight, Stigler, Polanyi, Popper, and dozens of others. The society's annual meetings continue to convene classical-liberal academics globally. Several Mont Pelerin presidents (Friedman, Buchanan, Coase, Vargas Llosa) have shaped public discourse far beyond academic economics.

question: In 1932, Lionel Robbins of the LSE published a famous methodological essay defining economics in subjectivist terms — as the study of human choice under scarcity, not the study of material wealth or specific resource categories. The essay made Robbins's reputation and provided Austrian-influenced methodological framework that influenced the subsequent decade. What is the essay's title?
answer: An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science
choices: An Essay on the Nature and Significance of Economic Science
An Essay on the Method of Economic Analysis
An Essay on the Theory of Economic Policy
An Essay on the Foundations of Welfare Economics
context: Robbins 1932 was the methodological essay that Hayek's 1932 LSE arrival reinforced. The definition — economics is the study of human action allocating scarce means with alternative uses — became the textbook standard for decades. The Austrian influence on Robbins via Mises and Hayek is well-documented. Robbins later softened his classical-liberal positions but the methodology persisted.

question: Alfred Schutz, an Austrian intellectual who attended both Mises's economics seminar and pursued phenomenological philosophy, developed a phenomenological foundation for the methodological subjectivism of Austrian economics — explaining how subjective meanings become intersubjectively shared. What was his most influential work?
answer: The Phenomenology of the Social World (Der sinnhafte Aufbau der sozialen Welt, 1932)
choices: The Phenomenology of the Social World (Der sinnhafte Aufbau der sozialen Welt, 1932)
The Crisis of European Sciences, which is Husserl's later work
Being and Time, which is Heidegger's work
The Theory of Communicative Action, which is Habermas's much later work
context: Schutz's bridge between phenomenology and economic methodology shaped Austrian thinking — most explicitly in Don Lavoie and Pete Boettke's hermeneutic-Austrian tradition. Schutz later emigrated to the US and taught at the New School in New York. His students included Peter Berger and Thomas Luckmann (The Social Construction of Reality 1966).

question: Don Lavoie's 1985 book Rivalry and Central Planning revisited the socialist calculation debate and argued that the late-1930s 'market socialist' responses (Lange, Lerner) had not actually solved the Misesian-Hayekian challenge — they had merely changed the subject. The book defended the Misesian conclusion. What is Lavoie's institutional legacy?
answer: He shaped the George Mason hermeneutic-Austrian tradition continued by Pete Boettke
choices: He shaped the George Mason hermeneutic-Austrian tradition continued by Pete Boettke
He shaped the Auburn Mises Institute praxeological tradition
He had no institutional legacy
He shaped the Chicago monetarist tradition
context: Lavoie's 1985 book updated the socialist calculation debate for late-20th-century audiences. His GMU position trained Boettke and others. His untimely 2001 death cut short a substantial career. The hermeneutic-Austrian tradition Lavoie advanced has been one of the more methodologically interesting strands of contemporary Austrian thought.

question: Israel Kirzner's entrepreneurial alertness framework was challenged by Misesian-Rothbardian Austrians who argued that alertness alone is too passive a description of what entrepreneurs do. The alternative emphasized that entrepreneurs exercise judgment under genuine uncertainty about future conditions. Who has developed this critique most fully?
answer: Peter Klein and Nicolai Foss in their work on entrepreneurial judgment
choices: Peter Klein and Nicolai Foss in their work on entrepreneurial judgment
Mark Skousen in his work on capital accumulation
Walter Block in his work on radical libertarianism
Murray Rothbard, posthumously through his unpublished papers
context: Klein and Foss's entrepreneurial judgment framework (Organizing Entrepreneurial Judgment 2012) extends Knight 1921 and Mises against the Kirznerian alertness focus. The two frameworks are not entirely incompatible but emphasize different aspects: Kirzner stresses arbitrage discovery; Klein-Foss stress capital deployment under uncertainty.

question: Steven Horwitz, a longtime Austrian economist at St Lawrence University (and later Ball State), spent his career making Austrian macroeconomic theory tractable in microeconomic foundations — including the Garrison-style capital-based macro framework. What is his best-known book?
answer: Microfoundations and Macroeconomics: An Austrian Perspective (2000)
choices: Microfoundations and Macroeconomics: An Austrian Perspective (2000)
Hayek's Modern Family (his 2015 book on family economics)
Macroeconomics for Engineers (which is not a real title)
The Austrian School: Market Order and Entrepreneurial Creativity (which is Huerta de Soto's title)
context: Horwitz 2000 made Austrian macroeconomic claims comparable to mainstream macro frameworks. Horwitz died in June 2021 at age 57 — a major loss to the Austrian academic community. His work was particularly important in extending the GMU-Hayekian Austrian tradition into rigorous microfoundations.

question: Bitcoin's first halving event occurred on November 28, 2012, when block 210,000 was mined and the block subsidy dropped from its original level. What did the subsidy become?
answer: 25 BTC per block (down from 50)

12.5 BTC per block, which is the post-2016 amount
6.25 BTC per block, which is the post-2020 amount
100 BTC per block, doubling instead of halving

The 2016 halving brought BTC to roughly $700; the 2020 to roughly $9,000; the 2024 to roughly $63,000. The halving pattern continues to be one of the most predictable monetary events in history.

question: Bitcoin's second halving occurred on July 9, 2016, when block 420,000 was mined. What did the block subsidy drop to?
answer: 12.5 BTC per block (down from 25)

25 BTC per block, which was the pre-halving rate
6.25 BTC per block, which is the post-2020 amount
50 BTC per block, the original rate

The halving's role in the price cycle is endlessly debated — supply reduction is real but timing of price effects varies. The third (2020) and fourth (2024) halvings continued the pattern.

question: Bitcoin's third halving occurred on May 11, 2020, when block 630,000 was mined. The block subsidy dropped to what level?
answer: 6.25 BTC per block (down from 12.5)

12.5 BTC per block, the pre-halving rate
3.125 BTC per block, which is the post-2024 amount
25 BTC per block, going backward
context: The 2020 halving came two months into the COVID pandemic, with the Fed's emergency monetary expansion just beginning. BTC was around $8,500 at the halving and rose to $69,000 by November 2021. The macro context — unprecedented monetary expansion — made the halving's supply-discipline argument particularly resonant.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto's true identity has been the subject of intense speculation for over a decade. Various journalists and researchers have proposed candidates. Which of these has been most thoroughly investigated and remains a prime candidate?

Newsweek's Dorian Nakamoto story (March 2014) appears to have been wrong. Craig Wright's claims have been judicially rejected. The Satoshi puzzle is one of the great unsolved mysteries of modern technology.

question: Craig Wright, an Australian computer scientist, has publicly claimed for years to be Satoshi Nakamoto. In 2024, a UK court ruled definitively on the question after a long civil trial. What did the court conclude?
answer: Wright is not Satoshi Nakamoto; the evidence presented was fabricated or forged

Multiple forged documents and contradictions in Wright's narrative were identified. The case ended what had been a decade of Wright-as-Satoshi claims, though Wright himself has not accepted the verdict.

question: After Hanyecz's 2010 pizza purchase, Bitcoin slowly developed a market price tracked across the early exchanges. In what month did BTC first trade at parity with the US dollar?
answer: February 2011 (BTC first exceeded $1 on February 9, 2011)

May 2010, simultaneous with the pizza day
January 2010, much earlier than actually
December 2013, when BTC actually hit $1000

By June 2011 BTC had spiked to $32 before crashing. The volatility from the earliest days of Bitcoin price discovery has been a defining feature of the asset.

question: From February 2011 to October 2013, an online marketplace operating on the Tor network used Bitcoin as its primary payment method for drugs, contraband, and various restricted goods. The marketplace's existence drove significant early Bitcoin adoption and brought the technology to FBI attention. What was it called?
answer: The Silk Road (run by Ross Ulbricht as 'Dread Pirate Roberts')

The Silk Road's role in early Bitcoin adoption is complex: it provided real-world use cases but also branded Bitcoin with crime associations that took years to fade.

question: Ross Ulbricht, the founder of the Silk Road, operated the marketplace under a pseudonym borrowed from a famous novel and 1987 film. What was the pseudonym?
answer: Dread Pirate Roberts (from The Princess Bride)

Tyler Durden (from Fight Club)
Hal Jordan (from Green Lantern)
Walter White (from Breaking Bad)

The novel's running joke — that the Dread Pirate Roberts is a transferable identity, not a single person — is a clever literary reference to the cypherpunk philosophy of anonymous identity. The October 2013 arrest at a San Francisco public library while logged into Silk Road as administrator ended the cleverness.

question: Bitcoin first crossed $1,000 in late November 2013, during a frenzied bull run that took BTC from below $200 in October to a December peak around $1,150. What contributed to the run?
answer: Senate Banking Committee testimony from FBI and other officials acknowledging Bitcoin had legitimate uses
choices: Senate Banking Committee testimony from FBI and other officials acknowledging Bitcoin had legitimate uses
El Salvador's adoption of Bitcoin as legal tender, which was actually in 2021
Approval of a Bitcoin ETF by the SEC, which actually came in 2024
MicroStrategy's purchases of Bitcoin for treasury, which actually began in 2020
context: The November 18, 2013 Senate hearings on virtual currencies (with Ben Bernanke's letter acknowledging legitimate uses) helped legitimize Bitcoin and contributed to the late-2013 spike. The peak was followed by a multi-year bear market — BTC didn't reclaim the $1000 level until early 2017.

question: When Mt. Gox collapsed in February 2014, the exchange had been handling roughly what fraction of global Bitcoin trading volume at its peak?
answer: Roughly 70% of all Bitcoin trading volume by 2013-early 2014
choices: Roughly 70% of all Bitcoin trading volume by 2013-early 2014
Roughly 5% of all Bitcoin trading volume
Roughly 100% — Mt. Gox was the only exchange operating
Roughly 0.1% — Mt. Gox was a minor exchange
context: Mt. Gox's dominance of global Bitcoin trading at peak made its February 2014 collapse a near-existential moment for Bitcoin. The 850,000 BTC lost was equivalent to roughly 7% of all bitcoin in existence at the time. The bankruptcy proceedings continued for a decade. Distributions to creditors began in 2024 — long after most assumed the funds were permanently lost.

question: On August 1, 2017, the Bitcoin blockchain experienced a contentious 'hard fork' — splitting into two separate chains. The faction favoring larger block sizes created a new chain. What was this fork called?
answer: Bitcoin Cash (BCH), at block 478,558
choices: Bitcoin Cash (BCH), at block 478,558
Bitcoin Gold (BTG), which is a different and later fork
Bitcoin SV (BSV), which is a 2018 fork of Bitcoin Cash
Litecoin (LTC), which is an unrelated separate cryptocurrency

The market overwhelmingly preferred Bitcoin (with SegWit and Lightning) over Bitcoin Cash (with bigger blocks). By 2024, BCH traded at roughly 1-2% of BTC's value.

question: In November 2018, Bitcoin Cash itself underwent a contentious split. One faction — led by Craig Wright and Calvin Ayre — favored even larger block sizes and a return to 'original Satoshi vision'. What was the new fork called?
answer: Bitcoin SV (Satoshi's Vision)

Bitcoin Gold, which is a different earlier 2017 fork
Bitcoin Diamond, which is a different earlier 2017 fork
Bitcoin Plus, which is not a major fork

BSV by 2024 trades at a tiny fraction of BTC. The successive forks (BCH 2017, BSV 2018) successively rejected market consensus and successively lost market value — vindicating the small-blocker camp.

question: The Lightning Network was first formally described in a January 2016 white paper by two cryptographic engineers who proposed using payment channels to scale Bitcoin off-chain. Who were the authors?
answer: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja

Hal Finney and Wei Dai
Nick Szabo and Adam Back
Vitalik Buterin and Charles Hoskinson (who actually worked on Ethereum)
context: Poon-Dryja 2016 white paper laid out Lightning's architecture: bilateral payment channels secured by hashed time-locked contracts (HTLCs). Mainnet launch came in January 2018. The Lightning Network has grown to handle millions of transactions monthly. The success has validated Bitcoin's layered architecture: a settlement layer plus payment layer.

question: In May-June 2021, the Chinese government announced major restrictions on Bitcoin mining. Mining facilities in Sichuan, Xinjiang, and Inner Mongolia ceased operations within weeks. Global Bitcoin hashpower dropped by roughly half before rapidly recovering. Where did most of the displaced mining operations relocate?
answer: Primarily Texas (USA), with significant amounts to Kazakhstan and Russia
choices: Primarily Texas (USA), with significant amounts to Kazakhstan and Russia

Texas's combination of cheap stranded energy, supportive politicians, and grid-balancing role became the new mining capital. The episode demonstrated Bitcoin's resilience: a 50% hashpower drop was fully recovered within months as miners relocated. The network kept producing blocks throughout.

question: Texas has become the largest US state for Bitcoin mining, with miners playing a particular role in the state's deregulated electricity grid. What grid function do Texas Bitcoin miners commonly perform?
answer: Demand response: powering down during peak grid demand and getting paid for grid stability
choices: Demand response: powering down during peak grid demand and getting paid for grid stability
Frequency regulation: directly providing grid frequency control services
Voltage regulation: directly providing voltage control to the grid
Spinning reserve: providing rotating mass for grid inertia
context: Texas's deregulated ERCOT grid pays Bitcoin miners to power down during peak demand. The economic logic: miners are uniquely flexible loads that can ramp down without harming production processes. During the February 2021 winter storm, Texas miners shut down and helped grid stability. The model has been controversial but operationally important for ERCOT.

question: Iceland was an early Bitcoin mining destination due to specific natural endowments. What combination of factors made Iceland an attractive early mining location?
answer: Abundant geothermal and hydroelectric energy plus naturally cold climate for cooling
choices: Abundant geothermal and hydroelectric energy plus naturally cold climate for cooling
Cheap coal-fired electricity
Subsidies from the Icelandic government targeting Bitcoin specifically
Tax exemptions exclusive to cryptocurrency mining
context: Iceland's geothermal-and-hydro grid produces some of the world's cleanest electricity per kWh, and its cold climate reduces cooling costs. The country became a mid-2010s mining hub. As mining has scaled globally, Iceland's relative share has shrunk — but the country remains an example of how renewable-rich regions can host Bitcoin mining sustainably.

question: Norway has hosted significant Bitcoin mining operations, taking advantage of the country's near-100% renewable electricity grid. What is the primary source of Norway's electricity?
answer: Hydroelectric power (over 90% of Norwegian electricity)
choices: Hydroelectric power (over 90% of Norwegian electricity)
Coal-fired power, which Norway phased out decades ago
Nuclear power, which Norway has not pursued
Wind power, which is significant but secondary to hydroelectric
context: Norway's hydroelectric grid (with significant wind addition) makes it one of the cleanest electricity sources in the world. Norwegian Bitcoin mining is largely hydroelectric. Critics arguing Bitcoin mining is environmentally harmful typically ignore the specific energy sources powering mining — Bitcoin miners chase cheap energy, and cheap energy is increasingly renewable.

question: When El Salvador adopted Bitcoin as legal tender in September 2021, the government launched a native wallet for citizens to receive an initial Bitcoin distribution and conduct everyday transactions. What is this wallet called?

choices: Chivo (Spanish slang for 'cool' or 'awesome')

context: Chivo's launch was rocky: the wallet had multiple outages, identity-theft concerns, and adoption challenges. Each adult Salvadoran citizen received $30 in BTC. The volcano bond — supposedly backed by Salvadoran geothermal Bitcoin mining — was promised but not delivered as of 2024. Whether El Salvador's experiment ultimately succeeds remains a live question.

question: President Bukele of El Salvador proposed in late 2021 issuing a sovereign bond partially backed by Bitcoin and funded partly through geothermal-powered Bitcoin mining at a volcano. The bond was supposed to launch in 2022 but has been repeatedly delayed. What is the proposal called?
answer: The Bitcoin Volcano Bond (formally the 'Volcano Bond')
choices: The Bitcoin Volcano Bond (formally the 'Volcano Bond')

The Bukele Bond, which is not the actual name
The Geothermal Mining Bond, which is not the actual name
context: The Volcano Bond's repeated delays reflect skepticism about the underlying economics. Salvadoran geothermal mining capacity is limited. The bond's collateralization mechanism is unclear. Whatever one thinks of the broader Bitcoin-legal-tender experiment, the Volcano Bond has been more performance than substance through 2024.

question: In February 2024, El Salvadoran President Nayib Bukele won re-election in a landslide despite constitutional concerns about whether consecutive terms were permissible. What was his approximate vote share?

question: Following the October 2013 takedown of the Silk Road, US federal authorities seized large quantities of Bitcoin from the marketplace's hot wallets. question: Caroline Ellison was the CEO of Alameda Research at the time of its November 2022 collapse alongside FTX. After cooperating with federal prosecutors against Sam Bankman-Fried, she was sentenced in September 2024. What was her sentence?

question: Sam Bankman-Fried was a high-profile donor to the effective altruism movement, having pledged to give away most of his fortune. question: Among the largest US asset managers, one major firm pointedly refused to either offer its own spot Bitcoin ETF or to make competing ETFs available on its brokerage platform when they launched in January 2024. Which firm took this stance?

Vanguard's institutional culture and Jack Bogle's known views on Bitcoin (he warned against it in 2017) likely played a role. The position will be reviewed but as of 2024 stands.

question: In February 2021, Tesla announced it had purchased $1.5 billion in Bitcoin for its treasury — making it the second major public-company Bitcoin treasury after MicroStrategy. Tesla later sold most of its Bitcoin treasury. The episode marked a high point of environmental criticism of Bitcoin mining. Subsequent analysis (energy mix, methodology) has substantially rehabilitated Bitcoin's environmental profile, but the May 2021 reversal stands.

question: Jack Dorsey's Block (formerly Square) was another early corporate-treasury Bitcoin adopter, with significant purchases beginning in 2020. Dorsey has been one of the most vocal Bitcoin advocates among Silicon Valley CEOs. What does Block's main consumer Bitcoin product do?

Dorsey's vision: a Bitcoin-denominated everyday financial system.

question: The 2017 Bitcoin bull run took BTC from below $1,000 in January to a December peak. What was the approximate peak price reached in mid-December 2017?

The subsequent 2018 bear market took BTC to roughly $3,200 by year-end — an 84% drawdown. The pattern (bull run, mania, deep correction, multi-year accumulation) has repeated through 2024.

question: Bitcoin reached its all-time high of late 2021 in November of that year — alongside peak NFT mania, the SBF/FTX celebrity tour, and broad crypto-cycle frenzy. What was the November 2021 peak price?

question: In late January 2023, software developer Casey Rodarmor activated a protocol on Bitcoin mainnet that enabled inscribing arbitrary data (images, text, video) directly onto individual satoshis. The protocol generated controversy within the Bitcoin community over whether it was legitimate use of block space. What is this protocol called?
answer: Ordinals (or specifically the 'Ordinal Theory' of satoshi-tracking)
choices: Ordinals (or specifically the 'Ordinal Theory' of satoshi-tracking)
Counterparty, which is a different and much older protocol
Stamps (SRC-20), which is a different and later protocol
Liquid, which is a Bitcoin sidechain not an inscription protocol
context: Ordinals launched January 2023 and immediately split Bitcoin opinion. Inscriptions drove transaction fees up. Supporters: legitimate use case. Detractors: spam clogging the mempool. By 2024, the controversy had partially resolved — ordinals are part of Bitcoin's reality even if many Bitcoiners find them aesthetically displeasing. Miner revenue benefited substantially.

question: Following the Ordinals launch in January 2023, developers created token standards using Ordinals to represent fungible tokens on Bitcoin. What is the most-used such standard called?

choices: BRC-20 (Bitcoin Request for Comment 20)

context: BRC-20 tokens use Ordinal inscriptions to track fungible-token states on Bitcoin. The standard has been heavily criticized by Bitcoin developers for inefficiency but used by enthusiasts. Whether BRC-20 represents the future or a passing speculation remains contested. The deeper question: should Bitcoin host non-monetary token systems? Different answers from different camps.

question: In 2023, the Lightning Labs team announced a protocol enabling Lightning Network channels to carry assets other than Bitcoin — including stablecoins. The protocol uses Taproot upgrades for this functionality. What is it called?

Whether stablecoins on Lightning gain real adoption remains to be seen. The protocol is one of several Bitcoin-layer developments attempting to add functionality without compromising base-layer security.

question: RSK (Rootstock) is a Bitcoin sidechain that launched in 2018, aiming to bring Ethereum-style smart contract functionality to Bitcoin via a federated peg. What is RSK's relationship to Bitcoin mining?
answer: RSK uses merged mining, allowing Bitcoin miners to simultaneously mine RSK blocks without additional energy cost
choices: RSK uses merged mining, allowing Bitcoin miners to simultaneously mine RSK blocks without additional energy cost
RSK is mined entirely separately with its own proof-of-stake mechanism
RSK is mined exclusively by RSK Labs employees
RSK uses proof-of-history instead of proof-of-work
context: RSK's merged mining means Bitcoin miners can mine RSK blocks 'for free' by including RSK's merkle root in their Bitcoin block templates. The architecture provides security but means RSK's security is parasitic on Bitcoin's. The federated peg has been criticized as centralizing. RSK has technical merit but limited adoption — like many Bitcoin sidechain proposals.

question: After the June 2016 DAO hack drained roughly $50 million worth of ether from a flagship Ethereum smart contract, the Ethereum community faced a choice. The decision they made fundamentally distinguished Ethereum from Bitcoin's 'code is law' commitment. What did they choose?

context: The Ethereum hard fork in July 2016 was the foundational moment distinguishing the project from Bitcoin's immutability commitment. The minority chain that refused the fork survives as Ethereum Classic. Bitcoiners frequently cite the DAO fork as evidence that Ethereum's governance is fundamentally different from Bitcoin's — for better or worse.

question: On September 15, 2022, Ethereum completed its transition from proof-of-work consensus (like Bitcoin) to proof-of-stake consensus. The event had been long-anticipated under the codename 'The Merge'. What was the most-cited justification for the transition?
answer: Energy consumption reduction (estimated 99.9% reduction)

Lower transaction fees (which the Merge did not directly produce)
Faster transaction throughput (which the Merge did not directly produce)
More decentralized network (which the Merge did not directly produce)
context: The September 2022 Merge reduced Ethereum's energy consumption dramatically. Other claimed benefits (lower fees, faster speeds, more decentralization) were either not delivered or were arguably reduced. The proof-of-stake mechanism introduces capital-lockup centralization concerns that proof-of-work avoids. The Bitcoin-vs-Ethereum design philosophical split widened with the Merge.

question: The August 2022 sanctions on the Tornado Cash smart contract were followed in 2023 by criminal charges against the smart contract's developers — not the users, but the people who wrote the open-source code. Whose case is the most prominent?

question: Various analytical efforts have attempted to estimate the size of Satoshi Nakamoto's bitcoin holdings — never moved since mining. The most widely-cited estimate comes from analysis of the 'Patoshi pattern' in early block nonce distributions. What is the approximate Patoshi estimate?

question: October 31 is informally celebrated in the Bitcoin community as the anniversary of Satoshi Nakamoto's release of the Bitcoin white paper in 2008. The day is sometimes called 'Bitcoin Whitepaper Day' or by another name. What event in Bitcoin culture coincides with this date?

question: Trace Mayer, an early Bitcoin advocate, popularized in 2019 the practice of withdrawing Bitcoin from exchanges on a particular date each year as a demonstration that holders rather than custodians control their coins. What is this annual event called?

context: Proof of Keys on January 3 reminds holders annually to test whether their exchange-held bitcoin can actually be withdrawn. The principle: an exchange that can't process your withdrawal doesn't actually hold your bitcoin. The 2022 collapses (Celsius, FTX) demonstrated the principle's importance. Trace Mayer's contribution to Bitcoin culture extends to this annual reminder.

question: After FDR's April 1933 gold confiscation, the Treasury then formally devalued the dollar against gold. What was the new official gold price, and what was the percentage devaluation from the pre-1933 level?
answer: $35 per troy ounce — a 41% devaluation from the previous $20.67
choices: $35 per troy ounce — a 41% devaluation from the previous $20.67
$20 per troy ounce — no devaluation
$100 per troy ounce — a much larger devaluation
$50 per troy ounce — a different percentage
context: The $20.67-to-$35 devaluation came in January 1934. Citizens who had complied with EO 6102 received the old $20.67 price; the Treasury captured the difference. The episode is the founding modern case of US monetary confiscation. The new $35 price held through the Bretton Woods era until Nixon's August 1971 closure of the gold window.

question: Private US gold ownership remained illegal under EO 6102 (1933) for over four decades. The legal restriction was finally lifted under what president and in what year?
answer: Gerald Ford in December 1974 (effective January 1, 1975)
choices: Gerald Ford in December 1974 (effective January 1, 1975)
Richard Nixon in August 1971 (alongside the gold window closure)
Ronald Reagan in 1981 (after taking office)
Jimmy Carter in 1977 (after taking office)
context: Ford's December 31, 1974 effective-1975 restoration of private gold ownership was a quiet but significant moment. The 1933 confiscation had become anachronistic since the 1971 gold window closure made the prohibition pointless. American Eagle gold coins now sold at US Mint shops have no historical analog before 1975 — gold ownership had been illegal for the prior 42 years.

question: At the absolute peak of the Weimar German hyperinflation in November 1923, the official exchange rate against the US dollar reached an astronomical level. Approximately what was the rate?
answer: Roughly 4.2 trillion marks per US dollar
choices: Roughly 4.2 trillion marks per US dollar
Roughly 42 marks per US dollar (the postwar pre-hyperinflation level)
Roughly 4,200 marks per US dollar
Roughly 420 trillion marks per US dollar
context: 4.2 trillion marks per dollar — November 1923, the absolute peak. The Rentenmark introduction at that point traded at 1 trillion paper marks = 1 Rentenmark = 1 reichsmark = the old pre-WWI mark. The fixed rate held; the Reichsbank credibly committed to stop printing. The German economic recovery 1924-1929 followed before the broader European collapse in 1929-1933.

question: At the peak of Hungary's 1946 hyperinflation — the worst in recorded history — daily inflation reached truly extraordinary levels. What was the price-doubling time at the peak?
answer: Approximately 15 hours (the worst price-doubling time ever recorded)
choices: Approximately 15 hours (the worst price-doubling time ever recorded)
Approximately 15 minutes (which would actually be impossibly fast)
Approximately 15 days (which is roughly Weimar-era pace)
Approximately 15 months (which would be modest inflation)
context: Hungary 1946: 207% daily inflation at peak. The monthly inflation rate exceeded 13.6 quadrillion percent. The August 1946 forint introduction stabilized matters with a 4 x 10^29 pengo to 1 forint exchange — currency reform on an unprecedented scale. The Hungarian episode remains the worst hyperinflation ever recorded — though Zimbabwe 2008 came close in some metrics.

question: In 1985, Argentina under President Raul Alfonsin attempted a major currency reform to break out of accelerating inflation. The new currency replaced the peso argentino at 1,000:1. What was the new currency called?
answer: The austral (running 1985-1991)
choices: The austral (running 1985-1991)
The peso convertible (which was the later 1992-2001 currency)
The peso (which is the current currency since 1992)
The peso ley (which was the earlier currency)
context: The austral was Argentina's third major postwar currency reform. It failed: by 1989-1990 the austral itself was in hyperinflation, with monthly rates exceeding 100%. The 1991 convertibility plan (peso pegged to dollar 1:1) replaced the austral. The convertibility plan itself collapsed in 2001-2002, leading to the modern peso. Each currency chapter in Argentina has been a chapter of monetary failure.

question: In December 2001, after a decade of Argentine convertibility plan (1991-2001) tying the peso 1:1 to the US dollar, the system collapsed. The government imposed restrictions on bank withdrawals that locked depositors out of their savings. What was this restriction called?
answer: El corralito ('the little corral')
choices: El corralito ('the little corral')
El corralon, which is a different policy
La cacerolazo, which refers to protest pot-banging
La devaluacion, which is the broader currency event
context: The corralito (December 1, 2001) restricted weekly withdrawals to 250 pesos. The collapse of the convertibility plan, default on $93B in sovereign debt (largest to that point), bank-account freezes, and a wave of unemployment created Argentina's worst peacetime economic crisis. Five presidents in two weeks. The trauma remains alive in Argentine politics.

question: Venezuela has redenominated its currency three times during the Chavismo-era hyperinflation. The current bolivar soberano (introduced August 2018) was followed by the bolivar digital (October 2021) — and each redenomination lopped zeros off the previous. What is the cumulative redenomination factor since the bolivar fuerte (2008)?
answer: Roughly 100 trillion to one (10^14)
choices: Roughly 100 trillion to one (10^14)
Roughly 1000 to one (10^3)
Roughly 1 million to one (10^6)
Roughly 100 billion to one (10^11)
context: Venezuela's bolivar fuerte (2008) cut three zeros from the prior bolivar. The bolivar soberano (2018) cut five more. The bolivar digital (2021) cut six more. Cumulative: 10^14 — comparable to Argentine cumulative redenominations. Each redenomination is a formal political acknowledgment that the currency has been destroyed. The currency redenominations are essentially state confessions of monetary failure.

question: Between roughly 2008 and 2019, Lebanon's central bank (Banque du Liban under Riad Salameh) operated a complex 'financial engineering' system that critics later described as Ponzi-like. The system channeled new dollar deposits to pay off earlier ones. When did it collapse?
answer: Late 2019, with a banking crisis and informal capital controls
choices: Late 2019, with a banking crisis and informal capital controls
2008, alongside the global financial crisis
2022, alongside global inflation
1990, alongside the end of the civil war
context: Lebanon's October 2019 protests and subsequent banking failure unfolded as the BDL scheme collapsed. The lebanese pound lost over 98% of its dollar value over the following four years. Depositors lost most of their savings. Salameh was indicted in multiple jurisdictions. The case is among the worst peacetime monetary catastrophes in modern history.

question: By mid-2024, the Turkish lira had depreciated against the US dollar from approximately 4 lira per dollar at the start of 2018 to approximately what rate?
answer: Approximately 32 lira per dollar (87% depreciation against the dollar)
choices: Approximately 32 lira per dollar (87% depreciation against the dollar)
Approximately 4 lira per dollar (no depreciation)
Approximately 100 lira per dollar (more severe depreciation than actual)
Approximately 0.4 lira per dollar (which would be appreciation)
context: The lira's 2018-2024 depreciation reflects President Erdogan's unorthodox monetary policy combined with chronic inflation. Erdogan's claim — that high interest rates cause inflation, requiring rate cuts to fight inflation — has been thoroughly empirically falsified. The June 2023 turn (new central bank governor Erkan, dramatic rate hikes) has begun stabilizing matters but at enormous cost.

question: By 2024, the Pakistani rupee was trading at over 280 PKR per US dollar — having lost nearly two-thirds of its dollar value from 2018-2024 levels. The country signed its 24th IMF program in September 2024. What was the size of that IMF package?
answer: Approximately $7 billion (37-month Extended Fund Facility)
choices: Approximately $7 billion (37-month Extended Fund Facility)
Approximately $700 million
Approximately $70 million
Approximately $70 billion (vastly larger than actual)
context: Pakistan's September 2024 IMF program ($7 billion) was its 24th since 1958 — a remarkable institutional record. The structural issues (chronic trade deficits, fiscal indiscipline, energy subsidies, low tax-to-GDP ratio) have repeated through political administrations. The IMF program is essentially recurring debt restructuring with conditions. Whether Pakistan ever exits this cycle remains the long-run question.

question: The Iranian rial has been one of the most consistently depreciating major currencies of the 21st century. By 2024, black market rates exceeded official rates by what factor?
answer: Approximately 10x — official rate of 42,000 IRR/USD vs black market rate exceeding 600,000 IRR/USD
choices: Approximately 10x — official rate of 42,000 IRR/USD vs black market rate exceeding 600,000 IRR/USD
Approximately 1x — official and black market rates roughly aligned
Approximately 1000x — far larger gap than actual
Approximately 0.5x — black market lower than official
context: Iran's dual exchange rate system has divergence factors that vary but typically run 10-15x. Sanctions have driven the divergence. The Iranian middle class has fled into gold, dollars, and Bitcoin as inflation hedges. Iranian Bitcoin mining is significant — estimated to account for some single-digit percentage of global hashrate even with periodic regulatory restrictions.

question: Cuba's dual-peso system (CUP for ordinary use, CUC pegged to the US dollar for tourism and foreign exchange) ended in January 2021. What was this unification called?
answer: Tarea Ordenamiento ('Ordering Task')
choices: Tarea Ordenamiento ('Ordering Task')
The Cuban Reform, which is not the official name
The Castro Reform, which is not the official name
The Special Period, which was a different earlier event
context: Tarea Ordenamiento on January 1, 2021 unified the two pesos at 24 CUP per old CUC — a massive overnight price adjustment for ordinary Cubans. Subsequent inflation, dollar shortages, and economic hardship have followed. Cuba's monetary trajectory under Diaz-Canel has continued the long pattern of socialist-system economic failures. The episode illustrates how protracted currency dysfunction can be in Cuba's planning economy.

question: The Bretton Woods Conference of July 1944 was attended by delegates from 44 Allied nations meeting at a New Hampshire resort hotel. What were the two main institutional outcomes?
answer: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD, now part of the World Bank)
choices: The International Monetary Fund (IMF) and the International Bank for Reconstruction and Development (IBRD, now part of the World Bank)
The World Trade Organization (founded 1995) and the United Nations (founded 1945)
The Federal Reserve System (founded 1913) and the European Central Bank (founded 1999)
The Bank for International Settlements (founded 1930) and the OECD (founded 1961)
context: Bretton Woods created the IMF (currency stabilization) and the IBRD/World Bank (reconstruction finance). Both institutions persist with substantially evolved mandates. The Soviet Union attended Bretton Woods but did not join the resulting institutions; the Cold War froze a more global cooperation framework. The dollar-gold standard that Bretton Woods established collapsed in August 1971.

question: At Bretton Woods 1944, the main negotiating dispute was between two figures representing the UK and US respectively. Keynes wanted a supranational reserve currency (the bancor); the US representative wanted a dollar-anchored system. Who was the US negotiator?
answer: Harry Dexter White (assistant secretary of the US Treasury)
choices: Harry Dexter White (assistant secretary of the US Treasury)
Henry Morgenthau, who was Treasury Secretary
Cordell Hull, who was Secretary of State
Henry Stimson, who was Secretary of War
context: White's design (dollar-anchored, gold-convertible) prevailed over Keynes's bancor proposal. White's later post-1944 trajectory was complicated by allegations he had been a Soviet sympathizer or agent. Bretton Woods established the dollar's role as world reserve currency — exorbitant privilege that has lasted (with the 1971 modification) for 80 years.

question: President Nixon's August 1971 decision to close the gold window was made during a weekend retreat at Camp David, Maryland. Who else was present, and what were the other major policy components announced?
answer: Treasury Secretary John Connally, Fed Chair Arthur Burns, Volcker (Treasury under-secretary); plus wage-price controls and 10% import surcharge
choices: Treasury Secretary John Connally, Fed Chair Arthur Burns, Volcker (Treasury under-secretary); plus wage-price controls and 10% import surcharge
Only the President and his economic advisor Herbert Stein
Only the President and Henry Kissinger (who was actually focused on China policy at the time)
Only the President and Vice President Spiro Agnew
context: The 'Camp David weekend' August 13-15, 1971 was a coordinated regime change: gold window closure, 90-day wage and price freeze, 10% import surcharge, 10% investment tax credit. The combination was an emergency response to the dollar-gold-confidence crisis. The temporary suspension has lasted 53 years and counting. The wage-price controls were a Keynesian-era misadventure that failed quickly.

question: The Roman silver denarius started its life around 211 BC at roughly 95% silver content and maintained that standard for over two centuries. By the time of Aurelian (270-275 AD), the silver content had collapsed to what level?
answer: Roughly 5% silver — the coin had become essentially a base-metal alloy
choices: Roughly 5% silver — the coin had become essentially a base-metal alloy
Roughly 50% silver — significant debasement but not the full collapse
Roughly 25% silver — intermediate debasement
Still roughly 95% silver — no significant debasement
context: The denarius's collapse from 95% to 5% silver over two centuries is the textbook ancient debasement. The third-century crisis (235-284 AD) accelerated the trajectory. Diocletian's reforms ended the denarius and introduced new coinage. The cycle — debasement, inflation, attempted price controls, eventual currency reform — is one history's most consistent patterns of fiscal-monetary failure.

question: After Diocletian's failed price-control experiment, the Emperor Constantine introduced a new gold coinage standard around 312 AD that lasted for over 700 years and became the international reserve currency of the medieval Mediterranean. What was the coin called?
answer: The solidus (later the nomisma; in Latin sources, the bezant)
choices: The solidus (later the nomisma; in Latin sources, the bezant)
The denarius (which was the silver coin Constantine's reforms replaced)
The aureus (which was an earlier Roman gold coin)
The drachma (which was the ancient Greek silver coin)
context: The solidus's 700-year stability is one of monetary history's greatest achievements. Constantine's reforms (along with monetary discipline) made the Eastern Roman Empire's gold coinage the trusted reserve from roughly 312 AD to the 11th century. The eventual debasement under Alexios I Komnenos in the late 11th century coincided with the empire's broader decline. The pattern — monetary stability and political success — recurs.

question: From the 1500s through the 1800s, the dominant globally-circulating coin was struck from Bolivian and Mexican silver. Its standardized weight and 90%+ purity made it the universal trade medium. From Macao to Boston, merchants used it. What was the coin called and what's the global circulation period?
answer: The Spanish silver dollar (or 'eight reales' / 'piece of eight'), dominant approximately 1500s-1850s
choices: The Spanish silver dollar (or 'eight reales' / 'piece of eight'), dominant approximately 1500s-1850s
The Dutch guilder, important regionally but never globally dominant
The Venetian sequin, dominant only in the Mediterranean
The Portuguese cruzado, important but not globally dominant
context: Spanish pieces of eight provided the longest period of global currency stability in modern history — roughly 350 years. The Mexican (Carolus IIII) dollar was US legal tender until 1857. The $ symbol derives from the Spanish dollar. Until WWI and the rise of paper currencies, silver coinage on the Spanish standard was the dominant world currency.

question: Sir Isaac Newton lost a significant portion of his savings in the 1720 South Sea Bubble. The episode produced one of his most famous remarks. What did Newton reportedly say after the crash?
answer: 'I can calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people.'
choices: 'I can calculate the motions of the heavenly bodies, but not the madness of people.'
'Trust no man but consult thy wallet.'
'Markets are always efficient in the long run.'
'The animal spirits of investors drive all financial markets.'
context: Newton's famous quote about the madness of people captures something deep about speculative manias. He had sold his South Sea holdings at a profit early, then bought back at the peak as the bubble continued — losing roughly £20,000 (a fortune). The lesson — that even great minds can be caught up in financial manias — remains relevant for every generation. Buffett's 'be fearful when others are greedy' captures the same insight.

question: The Panic of 1837 — one of the worst financial crises in early American history — followed Andrew Jackson's 1832-1836 destruction of the Second Bank of the United States. What was the typical Hamiltonian-school interpretation of the panic's cause?
answer: That Jackson's destruction of the Second Bank had removed monetary discipline and created banking instability
choices: That Jackson's destruction of the Second Bank had removed monetary discipline and created banking instability
That Jackson had prevented an even worse panic by destroying the Bank
That British policy alone caused the panic with no domestic component
That Mexico's silver supply alone caused the panic
context: The 1837 panic's causation has been argued for nearly two centuries. Whig-Hamiltonian interpretations blamed Jackson's bank war. Jacksonian-democratic interpretations cited British policy, state-bank speculation, and other factors. Modern scholarship (Peter Temin, others) tends toward multi-causal explanations including British silver flows and state banking practices. The political-monetary linkage remains contested.

question: During the Civil War, Congress passed the National Banking Act of 1863 — establishing the framework for federally chartered national banks issuing standardized currency. What problem was this trying to solve?
answer: Replacing the proliferation of varied state-bank notes circulating at varying discounts
choices: Replacing the proliferation of varied state-bank notes circulating at varying discounts
Establishing the Federal Reserve System (which actually came in 1913)
Funding World War I (which was over fifty years later)
Implementing the gold standard (which came in 1900)
context: The 1863 National Banking Act created a standardized national currency for the first time since the Second Bank's destruction in 1836. National-bank notes backed by federal bonds replaced the chaotic state-bank-note period. The architecture would remain in place until the Federal Reserve Act of 1913 layered central banking on top. The Civil War's funding crisis drove the institutional innovation.

question: Alongside the National Banking Act, Congress in 1862 authorized direct US Treasury issuance of paper currency to fund the Civil War. The notes were not backed by gold or silver and depreciated significantly against specie. What were they called?
answer: Greenbacks (officially 'United States Notes')
choices: Greenbacks (officially 'United States Notes')
Continentals, which were the Revolutionary War paper
Federal Reserve Notes, which is the modern paper
Silver Certificates, which were redeemable in silver
context: Greenbacks (1862) depreciated to roughly 35-40 cents on the gold-dollar at the war's worst. The Legal Tender Acts forced their acceptance. Post-war the question was when to redeem at gold parity. Resumption was finally completed in 1879. The greenback experience shaped subsequent American monetary politics — and the 1873 demonetization of silver came in this monetary-policy context.

question: After Japan's surrender in 1945 and the postwar occupation, the Japanese yen faced massive inflation — the yen lost over 90% of its prewar value by 1949. What stabilization framework was adopted under the Dodge Plan?
answer: Fixed exchange rate of 360 yen per US dollar (held until 1971 Nixon shock)
choices: Fixed exchange rate of 360 yen per US dollar (held until 1971 Nixon shock)
Floating exchange rate from 1949 onward
Direct adoption of the US dollar as legal tender
Direct adoption of British sterling
context: The Dodge Plan (1949) established the 360-yen-per-dollar rate that held for 22 years until the August 1971 Nixon shock. The rate was set at a level that initially overvalued the yen, contributing to mild deflation in the 1950s. By the 1960s, Japan's productivity growth had made the rate undervalued, fueling the export boom. Bretton Woods's collapse forced the move to floating rates.

question: Japan's asset-price bubble collapsed dramatically in 1990. The Nikkei stock index peaked at 38,915 in December 1989 and subsequently lost over 80% of its value over the following decade. What is the period of sustained low growth that followed commonly called?
answer: The Lost Decade (later extended to 'Lost Decades' as the trend persisted)

The Japanese Miracle (which refers to the earlier 1950s-1980s growth)
The Heisei Stagnation (a less-common term)
The Bubble Era (which refers to the pre-1990 bubble itself)
context: Japan's Lost Decade (later Lost Decades) has been the macroeconomics laboratory for unconventional monetary policy. Zero rates from 1999; QE from 2001; massive expansion under Kuroda from 2013. The Nikkei finally exceeded its 1989 peak in early 2024 — 34 years later. Whether Japan's experience has lessons for Western central banks remains debated. The slow-then-sudden trajectory recurs.

question: In January 2016, the Bank of Japan under Governor Haruhiko Kuroda introduced negative interest rates on certain reserve balances — joining the ECB in negative-rate experimentation. When did Japan finally exit NIRP?
answer: March 2024, ending eight years of negative rates

March 2017, just one year after introduction
March 2030 (not yet exited as of 2024)
context: Japan exited NIRP in March 2024, eight years after entry. The exit was carefully signaled to avoid market disruption. The yen's subsequent behavior has been complicated by the macro context. Japan's experiment with NIRP and yield curve control (introduced September 2016) has provided extensive data on what unconventional monetary policy can and cannot do in a deflationary environment.

question: In 2024, the Japanese yen weakened to multi-decade lows against the US dollar, approaching 160 yen per dollar in some sessions. The Bank of Japan intervened in foreign exchange markets — buying yen and selling dollars. How much did Japan reportedly spend on intervention in 2024?
answer: Approximately $100 billion across multiple intervention episodes
choices: Approximately $100 billion across multiple intervention episodes
Approximately $1 trillion in a single intervention
Approximately $10 million (negligible)
No intervention occurred
context: Japan's 2024 yen-defense interventions totaled approximately $100B. The interventions illustrated how even reserve-rich major economies face limits when fighting market trends. The yen ultimately strengthened back to 140-range by late 2024 as US Fed cuts and Japan's BOJ rate hikes narrowed the rate differential. The episode is one of the major FX events of the year.

question: Before the 2022 turn against negative rates, Switzerland had the longest-running negative-interest-rate regime among major economies. When did Swiss negative rates begin?
answer: December 2014 (with rates as low as -0.75%)
choices: December 2014 (with rates as low as -0.75%)
December 2008 (much earlier)
December 2020 (much later)
Switzerland never had negative rates
context: Swiss negative rates (2014-2022) were the longest such experiment among major economies. The -0.75% rate held for years. The SNB exited negative rates in September 2022 — alongside the ECB and Japan exits. The case provides extensive data on what NIRP can and cannot accomplish. The Swiss experience particularly informs Austrian critiques of NIRP's effects on savers, banks, and capital allocation.

question: China's current currency, the renminbi (RMB or 'yuan' for the unit), was introduced in December 1948 — before the People's Republic was even formally founded. What did the renminbi replace?
answer: The Nationalist (KMT) gold yuan and various regional currencies
choices: The Nationalist (KMT) gold yuan and various regional currencies
The Japanese yen (which was the occupying currency)

The British pound (which was used only in Hong Kong)

China's monetary management has been generally disciplined compared to the KMT-era hyperinflation, though specific episodes (Great Leap Forward, Cultural Revolution) saw economic distress. The renminbi's eventual internationalization (SDR inclusion 2016) remains a major macro question.

question: After Russia's February 2014 annexation of Crimea and the resulting Western sanctions, the Russian ruble depreciated sharply. The ruble lost approximately what fraction of its dollar value by December 2014?
answer: Roughly 50% — from about 33 rubles per dollar to about 65 per dollar
choices: Roughly 50% — from about 33 rubles per dollar to about 65 per dollar

Roughly 0% — no depreciation
context: The 2014 ruble depreciation was driven by oil-price collapse, sanctions, and capital flight. Russian Central Bank emergency rate hikes (to 17%) in December 2014 stabilized matters. The ruble subsequently recovered partially. The 2022 post-invasion sanctions caused another collapse but were also partially recovered. The pattern — sanctions-induced FX volatility followed by adaptation — has been the recurring Russian-monetary story.

question: The European Central Bank introduced negative deposit rates in 2014 — being the first major central bank to do so. The deposit rate eventually reached what level by 2019, before reversing in 2022?
answer: -0.5% (the deepest negative reached before the 2022 reversal)
