choices: The Cryptography Mailing List hosted by Metzdowd.com — an obscure forum read by maybe a few hundred people including hashcash inventor Adam Back
The Cypherpunks Mailing List originally founded by Eric Hughes in 1992 — though it had declined in activity by the late 2000s
The IEEE Computer Society's published proceedings, where it was submitted for academic peer review before public posting
His personal blog at satoshinakamoto.org, which was registered earlier in October 2008 and remained active for years afterward
context: The white paper is dated October 31, 2008. It cited Adam Back's hashcash (1997), Wei Dai's b-money (1998), and Ralph Merkle's tree structures (1979). Hal Finney, who would mine block 70 in January 2009, was reading. The paper combined existing primitives into something none of them had achieved — provable digital scarcity without a central issuer.

question: Bitcoin's Genesis Block was mined on January 3, 2009 at 18:15:05 UTC. Satoshi embedded a piece of text in the coinbase transaction's input script — text not strictly required by the protocol. What did it say?
answer: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — a UK newspaper headline timestamping the block and signaling Bitcoin's political moment
choices: 'The Times 03/Jan/2009 Chancellor on brink of second bailout for banks' — a UK newspaper headline timestamping the block and signaling Bitcoin's political moment

question: Adam Back published a paper in 1997 describing a system to discourage email spam by requiring senders to perform a small computational task before sending. The task — finding a hash with specific properties — would be cheap for legitimate users but expensive for bulk spammers. Satoshi cited this work in the Bitcoin white paper. What did Back call the system?
answer: Hashcash — a proof-of-work scheme using partial SHA-1 hash collisions that became the conceptual ancestor of Bitcoin mining
choices: Hashcash — a proof-of-work scheme using partial SHA-1 hash collisions that became the conceptual ancestor of Bitcoin mining

Bit gold — Nick Szabo's 2005 proposal for unforgeable digital scarcity that more closely resembles Bitcoin's actual mechanics
Digicash — David Chaum's commercial digital-cash system that operated from 1989 until bankruptcy in 1998
context: Hashcash used SHA-1 (Bitcoin uses SHA-256 doubled). Email never adopted it widely, but Bitcoin's mining is conceptually Hashcash repurposed: each block requires finding a nonce that makes the block header hash below a target. Back is now CEO of Blockstream and one of the most respected Bitcoin technologists.

question: Wei Dai posted a proposal to the cypherpunks mailing list in November 1998 describing a digital currency system maintained by a pseudonymous network. The system was never implemented. Satoshi cited it in the Bitcoin white paper as a key intellectual ancestor. What was the proposal called?

Cybercash — a commercial 1990s digital payment system that operated until being acquired by VeriSign in 2001
context: Wei Dai's b-money included unsolved problems Bitcoin later resolved: how do nodes agree on the ledger? How is issuance distributed? Satoshi emailed Dai in 2008 before the white paper. Dai later said Satoshi had taken an idea he had abandoned and made it work. The cypherpunk lineage from Hashcash to b-money to Bit Gold to Bitcoin is direct.

question: Nick Szabo, a polymathic legal scholar and cryptographer, published a proposal in 2005 for a digital currency system using proof-of-work to create unforgeable scarcity. The proposal anticipated Bitcoin's mechanics so closely that many in the community have suspected Szabo of being Satoshi. What did Szabo call his proposal?

context: Bit Gold was never implemented. Szabo's 2008 essay 'Bit gold' (lowercase) is one of the most prescient pre-Bitcoin documents. Szabo's writing style and Satoshi's have been compared by linguistic analysts who found similarities. Szabo has consistently denied being Satoshi but is widely respected as one of the deepest thinkers on monetary theory in the Bitcoin space.

question: In 1992, three cryptographers — Eric Hughes, Timothy May, and John Gilmore — started a mailing list to discuss using cryptography to defend privacy and individual liberty against state and corporate surveillance. The list ran from 1992 until roughly 2001 and produced ideas that would shape Bitcoin a decade later. What was the list called?
answer: The Cypherpunks Mailing List — host to Hughes's 1993 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' and a forum where Hashcash, b-money, and other Bitcoin precursors were first discussed
choices: The Cypherpunks Mailing List — host to Hughes's 1993 'A Cypherpunk's Manifesto' and a forum where Hashcash, b-money, and other Bitcoin precursors were first discussed
The Crypto-Anarchy List — Timothy May's earlier 1988 venue where his 'Crypto Anarchist Manifesto' was first distributed publicly
The Electronic Frontier Forum — John Gilmore's separate venue connected to the Electronic Frontier Foundation he co-founded in 1990
The CryptoMail List — a security-research mailing list operated by Phil Zimmermann following his PGP work in the early 1990s
context: The cypherpunks list was the spiritual home of the movement that produced PGP, mixmaster remailers, blinded signatures, and eventually Bitcoin. Hughes coined the term 'cypherpunk' (riffing on cyberpunk fiction). The list is closely associated with the libertarian and crypto-anarchist political positions that many early Bitcoiners shared.

question: In March 1993, Eric Hughes published a short manifesto laying out the philosophical foundations of the cypherpunk movement. The most-quoted line distilled the movement's program. What did Hughes write?
answer: 'Cypherpunks write code' — open-source cryptographic tools to defend privacy must be built rather than waited for from governments or corporations
choices: 'Cypherpunks write code' — open-source cryptographic tools to defend privacy must be built rather than waited for from governments or corporations
'In code we trust' — adapting the US dollar motto to express the cypherpunk replacement of state authority with cryptographic verification
'Cryptography is freedom' — the central slogan of the movement that connected mathematical privacy tools to political liberty
'Privacy is a human right' — Hughes's framing that became central to later international privacy-rights advocacy and policy
context: Hughes's manifesto begins: 'Privacy is necessary for an open society in the electronic age.' It champions open-source crypto, anonymous transactions, and resistance to surveillance. The cypherpunk ethos — build it rather than ask permission — runs straight through to Bitcoin. Hughes was a Berkeley mathematician who co-founded the list with May and Gilmore.

question: In 1991, Phil Zimmermann released a software package allowing ordinary users to encrypt email with strong public-key cryptography. The release violated US export-control regulations treating encryption as a 'munition.' Zimmermann was investigated by a federal grand jury from 1993-1996 but never charged. What did he name the software?
answer: Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) — a public-key email encryption system that became the de facto standard and inspired the cypherpunk movement
choices: Pretty Good Privacy (PGP) — a public-key email encryption system that became the de facto standard and inspired the cypherpunk movement
Secure Email Standard (SES) — Zimmermann's later commercial product after returning from his federal investigation period
The Privacy Project — Zimmermann's umbrella name for his various cryptographic and privacy-related software releases
Electronic Frontier Mail (EFM) — the original name before Zimmermann shortened it for commercial release purposes
context: Zimmermann's case was a major moment in the crypto wars of the 1990s. The government argued that exporting strong crypto was a national-security risk; cypherpunks responded by printing the PGP source code in a book (protected by First Amendment freedom of the press) and exporting copies legally. The government dropped the case in 1996. Public-key crypto became unrestricted.

question: In 1982, Leslie Lamport, Robert Shostak, and Marshall Pease published a paper formalizing a fundamental problem in distributed computing. Several generals must coordinate an attack via messengers; some generals may be traitors sending false messages. Under what conditions can the loyal generals reach agreement? What is the problem called?
answer: The Byzantine Generals Problem — the canonical formulation of consensus under arbitrary failures including malicious actors trying to deceive the system
choices: The Byzantine Generals Problem — the canonical formulation of consensus under arbitrary failures including malicious actors trying to deceive the system
The Two Generals Problem — the simpler related problem of coordinated action with unreliable but non-malicious communication channels
The Dining Philosophers Problem — Dijkstra's 1965 resource-allocation problem in concurrent computing systems
The Halting Problem — Turing's 1936 result about uncomputability that Lamport extended to distributed-system contexts
context: Bitcoin's central technical achievement is solving the Byzantine Generals Problem at internet scale without a trusted coordinator. Proof of work + longest valid chain rule allows mutually distrusting nodes to converge on a single consistent history. Lamport's 2024 ACM Turing Award citation specifically mentioned the impact of his consensus work on blockchain systems.

question: On January 12, 2009 — nine days after the Genesis Block — Satoshi Nakamoto sent 10 BTC to one of the first people to download and run the Bitcoin software. The transaction was block 170, one of the earliest non-trivial Bitcoin transactions. Who was the recipient?
answer: Hal Finney — the legendary cypherpunk who tweeted 'Running bitcoin' on January 11, 2009 and was likely the second person to run the network

context: Hal Finney had worked on PGP at Zimmermann's company and was a cypherpunks regular. He was diagnosed with ALS in 2009 and died in August 2014. His body was cryopreserved. His 2009 tweet remains one of the most-cited moments in Bitcoin history. Some speculate Finney was Satoshi, but the timing of his ALS progression argues against it.

question: On May 22, 2010, a programmer in Florida named Laszlo Hanyecz made a post on the BitcoinTalk forum offering to pay someone in BTC to deliver him two pizzas. A nineteen-year-old in California named Jeremy Sturdivant ordered the pizzas from Papa John's and was paid. How many BTC did Laszlo pay for two pizzas?
answer: 10,000 BTC — worth roughly $41 at the time and over $600 million at the 2021 all-time high, commemorated annually as Bitcoin Pizza Day

5,000 BTC — the negotiated price reached after some bargaining between Laszlo and Sturdivant in the forum thread
context: The transaction is the first known commercial purchase using Bitcoin. May 22 is now Bitcoin Pizza Day worldwide. Laszlo continued mining and accumulating BTC; he reportedly never regretted the trade because the pizzas were 'real' and the BTC was a hobby experiment at the time. Sturdivant sold his BTC eventually too.

question: From February 2011 to October 2013, an online marketplace operated as a hidden service on the Tor network where drugs and other contraband were sold with Bitcoin as the exclusive currency. The site demonstrated that Bitcoin could function as digital cash in a hostile environment. What was it called?

context: The FBI estimated Silk Road transacted roughly $1.2 billion in BTC over 2.5 years. Ulbricht was convicted in 2015 and sentenced to two life sentences plus 40 years without parole. His case became a major libertarian cause; the harsh sentence has been criticized as disproportionate. He was pardoned in 2025 by President Trump after years of advocacy.

question: On February 7, 2014, a Tokyo-based cryptocurrency exchange that had handled roughly 70% of all global Bitcoin trading volume in 2013 halted all withdrawals citing 'technical problems.' On February 24 it suspended trading entirely; on February 28 it filed for bankruptcy. How much customer Bitcoin had been lost?
answer: About 850,000 BTC — worth roughly $450 million at the time and over $50 billion at the 2021 all-time high
choices: About 850,000 BTC — worth roughly $450 million at the time and over $50 billion at the 2021 all-time high

About 3 million BTC — including all customer balances and exchange operating funds combined together
context: Mt. Gox's collapse remains the largest Bitcoin theft in history. CEO Mark Karpeles was later convicted of data manipulation but acquitted of embezzlement. Years of bankruptcy proceedings led to creditor distributions starting in 2024. The phrase 'not your keys, not your coins' became central Bitcoin wisdom after Mt. Gox showed why self-custody matters.

question: Bitcoin's protocol cuts the block-subsidy reward in half every 210,000 blocks (approximately every four years). The first such event occurred on November 28, 2012 at block 210,000. The mining reward dropped at that moment. From what to what?
answer: From 50 BTC per block to 25 BTC per block — the first halving in Bitcoin's monetary policy cementing its disinflationary schedule

context: Subsequent halvings: July 9, 2016 (25 to 12.5); May 11, 2020 (12.5 to 6.25); April 19, 2024 (6.25 to 3.125). The schedule reaches zero new supply around 2140, when transaction fees must fully fund mining. The 21M supply cap is hard-coded; the halving cycle defines Bitcoin's predictable scarcity, which has driven its sound-money narrative.

question: On April 19, 2024, Bitcoin's fourth halving occurred at block 840,000. The block subsidy dropped from 6.25 BTC to 3.125 BTC. The annualized inflation rate of new Bitcoin supply fell from roughly 1.7% to 0.85% — below gold's typical 1.5% annual supply growth rate. What is the next halving expected to do?

context: By 2028, Bitcoin's annualized supply growth will be approximately 0.4%. By the late 2040s it will be effectively zero, well below any plausible measure of inflation in fiat money systems. The halving schedule is what makes Bitcoin's 21M cap meaningful — issuance follows a known, immutable schedule that no human can change.

question: On June 9, 2021, El Salvador's Congress passed a law making Bitcoin legal tender alongside the US dollar. The law took effect on September 7, 2021. The launch was rocky — the Chivo wallet had bugs, polls showed limited public adoption — but the symbolic global precedent of a state adopting Bitcoin as legal tender is significant. Bukele continued accumulating BTC on the country's balance sheet.

question: Bitcoin miners compete to find a number called a 'nonce' that, when combined with the rest of the block header and hashed twice with SHA-256, produces a number below the network's current difficulty target. The miner who finds it first wins the block reward. What hash output do miners need?
answer: A number whose binary representation begins with a specific number of zero bits — the more zeros required, the higher the difficulty
choices: A number whose binary representation begins with a specific number of zero bits — the more zeros required, the higher the difficulty
A number that ends with a specific number of digits — increasing in difficulty as more trailing digits are required by the protocol
A number that exactly matches a target set by the protocol — though near-misses are valued for partial credit by mining pools
A number that, when divided by the previous block's hash, produces an integer result without remainder values
context: Mining is brute-force computation: try a nonce, hash, check if result is below target, try another. Modern ASICs perform trillions of attempts per second. The collective hashrate of Bitcoin in 2024 exceeded 500 exahashes per second — more computing power applied to a single problem than any other in human history. The system's security comes from this prohibitive cost to attack.

question: Bitcoin's protocol automatically adjusts mining difficulty to maintain an average block time of 10 minutes regardless of how much hashpower is currently mining. The adjustment happens at a regular interval. How often does Bitcoin re-target difficulty?
answer: Every 2,016 blocks — approximately every two weeks at the target ten-minute block time, based on actual blocks-per-time observed
choices: Every 2,016 blocks — approximately every two weeks at the target ten-minute block time, based on actual blocks-per-time observed
Every 144 blocks — approximately once per day, providing finer-grained adjustment to hashrate changes
Every 4,032 blocks — approximately every four weeks, providing more stable difficulty between adjustments
Every 210,000 blocks — coinciding with the halving schedule that occurs every four years on average
context: If hashrate doubles, blocks come faster than 10 minutes; the next difficulty adjustment raises the target hash threshold proportionally. If hashrate collapses (as during the 2021 China mining ban), difficulty drops to maintain block time. The 2,016-block window prevents reactive overshooting and protects the network from rapid hashrate manipulation attempts.

question: Bitcoin's monetary policy has one feature that distinguishes it from every state-issued currency in human history. The protocol is hard-coded to produce a total supply that converges to a specific maximum number that will never be exceeded. What is this maximum?

context: By April 2024 over 19.7 million BTC had been mined. The final satoshi will be mined around 2140 at block 6,929,999. Lost coins (estimated 3-4 million BTC) further reduce circulating supply permanently. The fixed cap is what makes Bitcoin 'digital gold' — it cannot be debased by issuance, only by losing access to private keys.

question: Bitcoin tracks balances differently than traditional banking. Rather than maintaining account balances that increase and decrease, the protocol maintains a set of discrete outputs that have not yet been spent. Each transaction consumes some outputs and creates new ones. What is this model called?
answer: UTXO (Unspent Transaction Output) model — every wallet's 'balance' is the sum of UTXOs it controls, each spent in full when used
choices: UTXO (Unspent Transaction Output) model — every wallet's 'balance' is the sum of UTXOs it controls, each spent in full when used

Ledger model — Ripple's accounting approach where balances are recorded in a more conventional database structure
Token model — Solana's account approach where each token has its own associated record in the program state
context: UTXO is more like physical cash: you can spend a $20 bill, get $13 back as change. You cannot spend half a UTXO. The model has privacy and parallelization advantages over the account model but is harder for smart contracts. Bitcoin Script (the limited scripting language) works on UTXOs; Ethereum's Turing-complete EVM works on accounts.

question: From 2015 to 2017, Bitcoin's user community engaged in a bitter public dispute about whether to increase the protocol's 1MB block-size limit. One side wanted larger blocks for greater throughput; the other side wanted to preserve smaller blocks to keep nodes affordable to run, ensuring decentralization. What was the eventual outcome?

context: The block size war was decided by user consensus, not the loudest miners or developers. SegWit activated August 24, 2017. Bitcoin Cash forked August 1, 2017 and now trades at roughly 1% of BTC's price. The Bitcoin Cash side later forked again into Bitcoin SV. The episode demonstrated Bitcoin's social-consensus resilience against capture by any single faction.

question: On November 14, 2021 at block 709,632, Bitcoin activated its most significant protocol upgrade since SegWit four years earlier. The upgrade combined three Bitcoin Improvement Proposals (BIPs 340, 341, 342) and introduced new cryptographic capabilities. What was the upgrade called?

context: Taproot brought signature aggregation (multiple signers' signatures combine into one), provable script confidentiality (only the executed branch reveals), and small footprint. Adoption has been gradual; Taproot remains underused but enables next-generation Layer 2 protocols. Activation used 'Speedy Trial' deployment that allowed quick miner signaling.

question: The Lightning Network, proposed in a 2015 white paper by Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja and launched on Bitcoin mainnet in January 2018, is a Layer 2 protocol enabling instant low-fee Bitcoin payments. How does Lightning fundamentally work?
answer: Two parties open a payment channel by locking BTC in a multi-sig output, then exchange signed off-chain updates; only opening and closing transactions touch the blockchain

Lightning uses delegated proof-of-stake to confirm transactions instantly, with periodic anchoring to the Bitcoin chain for security
context: Lightning enables millions of transactions per second potential capacity by keeping most activity off-chain. Payments route through paths of channels using hashed-timelock contracts. As of 2024, Lightning capacity exceeds 5,000 BTC across 60,000+ channels. El Salvador's Chivo wallet, Strike, and Cash App all use Lightning for payments.

question: Taproot introduced a new digital signature scheme to Bitcoin alongside the existing ECDSA. The new scheme has cleaner mathematical properties: signatures from multiple keys can be aggregated into a single signature indistinguishable from a single-key signature. answer: Schnorr signatures — named for German mathematician Claus Schnorr who patented the original scheme; the patent expired in 2008 making it usable
choices: Schnorr signatures — named for German mathematician Claus Schnorr who patented the original scheme; the patent expired in 2008 making it usable

context: Schnorr's mathematical elegance enables MuSig (multi-signature aggregation), making 'is this 2-of-3 multisig or just one signer?' indistinguishable on-chain. This dramatically improves privacy for multi-sig wallets, threshold signing, and Lightning. Schnorr was always preferred to ECDSA but waited for patent expiry; Bitcoin's caution paid off when the patent lapsed safely.

question: Satoshi Nakamoto's last known communication with the Bitcoin community came in spring 2011. question: Bitcoin's protocol targets an average time between new blocks. The actual time can vary block-to-block based on luck, but on average it stabilizes via the difficulty adjustment mechanism. What is the target average block time?

The 10-minute target combined with the 2016-block difficulty adjustment produces the disinflationary, predictable supply schedule that defines Bitcoin's monetary properties.

question: Each Bitcoin block contains many transactions efficiently summarized in the block header by a single 32-byte hash. The hash represents all transactions in the block via a tree of hashes, with leaf hashes for individual transactions and root hash for the whole. What is the tree structure called?
answer: A Merkle tree — invented by Ralph Merkle in 1979; the root hash changes if any leaf transaction is modified

context: Merkle trees enable light clients (SPV nodes) to verify a transaction is included in a block without downloading the whole block. The block header is only 80 bytes; you can prove transaction inclusion with O(log n) hashes from leaf to root. Merkle's 1979 patent was foundational; he was a UC Berkeley grad student then.

question: Bitcoin uses elliptic curve digital signatures to prove ownership of UTXOs. The specific curve Satoshi chose is unusual — most cryptographic systems use curves with different parameters. What curve does Bitcoin use?

The choice has aged well; Bitcoin's cryptography has never been broken in 16 years of public scrutiny against trillion-dollar incentive.

question: Before Bitcoin, no one had solved the 'double-spend problem' for digital cash without a central server. Digital files can be copied; cash payments require ensuring the same dollar is not spent twice. What was Satoshi's insight that solved this in a peer-to-peer system?

Use proof-of-stake to make double-spending expensive — Ethereum's later approach that Bitcoin avoided for security reasons
context: Section 8 of the white paper proves an attacker controlling less than 50% of network hashpower has exponentially decreasing odds of reversing a transaction as confirmations accumulate. Six confirmations (about an hour) is generally considered final. Twenty-four hours of confirmations is practically irreversible. This is the core security model.

question: Modern Bitcoin wallets generate a 'seed phrase' of 12 or 24 English words that can fully recover all keys derived from that seed. The standard defining this is widely implemented across hardware wallets and software wallets. What is the standard called?
answer: BIP-39 — Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 39, using a 2,048-word list with checksum, allowing language-independent backup
choices: BIP-39 — Bitcoin Improvement Proposal 39, using a 2,048-word list with checksum, allowing language-independent backup
BIP-32 — the hierarchical deterministic wallet standard that BIP-39 builds upon for the actual key derivation
BIP-44 — the account-structure standard that organizes derived keys for multi-coin and multi-account use
BIP-141 — the SegWit standard that handles transaction format separately from seed phrase generation
context: Twelve words at 11 bits each = 132 bits, with last word containing 4-bit checksum = 128 bits of entropy. The 2,048-word list is shared across all major wallets, so a seed generated by Trezor can recover funds on a Coldcard or Ledger. The standard transformed Bitcoin self-custody from 'back up files' to 'back up these 12-24 words.'

question: Hardware wallets are dedicated devices for signing Bitcoin transactions while keeping private keys isolated from internet-connected computers. The first commercially successful hardware wallet was released in 2014 by a Czech company. What was its name?
answer: Trezor — released by SatoshiLabs in Prague, designed by Marek 'Slush' Palatinus, the inventor of mining pool concept (Slush Pool)
choices: Trezor — released by SatoshiLabs in Prague, designed by Marek 'Slush' Palatinus, the inventor of mining pool concept (Slush Pool)
Ledger — the French manufacturer founded in 2014 that became Trezor's main competitor; Ledger's Nano line came later
Coldcard — the Canadian-made hardware wallet by Coinkite, released later than Trezor and focused on Bitcoin-only support
BitBox — the Swiss-made hardware wallet from Shift Crypto, released after Trezor established the hardware wallet market
context: Trezor pioneered the seed-phrase-based recovery model that all subsequent hardware wallets adopted. The Trezor One remains in production today alongside the Trezor Model T touchscreen device. Ledger's 2020 customer database hack — which exposed names and addresses of buyers — pushed many privacy-focused users toward Trezor and Coldcard alternatives.

question: A common Bitcoin self-custody pattern uses multi-signature transactions requiring more than one private key to spend funds. A particularly popular configuration distributes three keys across three locations, requiring any two to sign. What is this pattern called?
answer: 2-of-3 multisig — providing redundancy (any 2 keys work) and security (no single key compromise suffices to steal funds)
choices: 2-of-3 multisig — providing redundancy (any 2 keys work) and security (no single key compromise suffices to steal funds)
3-of-3 multisig — requiring all three keys, providing maximum security but no redundancy if one key is lost permanently
1-of-3 multisig — requiring any single key to sign, providing maximum redundancy but minimum security against theft
Threshold 5-of-7 multisig — a more complex pattern used by exchanges and institutional custody operations exclusively
context: Casa, Unchained Capital, and other Bitcoin custody firms offer collaborative 2-of-3 setups: client holds two keys (one easily accessible, one in cold storage), custodian holds one. The setup protects against loss of one key and against unilateral seizure by the custodian. Taproot's MuSig will eventually make multisig setups indistinguishable from single-signer addresses on-chain.

question: Sophisticated Bitcoin self-custodians use 'cold storage' — keeping private keys on devices that have never been connected to the internet. The strongest version of this practice uses devices that physically cannot connect to the internet at all. What is this approach called?
answer: Air-gapped signing — using a device with no network capability that signs transactions via QR codes or microSD cards transferred manually
choices: Air-gapped signing — using a device with no network capability that signs transactions via QR codes or microSD cards transferred manually
Hot wallet storage — keeping keys on internet-connected devices for daily use, which is the opposite of cold storage practice
Paper wallet storage — printing keys on paper; once standard practice but now considered obsolete and error-prone
Brain wallet storage — memorizing a password from which keys are deterministically derived; abandoned due to brute-force vulnerability
context: Coldcard and SeedSigner are popular air-gapped devices. The trade-off is convenience: every transaction requires physically moving data between devices. For large holdings, the friction is worth the security. Bitcoin's largest known cold storage holders (exchanges, ETF custodians) use elaborate procedures involving multiple geographic locations and ceremonial signing events.

question: After repeated exchange collapses — Mt. Gox 2014, Cryptopia 2019, FTX 2022, Celsius 2022, BlockFi 2022 — the Bitcoin community settled on a six-word maxim summarizing the lesson. The maxim warns that funds held on an exchange are owned by the exchange, not the customer. What is the saying?
answer: 'Not your keys, not your coins' — if you don't control the private keys, you don't actually own the Bitcoin
choices: 'Not your keys, not your coins' — if you don't control the private keys, you don't actually own the Bitcoin
'Trust math, not men' — emphasizing cryptographic verification over institutional promises in handling Bitcoin
'Don't trust, verify' — the cypherpunk maxim that pre-dates Bitcoin but became prominent through self-custody advocacy
'Hold your own keys' — the imperative version of the maxim widely used in Bitcoin self-custody education materials
context: The saying captures Bitcoin's core insight: digital bearer instruments require self-custody. Andreas Antonopoulos popularized the formulation in the 2010s. Every major exchange failure has cost customers money — Mt. Gox creditors recovered partial value only a decade later. The 2022 wave of crypto-lender collapses retraumatized the community into emphasizing custody fundamentals.

question: Bitcoin's block subsidy declines geometrically through halvings until reaching effectively zero around 2140. After that, miners must be compensated by transaction fees alone. The economics of this transition is debated. What is the basic mechanism by which fees will sustain mining?
answer: Users compete for limited block space by paying higher fees; total fee revenue must justify hashpower to secure the network
choices: Users compete for limited block space by paying higher fees; total fee revenue must justify hashpower to secure the network
Miners will switch to alternative consensus mechanisms — proof-of-stake or others — to remove the need for fee-supported security
The protocol will automatically increase the supply cap above 21 million through emergency consensus action by then
Layer 2 networks like Lightning will subsidize Layer 1 miners through revenue-sharing mechanisms built into the protocol
context: Critics argue that without subsidy, security may be inadequate. Bitcoin proponents argue that as the network grows, transaction-fee revenue should rise proportionally with the value being secured. Lightning Network and other Layer 2s reduce on-chain transaction volume but also reduce fee revenue per user. The transition is the major open question in Bitcoin's monetary architecture.

question: Bitcoin's Script language includes an opcode that allows including arbitrary data in a transaction output that is provably unspendable. The output costs the data inserter standard transaction fees but is recognized by all nodes as a marker rather than spendable value. What is the opcode?
answer: OP_RETURN — limited to 80 bytes per transaction since 2014, used for timestamping, commitments, and protocol markers
choices: OP_RETURN — limited to 80 bytes per transaction since 2014, used for timestamping, commitments, and protocol markers
OP_CHECKSIG — the standard signature verification opcode used in every regular spending transaction on Bitcoin
OP_NOP — a no-operation opcode used for forward-compatibility in script upgrades like CLTV and CSV
OP_DUP — a stack duplication opcode used in the standard P2PKH script pattern for verification
context: OP_RETURN has been used for thousands of secondary protocols: Counterparty assets, Omni Layer (Tether's original implementation), Rare Pepe (early NFT-like), and Ordinals/inscriptions controversially using related techniques starting 2023. The 80-byte limit is a deliberate restriction to keep Bitcoin focused on monetary use rather than becoming a general data layer.

question: Bitcoin's transaction scripting language is intentionally limited compared to Ethereum's EVM. The limitation is a feature, not a bug — it prevents many classes of bugs and exploits that have plagued more powerful blockchains. What is the key limitation?
answer: Bitcoin Script is not Turing-complete — no loops, no recursion; every script terminates in bounded time and cannot create infinite-loop denial-of-service attacks
choices: Bitcoin Script is not Turing-complete — no loops, no recursion; every script terminates in bounded time and cannot create infinite-loop denial-of-service attacks
Bitcoin Script cannot do arithmetic — completely lacking add/subtract/multiply operations, requiring all logic to be sign-checking only
Bitcoin Script cannot verify signatures — relying entirely on transaction inputs for authentication rather than script-level checks
Bitcoin Script cannot reference external data — completely unable to interact with anything outside the immediate transaction context
context: Ethereum's Turing-completeness has caused countless smart-contract exploits worth billions of dollars. The DAO hack (2016), Parity multi-sig freeze (2017), and dozens of DeFi flash-loan attacks all involve unintended script execution paths. Bitcoin's restricted script prioritizes the function of a sound money over the function of a programmable platform.

question: Bitcoin's monetary policy combines a hard supply cap (21M) with a predictable issuance schedule. New BTC enters circulation only as block rewards to miners, decreasing geometrically through halvings. What is the cumulative effect on annualized inflation rate?
answer: Inflation falls geometrically from very high in the early years to below 1% after the 2024 halving and approaching zero by 2140
choices: Inflation falls geometrically from very high in the early years to below 1% after the 2024 halving and approaching zero by 2140
Inflation is constant at 2% per year — a deliberate design choice mirroring Fed inflation targets
Inflation rises slightly over time before falling — initial halvings produce modest deflation followed by gradual normalization
Inflation is variable based on demand — the protocol adjusts supply growth based on hashrate signals from the network
context: The 2024 halving brought Bitcoin's annual supply growth below gold's. By the 2028 halving it will be below 0.5%. The disinflationary schedule is what makes 'stock-to-flow' analysis (Plan B) appealing despite its methodological criticisms. The schedule is hard-coded; no human can change it without a protocol upgrade requiring vast user consensus.

question: Lightning Network was first described in a January 2016 white paper (work-in-progress drafts circulated 2015) that proposed using Bitcoin's existing transaction features to construct off-chain payment channels with strong security guarantees. Who were the authors?
answer: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja — both later founders of Lightning Labs, the Lightning protocol's primary implementation team
choices: Joseph Poon and Thaddeus Dryja — both later founders of Lightning Labs, the Lightning protocol's primary implementation team
Adam Back and Greg Maxwell — both senior Blockstream technologists working on Bitcoin protocol-level improvements at the time
Andreas Antonopoulos and Pieter Wuille — both Bitcoin Core contributors and educators in the technical community
Vitalik Buterin and Gavin Wood — though both are associated with Ethereum, not Bitcoin's Lightning Network protocol
context: The white paper proved Bitcoin's 1MB block-size limit need not constrain transaction throughput. By moving most activity off-chain into payment channels, Lightning enables effectively unlimited transactions per second. The first mainnet implementation launched January 2018. Lightning capacity and channels have grown steadily; Strike and El Salvador's Chivo wallet use Lightning for payments.

question: Segregated Witness (SegWit), activated August 2017, separated the witness data (signatures) from transaction inputs. The change had immediate benefits and enabled future improvements like Lightning Network. What was SegWit's most important immediate benefit?
answer: Effective block size increased to ~4MB through witness discount, enabling more transactions per block without changing the 1MB base limit
choices: Effective block size increased to ~4MB through witness discount, enabling more transactions per block without changing the 1MB base limit
Transaction fees reduced to near zero by eliminating signature data from transactions in addressed reformulation of the protocol
Mining difficulty adjusted automatically to match SegWit transaction volume, replacing the 2016-block adjustment cycle
Privacy improved dramatically by encrypting all transaction data using zero-knowledge proofs at the witness level only
context: SegWit also fixed transaction malleability (the ability to alter transaction IDs without invalidating signatures), which had blocked Lightning Network deployment. Activation came after the prolonged block-size war. Today most Bitcoin transactions use SegWit-compatible addresses (bech32 starting with bc1), reducing fees and improving security.

question: Lyn Alden, an independent macro analyst widely respected for her Bitcoin commentary, published a comprehensive 2023 book examining the history of money and arguing for Bitcoin's monetary properties from a long-historical perspective. What is the book's title?
answer: *Broken Money: Why Our Financial System Is Failing Us and How We Can Make It Better* — Alden's history of money from antiquity through modern fiat and Bitcoin
choices: *Broken Money: Why Our Financial System Is Failing Us and How We Can Make It Better* — Alden's history of money from antiquity through modern fiat and Bitcoin
*The Bitcoin Standard* — Saifedean Ammous's 2018 book, often confused with Alden's more recent and economically nuanced work
*The Bullish Case for Bitcoin* — Vijay Boyapati's essay-turned-book on Bitcoin's monetization through Mengerian saleability stages
*Layered Money* — Nik Bhatia's 2021 book on monetary hierarchy from gold through Lightning Network and beyond
context: Alden's work synthesizes traditional macro analysis with Bitcoin-native thinking better than perhaps any other contemporary writer. *Broken Money* traces monetary failures from Roman debasement through modern fiat through the cryptographic alternative Bitcoin offers. Alden writes from a non-ideological vantage point that many traditional macro audiences find more accessible than the more polemical Bitcoin literature.

question: Saifedean Ammous, a Lebanese-American economist, published a 2018 book that became one of the most-read introductions to Bitcoin's monetary properties. The book applies Austrian school economics to argue Bitcoin succeeds where state-issued money fails. What is the book's title?
answer: *The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking* — Ammous's application of Austrian economics to Bitcoin's monetary case
choices: *The Bitcoin Standard: The Decentralized Alternative to Central Banking* — Ammous's application of Austrian economics to Bitcoin's monetary case
*The Fiat Standard* — Ammous's 2021 sequel critiquing the fiat money system in depth and contrasting it with Bitcoin alternatives
*Principles of Economics* — Ammous's 2024 textbook covering basic Austrian economics intended for university and self-study use
*The Politics of Bitcoin* — David Golumbia's critical 2016 book on Bitcoin's libertarian politics, often confused with Ammous's work
context: *The Bitcoin Standard* has been translated into dozens of languages. Ammous argues Bitcoin's hard supply cap and verifiable scarcity make it monetarily superior to gold (which can be mined more if price rises) and to fiat (which can be debased by issuance). His follow-up *The Fiat Standard* (2021) details fiat money's distortions across food, science, energy, and culture.

question: An anonymous Dutch investor publishing under the name 'PlanB' developed a model attempting to predict Bitcoin's long-term price based on its scarcity. The model uses a ratio borrowed from commodity economics to compare different stores of value. What is the ratio?
answer: Stock-to-flow — total existing supply (stock) divided by annual new issuance (flow); higher ratios indicate scarcer monetary commodities
choices: Stock-to-flow — total existing supply (stock) divided by annual new issuance (flow); higher ratios indicate scarcer monetary commodities
Price-to-earnings — corporate valuation metric not normally applied to commodities or to monetary base assets like Bitcoin
Market-cap-to-volume — a liquidity measure used in traditional finance for evaluating market depth and stability
Hash-rate-to-supply — a Bitcoin-specific metric measuring network security per unit of monetary base
context: Stock-to-flow plots Bitcoin in the same framework as gold (S/F ratio ~60), silver (~22), and platinum (~0.5). Bitcoin's S/F was around 25 in 2020, projected to reach 100+ after the 2024 halving. The model accurately predicted price trajectories through 2021 but missed the 2022 crash. It remains influential despite methodological criticism from quantitative analysts.

question: Bitcoin's third halving occurred on May 11, 2020 at block 630,000. The block subsidy dropped from 12.5 BTC to 6.25 BTC. The halving occurred during a particularly unusual macroeconomic moment. What was happening in global monetary policy at the same time?
answer: Massive central-bank balance-sheet expansion in response to COVID-19 — the Fed alone expanded by trillions of dollars in March-April 2020
choices: Massive central-bank balance-sheet expansion in response to COVID-19 — the Fed alone expanded by trillions of dollars in March-April 2020
Major central banks were raising rates in response to building inflation pressure that began in early 2020 before COVID disruption
Quantitative tightening was underway — central banks were shrinking their balance sheets through bond rolloffs and asset sales
Gold standard pressure had been restored — major economies were committing to fixed monetary discipline through coordinated agreement
context: The contrast was stark: Bitcoin's supply growth rate cut in half by protocol; Fed balance sheet doubling in weeks. This contrast drove the 2020-2021 bull run from $9,000 in May 2020 to $69,000 in November 2021. The narrative of 'sound money meets crisis fiat' became central to institutional adoption (MicroStrategy began accumulating in August 2020 with Michael Saylor as CEO).

question: Bitcoin distinguishes itself from most other cryptocurrencies by one feature of its initial launch. The first 50 BTC mined (the Genesis Block) were even technically unspendable. No insiders received early allocations before public release. What is this called?
answer: Fair launch — no pre-mine, no insider allocation, no ICO; everyone had equal opportunity to mine from the Genesis Block onward
choices: Fair launch — no pre-mine, no insider allocation, no ICO; everyone had equal opportunity to mine from the Genesis Block onward
Stealth launch — Satoshi mined privately for months before announcing Bitcoin publicly, giving insiders a head start
Subsidized launch — early miners received discounted rates from the protocol that newcomers could not access later
Curated launch — Satoshi selected initial network participants from the cypherpunk community before public release
context: Bitcoin's fair launch contrasts sharply with Ethereum (60 million ETH pre-mined and sold in 2014 to insiders), Ripple (100 billion XRP pre-mined and partially distributed to founders), and most ICO-era tokens. The fair launch is foundational to Bitcoin's claim of being a 'neutral' monetary protocol comparable to gold's natural emergence.

question: Most software projects have a corporation, foundation, or other centralized entity that develops the software, holds copyright, and makes formal decisions. Bitcoin does not. What is Bitcoin's governance structure?
answer: No central entity — Bitcoin Core is one of several implementations; no foundation, CEO, or board controls the protocol
choices: No central entity — Bitcoin Core is one of several implementations; no foundation, CEO, or board controls the protocol
The Bitcoin Foundation governs Bitcoin Core development and represents the protocol legally to governments worldwide
MIT Digital Currency Initiative coordinates development through its housed Bitcoin Core team after Satoshi's departure
The Linux Foundation manages Bitcoin development through its Hyperledger umbrella organizational structure formally
context: Bitcoin Improvement Proposals (BIPs) require rough consensus among developers, miners, exchanges, and users to activate. There is no formal voting; there is no on-chain governance. The Bitcoin Foundation existed 2012-2015 but was never authoritative and is now defunct. This 'no leader' status is core to Bitcoin's credibility as truly neutral protocol money.

question: Every January 3 — the anniversary of the Genesis Block — Bitcoin holders are encouraged to verify control of their private keys by moving funds (or signing a proof message) from any exchange or custodian onto wallets they personally control. The practice was popularized by Trace Mayer. What is it called?
answer: Proof of Keys Day — withdrawing from exchanges and verifying self-custody on the anniversary of Bitcoin's launch each year
choices: Proof of Keys Day — withdrawing from exchanges and verifying self-custody on the anniversary of Bitcoin's launch each year
Bitcoin Independence Day — a separate informal holiday celebrated on November 28 (the first halving anniversary)
Halving Day — the four-year cycle anniversary of each block subsidy reduction event in Bitcoin's history
Hodlers' Day — an informal community celebration of long-term Bitcoin holders, on no specific calendar date
context: Trace Mayer started the tradition in 2019 partially as response to repeated exchange failures. The point is to test exchange solvency — if many users withdraw simultaneously, an exchange operating fractionally would fail. The annual practice reinforces self-custody culture and provides ongoing market check on custodial solvency claims by exchanges and lending platforms.

question: In February 2022, Canada invoked the Emergencies Act against truck-driver protests in Ottawa over COVID vaccine mandates. The order authorized banks to freeze accounts of protest supporters without court order. How did Bitcoin demonstrate its value proposition?
answer: Donors who gave to truckers via banking saw accounts frozen; Bitcoin donations could not be similarly frozen or confiscated
choices: Donors who gave to truckers via banking saw accounts frozen; Bitcoin donations could not be similarly frozen or confiscated
Canada banned Bitcoin transactions during the protests, demonstrating Bitcoin's vulnerability to coordinated state action
Trucker organizations refused Bitcoin donations as too volatile, undermining Bitcoin's narrative as protest-era resistance money
All Bitcoin exchanges in Canada complied with freezing orders, showing custodial Bitcoin offered no protection against state action
context: The Canadian episode put Bitcoin's censorship-resistance to real test in a Western democracy. Bitcoin in self-custody could not be frozen; Bitcoin on exchanges could be. The case taught separating Bitcoin's properties from custodial intermediaries that subject holders to traditional controls.

question: In late 2022 and early 2023, the Nigerian government attempted a rapid currency redesign and ATM cash withdrawal limits intended to push citizens onto the e-Naira CBDC. The transition caused massive cash shortages, hour-long ATM lines, and economic disruption. What was the Bitcoin and crypto consequence?
answer: Peer-to-peer Bitcoin volume in Nigeria surged as citizens routed around banking limitations and capital controls during the cash crisis
choices: Peer-to-peer Bitcoin volume in Nigeria surged as citizens routed around banking limitations and capital controls during the cash crisis
Nigerian citizens widely adopted the e-Naira CBDC, demonstrating that government-issued digital currencies can compete with Bitcoin
Bitcoin trading was banned successfully across Nigeria, demonstrating Bitcoin's vulnerability to determined state suppression
Stable coins replaced Bitcoin entirely as the Nigerian crypto preference, showing that volatility undermined Bitcoin's adoption
context: Nigeria's Paxful and Yellow Card volumes surged during the cash crisis. The 2023 episode demonstrated that in real currency stress, ordinary citizens turn to Bitcoin as a parallel financial system. Despite official restrictions, peer-to-peer trading thrived. Nigeria has one of the highest per-capita Bitcoin adoption rates outside the US.

question: In November 2023, Argentine voters elected Javier Milei, a self-described libertarian economist who had publicly criticized the central bank and the peso, and advocated for dollarization or full free banking. What was Milei's stated position on Bitcoin?
answer: Bitcoin is a return to private money — Milei has publicly praised Bitcoin's removal of money from state control as a positive development
choices: Bitcoin is a return to private money — Milei has publicly praised Bitcoin's removal of money from state control as a positive development
Bitcoin must be regulated heavily — Milei's libertarianism applies only to traditional currency, not cryptocurrencies
Bitcoin should be banned — Milei's economic plan rejected all decentralized digital assets as monetary alternatives
Bitcoin is irrelevant — Milei focused exclusively on the peso-dollar question without commenting on cryptocurrencies
context: Milei is the first national leader of a major Western country to be publicly Austrian-school in economic orientation. His government has reduced inflation from 211% annually (when he took office) toward more normal ranges. Argentina has not formally adopted Bitcoin as legal tender (unlike El Salvador) but has loosened restrictions and explored monetary alternatives substantially.

question: Nick Szabo, in writings extending back to the early 2000s, articulated a property he argued was essential for any commodity to function well as money. Gold has this property; counterfeit gold can be detected because real gold requires costly mining. What did Szabo call this property?
answer: Unforgeable costliness — the property that something cannot be cheaply faked because creating it requires significant real resources
choices: Unforgeable costliness — the property that something cannot be cheaply faked because creating it requires significant real resources
Convergent saleability — Menger's term for how a commodity gradually becomes accepted by more parties over time
Intrinsic value — the classical-economist position that money must have non-monetary uses to ground its value historically
Network monopoly — Hayek's concept that money tends toward winner-take-all dynamics in adoption competition
context: Bitcoin has unforgeable costliness via proof of work — creating a valid block requires real electricity and computation. This property is what distinguishes Bitcoin from pre-mined or proof-of-stake cryptocurrencies, which lack the costly anchoring to physical reality that Szabo identified as essential. The concept ties Bitcoin to a long tradition in Austrian monetary thought.

question: Bitcoin advocates often frame the protocol's significance using a phrase comparing it to a famous 17th-century political achievement. Just as the modern state separated religious authority from political authority, Bitcoin separates another function from the state. What separation does the phrase refer to?
answer: Separation of money and state — removing the issuance and control of currency from government, analogous to the separation of church and state
choices: Separation of money and state — removing the issuance and control of currency from government, analogous to the separation of church and state
Separation of bank and state — removing private banking from state control, focusing on commercial banking rather than monetary issuance
Separation of payment and state — removing transaction processing from state control while leaving currency issuance unchanged
Separation of regulation and state — removing financial regulation from state control through decentralized smart contracts
context: The phrase 'separation of money and state' was popularized by Andreas Antonopoulos and other early Bitcoin educators. The framing places Bitcoin in a Western political tradition of disestablishment — taking critical functions out of state hands and submitting them to private competition. The intellectual lineage runs through Hayek's *Denationalization of Money* (1976).

question: Vitalik Buterin (Ethereum's founder) coined a term to describe a property that successful base-layer protocols should have. The property requires that the protocol does not favor or disfavor any particular party — it operates by mechanical rules without human discretion. What is the term?
answer: Credibly neutral — the protocol's rules are predictable and apply equally to all users, with no discretionary intervention by any authority
choices: Credibly neutral — the protocol's rules are predictable and apply equally to all users, with no discretionary intervention by any authority
Permissionless — anyone can use the protocol without seeking authorization, which is necessary but not sufficient for full neutrality
Censorship-resistant — transactions cannot be selectively blocked, a related but narrower property than full neutrality
Immutable — the protocol cannot be changed by any party, the strongest form of neutrality but rarely achievable in practice
context: Bitcoin is more credibly neutral than Ethereum. Ethereum's leadership has intervened twice in major ways: the DAO hard fork (2016) reversed a hack, and major upgrades happen by foundation-led roadmap. Bitcoin's protocol changes only through community-wide consensus on improvements, with no foundation roadmap. Buterin himself acknowledges Bitcoin's greater credible neutrality.

question: Modern fiat governments fund a significant portion of their spending through the inflation tax — debasement of the currency transfers purchasing power from savers and wage earners to the government and its allied institutions. Bitcoin removes this option. What does this mean for governments operating on Bitcoin?
answer: Spending must equal taxation plus genuine borrowing — no money creation; budgets become real-time visible to citizens
choices: Spending must equal taxation plus genuine borrowing — no money creation; budgets become real-time visible to citizens
Spending is permanently constrained at exactly current tax levels with no growth flexibility regardless of economic conditions
Governments cannot exist at all — Bitcoin makes any government impossible because all taxation requires state currency to function
Governments must adopt CBDCs in parallel to Bitcoin — maintaining inflation tax capability through state-issued digital currency
context: On a Bitcoin standard, governments lose the seigniorage revenue from issuing currency and the indirect financing from debt monetization. This is precisely why the Austrian-libertarian tradition celebrates Bitcoin's monetary properties — it constrains the state to honest taxation, eliminating the hidden tax mechanism that has financed much of 20th-century government growth.

question: Ethereum launched its mainnet in July 2015 with one feature distinguishing it sharply from Bitcoin: a Turing-complete scripting language allowing arbitrary 'smart contracts' to run on chain. The platform was conceived by a young Russian-Canadian programmer who had written for *Bitcoin Magazine*. Who created Ethereum?
answer: Vitalik Buterin — proposed Ethereum in a 2013 white paper at age 19, co-founded with Gavin Wood, Joseph Lubin, and others
choices: Vitalik Buterin — proposed Ethereum in a 2013 white paper at age 19, co-founded with Gavin Wood, Joseph Lubin, and others
Charles Hoskinson — though he was an early Ethereum founder, he left in 2014 and created Cardano separately afterward
Gavin Wood — wrote the technical Yellow Paper for Ethereum but Buterin was the primary conceptualizer and public face
Joseph Lubin — co-founded Ethereum and ConsenSys but was the business side, not the technical visionary of the project
context: Ethereum's launch raised concerns from Bitcoin maximalists due to its 2014 pre-sale (60 million ETH allocated to early purchasers), its centralized founder team, and its Turing-complete scripting that proved repeatedly hackable. Ethereum's market role has shifted toward 'smart contract platform' rather than money — a different niche than Bitcoin claims.

question: In April 2016, a smart-contract project called The DAO launched on Ethereum, raising $150 million worth of ETH from investors who would vote on which startups to fund. On June 17, 2016, an attacker exploited a re-entrancy bug in the smart contract and drained about $50 million worth of ETH. What did the Ethereum community do?
answer: Hard-forked Ethereum on July 20, 2016 to reverse the hack — creating Ethereum Classic on the original chain that did not fork
choices: Hard-forked Ethereum on July 20, 2016 to reverse the hack — creating Ethereum Classic on the original chain that did not fork
Accepted the loss as a learning experience and continued without modification — maintaining immutability as a core principle
Pursued legal action against the hacker through coordinated international law enforcement cooperation efforts
Restored funds through community donations that voluntarily compensated DAO investors for their unrecovered losses
context: The hard fork was the original sin of Ethereum's credible neutrality. By demonstrating that the Ethereum Foundation could and would intervene to reverse a major transaction, Ethereum proved itself willing to bend rules when leadership preferred. Ethereum Classic remains as the chain that did not fork — the smaller faction that prioritized immutability.

question: On September 15, 2022, Ethereum executed 'The Merge,' transitioning from proof-of-work mining to proof-of-stake validation. The change had been planned since Ethereum's launch but took seven years to implement. What was the fundamental change?
answer: Block production moved from competing miners (PoW) to validators staking ETH (PoS); miners no longer secure the network
choices: Block production moved from competing miners (PoW) to validators staking ETH (PoS); miners no longer secure the network
Block production moved from validators (PoS) to mining (PoW), reversing Ethereum's earlier consensus mechanism
Block production became hybrid PoW and PoS, with both miners and stakers having a role in network security
Block production became fully centralized through a foundation-controlled set of approved validators only
context: The Merge reduced Ethereum's energy consumption by ~99.95%. Critics noted PoS validators are concentrated (Lido, Coinbase, Binance hold a majority of staked ETH) and that PoS lacks the unforgeable costliness of PoW. The Merge consolidated Ethereum's status as a different category of asset from Bitcoin — programmable platform versus sound money.

question: Ripple Labs launched XRP in 2012-2013 with a different supply mechanism than Bitcoin. All 100 billion XRP were created at launch and distributed to founders and early investors. Most cryptocurrencies modeled their economics on Ripple rather than Bitcoin. What is the technical name for this issuance pattern?
answer: Pre-mining — all tokens existed before public launch, with insider allocations preceding public availability or fair distribution
choices: Pre-mining — all tokens existed before public launch, with insider allocations preceding public availability or fair distribution
Fair distribution — though pre-mined, Ripple claims its initial distribution was fair through partnerships with banks
Algorithmic issuance — XRP supply changes via algorithm rather than human decisions made by Ripple Labs
Open mining — XRP was actually mined by community participants like Bitcoin, with similar fair-launch properties
context: Ripple founders Chris Larsen and Jed McCaleb together held billions of XRP at launch. The SEC sued Ripple in December 2020, alleging XRP was an unregistered securities offering. A partial Ripple win in 2023 limited the ruling. The Ripple/XRP case is paradigmatic of pre-mined tokens that resemble securities rather than commodity money.

question: In November 2022, the third-largest cryptocurrency exchange suddenly collapsed when a Coindesk article revealed its balance sheet was largely composed of its own native token (FTT). Customers attempted mass withdrawals; the exchange could not fulfill them. The CEO had been a major Democratic Party donor. Who was the CEO?
answer: Sam Bankman-Fried — 'SBF,' an MIT physics graduate convicted in October 2023 on seven federal fraud counts; sentenced to 25 years March 2024
choices: Sam Bankman-Fried — 'SBF,' an MIT physics graduate convicted in October 2023 on seven federal fraud counts; sentenced to 25 years March 2024
Changpeng Zhao — 'CZ,' Binance CEO, who triggered the FTX collapse by announcing he would liquidate his FTT holdings
Brian Armstrong — Coinbase CEO, whose company benefited from FTX collapse but did not cause it directly
Sam Trabucco — Alameda Research co-CEO who left before the collapse and avoided personal legal consequences
context: FTX customers lost roughly $8 billion in customer deposits that Alameda Research (FTX's affiliated trading firm) had used for proprietary trading and personal expenses including a $40M Bahamas penthouse. SBF had been a darling of Effective Altruism and earned-political-influence circles. His conviction was the largest financial fraud case since Bernie Madoff. The trial concluded in November 2023.

question: In May 2022, an algorithmic stablecoin called UST and its sister token LUNA collapsed in roughly a week, wiping out $60 billion of nominal value. The system had promised that 1 UST would always equal $1 USD through an algorithmic mint/burn mechanism with LUNA. What was the design flaw?
answer: The arbitrage mechanism could not handle large redemptions during a confidence crisis; LUNA hyperinflation crashed both tokens simultaneously
choices: The arbitrage mechanism could not handle large redemptions during a confidence crisis; LUNA hyperinflation crashed both tokens simultaneously
The Federal Reserve raised rates aggressively, breaking the algorithmic peg through monetary policy externally imposed
A hacker exploited a smart-contract vulnerability, draining the reserve fund that backed the stablecoin's peg directly
The Korean government banned UST trading, removing the primary demand source that had kept the algorithmic peg stable
context: Terra/Luna's collapse was the largest cryptocurrency failure of all time by nominal value. Founder Do Kwon was arrested in Montenegro in March 2023 and faces extradition proceedings between US and South Korea. The failure took down Three Arrows Capital (Asia-based hedge fund), Celsius, Voyager, and started the cascade that ultimately reached FTX six months later in November.

question: Celsius Network was a crypto lending platform promising users up to 18% yield on deposited Bitcoin and Ethereum. The platform paused withdrawals on June 12, 2022 and filed for Chapter 11 bankruptcy on July 13. What had happened?
answer: Celsius had taken depositor funds and made risky bets that lost when crypto markets crashed in 2022 — fractional reserve banking without disclosure
choices: Celsius had taken depositor funds and made risky bets that lost when crypto markets crashed in 2022 — fractional reserve banking without disclosure
Celsius was hacked by external attackers who drained customer funds in a sophisticated exchange-level cybersecurity breach
Celsius was shut down by SEC enforcement before any actual financial difficulties materialized in its operations
Celsius founders absconded with customer funds without warning, taking their assets to non-extradition jurisdictions
context: Celsius CEO Alex Mashinsky was charged in 2023 with fraud. The company's collapse was emblematic of the 2022 crypto lender meltdown: BlockFi, Voyager, Genesis, and others followed. The basic pattern — promising yield on customer deposits while taking on undisclosed risk — repeated lessons from 19th-century wildcat banking. Self-custody emerged stronger from the rubble.

question: On August 8, 2022, the US Treasury's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) added an Ethereum smart contract to its Specially Designated Nationals list. The sanction made it illegal for US persons to interact with the code. The contract was a privacy tool used to obscure Ethereum transaction histories. What was the tool's name?
answer: Tornado Cash — a privacy mixer for Ethereum and other chains that had become widely used by ordinary users and criminals alike
choices: Tornado Cash — a privacy mixer for Ethereum and other chains that had become widely used by ordinary users and criminals alike
Wasabi Wallet — a Bitcoin privacy wallet that uses CoinJoin but was not subject to US Treasury sanctions
Samurai Wallet — another Bitcoin privacy wallet that had been targeted by separate enforcement actions but not sanctioned
Monero — the privacy-focused cryptocurrency that has been delisted from exchanges but not formally sanctioned by Treasury
context: The Tornado Cash sanction was unprecedented — the first time the US government sanctioned code rather than people. Coin Center sued; in 2024 a federal court ruled the sanction unlawful, finding that smart contracts are not 'property' OFAC can sanction. The case became a landmark on whether code is speech and whether decentralized software can be illegal.

question: Tether (USDT) is the largest stablecoin, claiming each USDT is backed by US dollar reserves. The company has faced repeated questions about whether reserves actually exist. In February 2021, Tether settled with the New York Attorney General for $18.5 million and agreed to publish quarterly attestations. What was the central concern?
answer: Tether could not produce a full audit of its reserves; quarterly attestations show breakdowns suggesting partial backing by short-term commercial paper
choices: Tether could not produce a full audit of its reserves; quarterly attestations show breakdowns suggesting partial backing by short-term commercial paper
Tether holdings were entirely concentrated in cash at a single bank, creating a single point of failure for the largest stablecoin
Tether had over-collateralized its issuance, with reserves substantially exceeding circulating USDT supply — a positive concern
Tether was actually backed by gold rather than dollars, contrary to its claimed reserve composition publicly described
context: USDT supply grew from $4 billion to over $80 billion between 2020 and 2024. Despite the criticisms, USDT held its peg through the 2022 crypto crash that took down algorithmic stablecoins. Critics including Hindenburg Research have alleged Tether's audit transparency falls short of equivalent disclosures from regulated banks. The risk remains.

question: After conviction on seven federal fraud counts in October 2023, Sam Bankman-Fried received his sentence in March 2024. Judge Lewis Kaplan presided. The sentence ended the most prominent crypto-fraud case in history. How long was the sentence?
answer: 25 years in federal prison — substantially less than prosecutors' 50-year request but well above defense counsel's 6-year request
choices: 25 years in federal prison — substantially less than prosecutors' 50-year request but well above defense counsel's 6-year request
100 years in federal prison — matching Bernie Madoff's sentence for similar magnitude of fraud committed
5 years in federal prison — reflecting the judge's view that SBF's cooperation merited substantial leniency
Time served — reflecting the unusual decision to credit pretrial detention and impose only probation moving forward
context: SBF was incarcerated at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn before sentencing. He maintained his innocence at sentencing — refusing to express remorse — which Judge Kaplan cited in declining maximum leniency. Caroline Ellison (Alameda CEO) received 2 years for cooperating. Gary Wang received 0 years for cooperating. SBF's parents were named in civil suits.

question: QuadrigaCX was Canada's largest cryptocurrency exchange. In December 2018, its CEO died unexpectedly while traveling in India. Customer funds totaling roughly C$215 million became inaccessible because the CEO had been the sole holder of the cold wallet keys. What was his name?
answer: Gerald Cotten — whose death (or possibly faked death) caused one of the most bizarre exchange failures in cryptocurrency history
choices: Gerald Cotten — whose death (or possibly faked death) caused one of the most bizarre exchange failures in cryptocurrency history
Mark Karpeles — though Karpeles was the Mt. Gox CEO, not Quadriga; he survived his exchange's failure
Alex Mashinsky — Celsius CEO, not Quadriga; arrested 2023 for fraud unrelated to the Quadriga case
Dave Carlson — though Carlson founded MegaBigPower mining company, he was not affiliated with Quadriga
context: Cotten's widow could not access the cold storage. Later investigation by Ernst & Young found that the wallets had been empty before his death — Quadriga had operated as a Ponzi scheme. Whether Cotten is actually dead remains contested; conspiracy theories persist. The case became a teaching example of why centralized exchanges with single-point-of-failure operational structures are dangerous.

question: Throughout 2017, Initial Coin Offerings (ICOs) raised an estimated $5.6 billion as projects sold tokens to fund development. The vast majority of these projects later failed or were revealed as fraudulent. A 2018 study attempted to quantify the failure rate. What did it find?
answer: Roughly 80% of 2017 ICOs were either outright scams or failed to deliver any working product within two years
choices: Roughly 80% of 2017 ICOs were either outright scams or failed to deliver any working product within two years
Roughly 50% of 2017 ICOs succeeded in delivering working products that retained value through the 2018 bear market
Roughly 20% of 2017 ICOs were scams; the majority were legitimate but failed because of market conditions
Roughly 95% of 2017 ICOs were registered securities offerings that complied with applicable regulations of the time
context: The 2017 ICO boom and subsequent collapse demonstrated that pre-mined token launches without fair distribution rarely produce sustainable assets. SEC enforcement actions followed. The episode is the strongest data point in the Bitcoin-maximalist case that 'crypto' is mostly a different category than Bitcoin: speculation in poorly governed software projects rather than monetary innovation.

question: On August 11, 2020, a public corporation announced it had purchased $250 million worth of Bitcoin as its primary treasury reserve asset, replacing US dollar holdings. The decision was made by the CEO, who later became Bitcoin's most prominent corporate advocate. What company made this purchase?
answer: MicroStrategy — software company led by Michael Saylor; by 2024 it held over 200,000 BTC valued at over $14 billion
choices: MicroStrategy — software company led by Michael Saylor; by 2024 it held over 200,000 BTC valued at over $14 billion
Tesla — though it did purchase $1.5 billion in BTC in February 2021, it was not the first major corporate adopter
Block (Square) — Jack Dorsey's company did purchase $50 million in BTC October 2020, but two months after MicroStrategy
MassMutual — the insurance company purchased $100 million in BTC in December 2020, several months after MicroStrategy
context: Saylor became Bitcoin's leading institutional advocate after MicroStrategy's purchase. His firm's repeated purchases through 2021-2024 demonstrated corporate treasury demand for Bitcoin. Saylor's framing — 'Bitcoin is digital property,' 'thermodynamically sound money' — became standard among institutional Bitcoin adopters who followed MicroStrategy's lead.

question: On January 10, 2024, the US SEC approved 11 spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs), allowing American retail and institutional investors to gain Bitcoin exposure through standard brokerage accounts. The approval followed a decade of rejected applications and a 2023 court ruling. What did the ETFs initially attract?
answer: Massive inflows — within months ETFs held over 800,000 BTC, with BlackRock's IBIT becoming the fastest-growing ETF in history
choices: Massive inflows — within months ETFs held over 800,000 BTC, with BlackRock's IBIT becoming the fastest-growing ETF in history
Modest interest — initial inflows were below industry expectations and Bitcoin price fell after launch on the news
Outflows initially — Grayscale GBTC saw massive outflows that exceeded new ETF inflows in the first month after launch
Suspended trading — regulatory complications forced multiple ETFs to halt trading within the first weeks of launch
context: The ETF approval came after a DC Circuit ruling in August 2023 found the SEC's denial of Grayscale's application 'arbitrary and capricious.' The structural change brought Bitcoin into the standard wealth-management infrastructure: financial advisors can allocate to BTC like to any other asset class. Critics worry the ETF concentrates ownership and undermines self-custody norms.

question: Nik Bhatia's 2021 book *Layered Money* examined the historical structure of money — gold as base layer, fractional-reserve banknotes as second layer, central bank money as another layer — and argued Bitcoin establishes a new monetary base layer. What is Bitcoin's place in Bhatia's layered framework?
answer: Bitcoin is the base monetary layer; Lightning Network is second layer; custodial Bitcoin services and Bitcoin-denominated debt are higher layers
choices: Bitcoin is the base monetary layer; Lightning Network is second layer; custodial Bitcoin services and Bitcoin-denominated debt are higher layers
Bitcoin is a second-layer instrument; gold remains the base monetary layer with Bitcoin operating as a transferable claim
Bitcoin operates at the same layer as gold; both function as parallel base monies for different communities and use cases
Bitcoin replaces all higher layers; Bhatia argued there should be no layered structure above Bitcoin's base settlement
context: Bhatia's framework usefully maps how Bitcoin's adoption likely scales: most transactions occur on higher layers (Lightning, exchanges, custody services), with periodic settlement to the base layer. The model mirrors how gold worked historically — daily transactions happened with paper claims, not gold itself. Bhatia is a former US Treasury economist who applied that training to Bitcoin.

question: In February 2018, Bitcoin engineer Vijay Boyapati published a long-form essay titled 'The Bullish Case for Bitcoin' on Medium. The essay applied Menger's theory of money's evolution through saleability stages. Boyapati argued Bitcoin was progressing through stages. What were the stages?
answer: Collectible → Store of value → Medium of exchange → Unit of account — Menger's framework applied to Bitcoin's monetization
choices: Collectible → Store of value → Medium of exchange → Unit of account — Menger's framework applied to Bitcoin's monetization
Speculation → Investment → Currency → Standard — a finance-industry framework for new asset class adoption sequences
Cypherpunk → Libertarian → Mainstream → Universal — a sociological framework for community adoption patterns
Test → Pilot → Adoption → Maturity — a product-management framework borrowed from technology adoption curves
context: Boyapati's essay became one of the most-shared Bitcoin essays of the late 2010s. The Mengerian framework offered a non-financial way to think about why Bitcoin's price rises in jumps as it crosses adoption thresholds. The essay expanded into a 2021 book. The framework underlies much Bitcoin investment thinking even when not explicitly cited.

question: Hemingway's *The Sun Also Rises* (1926) contains a famous exchange about how a character went bankrupt: 'Two ways. Gradually, then suddenly.' Bitcoin advocate Parker Lewis (Unchained Capital) borrowed this framing for a famous series of essays. What is the framing applied to?
answer: How Bitcoin adoption proceeds and how fiat currencies collapse — both following the 'gradually, then suddenly' pattern
choices: How Bitcoin adoption proceeds and how fiat currencies collapse — both following the 'gradually, then suddenly' pattern
How regulatory crackdowns on Bitcoin will eventually fail — building gradually before sudden collapse of restrictions
How institutional Bitcoin adoption will unfold — gradually growing custody until sudden flooding of capital occurs
How Bitcoin's price discovery works — gradually finding value before sudden price jumps to new equilibria
context: Lewis's essays argued fiat collapse and Bitcoin adoption are mirror processes. Confidence in fiat erodes gradually until a sudden crisis; Bitcoin gains acceptance gradually until a sudden tipping point. The framing has become part of Bitcoin's cultural vocabulary. Lewis's essays are collected at Unchained Capital's blog and remain influential.

question: Bitcoin's launch had several properties that distinguished it from every cryptocurrency that followed. The Genesis block was an unspendable coinbase. Satoshi mined alone for a few days before others joined. No tokens were sold to anyone in advance. What term has the Bitcoin community used for this combination?
answer: Immaculate conception — the fair-launch, no-pre-mine, anonymous-founder origin that has never been replicated
choices: Immaculate conception — the fair-launch, no-pre-mine, anonymous-founder origin that has never been replicated
Decentralized birth — though the term is sometimes used, immaculate conception is the more common community shorthand
